It  now  occurred  to  me  that  if  the  main  advance  from  Suffolk  was 
successful  the  force  opposed  to  me  would  be  intercepted  between  Gen- 
eral Getty,  the  West  Branch,  and  myself,  and  I accordingly  resolved 
to  attract  their  attention  by  continual  skirmishing.  Captain  Cushing 
kindly  supplied  me  with  a boat  howitzer  and  a detachment  of  sailors. 
Colonel  Pease,  One  hundred  and  seventeenth  New  York,  also  sent  me, 
at  my  request,  100  men,  and  I once  more  advanced,  driving  the  enemy 
to  the  skirt  of  the  woods.  Skirmishing  continued  for  a couple  of  hours, 
when  the  enemy  brought  artillery  and  opened  fire  upon  me.  My  how- 
itzer having  expended  its  ammunition  I again  retired  with  slight  loss. 

During  the  engagement  the  officers  of  the  regiment  behaved  with 
great  coolness  and  bravery,  and  there  were  individual  instances  of  gal- 
iantry  among  the  men,  but  I regret  to  state  that  the  mass  of  the  meu 
exhibited  an  aversion  to  exposing  themselves,  a willingness  to  retreat, 
and  a contempt  for  good  order  that  I scarcely  expected  in  a regiment  of 
two  years’  experience  and  which  has  five  battles  inscribed  ui)on  its  flag. 

At  about  3 p.  m.  I received  a dispatch  from  Major  Crosby  announc- 
ing his  success.  I therefore  meditated  a joint  movement  of  the  two 
regiments  upon  the  enemy  near  Le  Compte’s  house,  which  I was  as- 
sured would  result  successfully  though  involving  considerable  loss; 
but  learning  that  the  Twenty-first  Connecticut  was  utterly  exhausted 
and  without  food  for  man  or  horse  I concluded  to  await  orders  from  the 
general  commanding.  After  dark,  by  order  of  General  Getty,  I with- 
drew the  troops  from  Hill’s  Point,  bringing  over  also  some  valuable 
pieces  of  timber,  which  I found  useful  the  following  day. 

On  the  4th  the  enemy  retired  altogether  from  our  front,  and  I with- 
drew Major  Crosby’s  force.  The  horses  and  artillery  were  embarked 
by  the  aid  of  an  improvised  floating  wharf  which  I constructed  out  of 
row-boats  and  loose  timber. 

Ever  since  the  commencement  of  the  siege  I have  been  generally  well 
seconded  by  the  officers  and  soldiers  under  my  command.  All  have 
nobly  done  their  duty,  but  some  have  done  more.  Among  these  I take 
ifleasure  in  mentioning  Maj.  H.  B.  Crosby,  of  the  Twenty-first  Connec- 
licut,  who  has  always  shown  himself  a zealous,  industrious,  brave,  and 
trustworthy  officer."  I would  also  specially  commend  Colonel  Derrorn, 
Twenty-fifth  New  Jersey,  to  whose  ability  as  an  engineer  the  service  is 
much  indebted ; Colonel  Donohoe,  of  the  Tenth  New  Hampshire,  to 
whom  I am  indebted  for  valuable  co-operation  in  su])erintemling  the 
river  defenses;  Major  Storer,  of  the  Thirteenth  New  Hampshire;  ( ap- 
tains  Brown  and  Keed,  of  the  Fourth  IMiode  Island,  and  Lieutenant 
Bruce,  of  my  staff,  for  their  faithful  and  soldierly  deportment  in  the 
various  trying  scenes  in  which  they  separately  i)artici})ated.  I am  in- 
debted for  repeated  and  valuable  favors  to  Lieutenants  Cushing  and 
Lamsou,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  flotilla.  I also  take  pride  in  calling

Report  of  Maj.  Hiram  B.  Crosby^  Twenty-first  Connecticut  Infantry. 

Hdqrs.  Twenty-first  Eegt.  Connecticut  Vols., 

SuffollCj  Va.j  May  5,  1863. 

Lieutenant  : I have  the  honor  to  report  that  in  compliance  with 
orders  from  the  general  commanding  1 crossed  the  Nansemond  on  Sun- 
day, at  4 o’clock  in  the  morning.  May  3,  having  under  my  command  the 
Twenty-first  Regiment  Connecticut  Yolunteers,  a section  of  the  Fourth 
Wisconsin  Battery  under  Lieut.  Martin  McDevitt,  and  a sergeant  with 
10  men  of  the  First  New  York  Mounted  Rifles.  My  orders  were  to 
march  to  Chuckatuck  and  from  thence  to  Reed’s  Ferry,  opening  com- 
munication with  the  Fourth  Rhode  Island  on  my  left. 

The  troops  were  under  way  for  Chuckatuck  at  4.30  o’clock  Sunday 
morning,  the  distance  being  2J  miles.  My  skirmishers  came  upon  the 
line  of  rebel  pickets  about  half  a mile  from  the  Nansemond,  their  fires 
still  burning.  The  rebel  pickets  fell  back  to  Chuckatuck  as  we  ad- 
vanced. When  within  half  a mile  of  the  village  we  saw  a company  of 
rebel  cavalry  drawn  up  in  the  main  street  leading  into  the  village.  I 
ordered  Lieutenant  McDevitt  to  open  fire  upon  them  with  artillery,  and 
the  rebels,  after  a few  rounds,  retired  to  the  farther  side  of  the  village, 
at  the  junction  ot  the  Reed’s  Ferry  and  Isle  of  Weight  roads.  I advanced 
the  skirmishers  to  the  village  and  moved  up  the  column.  Appearances 
indicated  that  the  enemy  would  make  a stand  at  that  point,  but  they 
again  retired,  a portion  of  their  force  taking  the  Isle  of  Wight  road, 
but  the  greater  number  retiring  by  the  Reed’s  Ferry  road. 

As  soon  as  my  command  were  in  the  village  I sent  Sergeant  Trow- 
bridge, of  the  Mounted  Rifles,  and  his  detachment  of  cavalry  to  recon- 
noiter  the  road  leading  to  the  Isle  of  Wight,  and  also  ordered  Captain 
Spittle,  acting  major  of  the  Twenty-first,  with  Companies  A and  K,  to 
skirmish  along  the  Reed’s  Ferry  road.  From  the  accounts  given  by 
contrabands  at  this  point  the  enemy’s  cavalry  were  estimated  at  about 
300  strong,  and  that  they  had  a camp  at  Isle  of  Wight  and  also  on  the 
Reed’s  Ferry  road.  I ordered  Lieutenant  McDevitt  to  put  the  artillery 
in  i)osition  to  command  both  roads  until  they  could  be  reconuoitered. 
On  discovering  that  the  enemy  intended  to  make  no  resistance  at  this 
point  the  column  was  moved  ahead  on  the  Reed’s  Ferry  road.  Captain 
Spittle  came  upon  the  camp  on  this  road  about  haff  a mile  beyond 
Chuckatuck.  The  enemy  had  but  just  left;  their  camp-fires  still  burn- 
ing. About  a mile  beyond  Chuckatuck  the  roads  branch  ofi*,  one  leading 
to  Reed’s  Ferry  the  other  to  Everett’s  Bridge.  The  foot-prints  indicated 
that  the  enemy’s  cavalry  had  retired  by  the  latter  road,  but  as  the  two 
roads  ran  near  together  for  quite  a distance  I halted  the  column  at  this 
point,  put  the  guns  in  position  commanding  both  roads,  and  ordered 
Captain  Spittle  to  reconnoiter  them.  The  enemy  were  then  reported 
nowhere  in  sight. 

The  column  was  at  once  ^et  in  motion  along  the  Reed’s  Ferry  road 
with  the  exception  that  Lieutenant  McDevitt,  with  one  piece  of  artillery 
and  a sufficient  support,  was  left  behind  to  command  the  Everett’s 
Rndge  road  until  an  advance  was  secured.  The  column  had  moved 
out  ail  eighth  of  a mile  in  advance  when  I ordered  Sergeant  Trow- 
bridge to  make  a reconnaissance  on  the  Everett’s  Bridge  road  for  about

Report  of  Brig.  Gen.  George  H.  Gordon.,  U.  8.  Army,  commanding  Reserve 
Division,  of  operations  May  1-4. 

Headquarters  Gordon’s  Division, 

Folly  Island,  8.  C.,  October  21,  1863. 

General  : Constant  service  in  the  field  has  delayed  a report  of  my 
])articipation  in  the  memorable  siege  of  Sufiblk,  V'a.,  during  portions  of 
tlie  months  of  April  and  May  in  the  present  year.  Deporting  to  Major- 
General  Dix,  commanding  the  Department  of  Virginia,  on  April  2!),  I 
was  ordered  to  join  you  at  Suffolk,  Va.,  to  assume  command  of  a division 
of  troops  within  the  almost  closely-invested  town.  I reported  on  May  1 
and  was  assigned  to  the  command  of  the  Deserve  Division,  consisting  of 
two  brigades,  the  Second  and  Third,  of  what  was  formerly  Abercrombie’s 
division,  the  Second,  commanded  by  Col.  Burr  Porter,  of  the  Fortieth 
Massachusetts  Degiment,  consisting  of  his  own  regiment,  the  Twenty- 
second  Connecticut,  One  hundred  and  forty-first  Dew  York,  and  Elev- 
enth Dhode  Island  Degiments;  the  Third,  commanded  by  Col.  William 
Gurney,  of  the  One  hundred  and  twenty-seventh  Dew  York  Degiment, 
consisting  of  that  regiment  and  the  One  hundred  and  forty-second.  One 
biindred  and  forty-third,  and  One  hundred  and  forty-fourth  Dew  York 
Degimentsj  in  all,  eight  regiments,  numbering  over  5,000  officers  and 
men.  The  siege  had  continued  for  some  days  before  my  arrival.  I fouiul 
tlie  enemy  holding  a belt  of  woods  that  surrounded  the  town  in  front 
and  fiank  from  the  Dansemond  on  the  right  to  the  Dismal  Swamp  on 
the  left.  His  rifle-pits  covered  his  line  far  to  the  front,  while,  his  sharp- 
shooters annoyed  not  only  our  gunners  at  their  pieces  but  the  men  in 
their  encampments. 

All  had  been  done  that  skill  could  suggest  to  strengthen  your  posi- 
tion. An  outer  and  inner  line  of  forts  protected  the  front;  strong 
inclosed  works  defended  the  flanks,  the  whole  connected  by  a line  of  in- 
trenchments  for  infantry  protected  by  ditches  and  abatis.  The  woods 
cleared  from  your  front  gave  a full  sweep  to  the  artillery.  Every  pre- 
caution by  artificial  works,  by  the  advantages  of  strong  natural  sites, 
and  by  a judicious  disposition  of  the  troops  to  repel  an  assault,  seemed 
to  me  to  have  been  taken.  The  sudden  flight  of  the  enemy  from  the 
front  on  the  night  of  May  3,  thus  raising  the  siege,  placed  my  division 
at  the  disposal  of  the  commander  of  the  department,  by  whom  I was 
immediately  ordered  on  the  important  duty  of  occupying,  holding,  and 
fortifying  West  Point  as  a military  base  for  future  operations.  The 
removal  of  the  enemy  from  our  front  developed  the  whole  of  his  opera- 
Itions  and  gave  me  a good  opportunity  of  judging,  from  the  extent  and 
character  of  his  works,  the  force  which  threatened  your  position. 

It  w^as  well  known  that  Generals  Longstreet  and  Hill,  of  the  rebel 
service,  had  united  their  forces  in  front  of  Suffolk.  Without  taking 
into  consideration  the  reports  of  deserters  and  facts  revealed  by  recon- 
|tiaissances,  special  as  well  as  in  force,  but  simply  judging  from  the 
imount  of  labor  performed  in  completing  their  lines  of  investment,  the 
Jesieging  force  could  not  have  been  less  than  30,000.  Everywhere  in 
rout,  from  the  Dansemond  to  the  swamp,  they  had  thrown  up  heavy 
ntrenchments  for  infantry.  On  all  the  roads  batteries  for  artillery,  in 
cnibrasure,  well  revetted,  with  ditches  wide  and  deep,  and  abatis  skill- 
mlly  hiid  and  thickly  interwoven,  rendered  a sortie  almost  hopeless. 
Mot  only  one  line  of  such  defenses  covered  the  enemy’s  front  but  on 
Jome  roads  three,  four,  and  even  five  i)arallel  lines  of  formidable  works

opposite  side  of  the  river. 

i^out  10  a.  m.  the  four  gunboats  above  and  the  land  batteries  opened

halt  before  the  guns  were  lost.  In  that  time  he  might  have  been  near 
the  work,  so  far  as  distance  is  concerned,  but  I have  my  doubts  if  any 
regiments  could  have  passed  the  wide  plain  and  rendered  any  real  sup- 
port under  the  fire  that  was  or  could  have  been  brought  to  bear  on  their 
approach.  The  manner  of  attack  appears  to  have  been  to  have  sent  one 
gunboat  down  as  though  she  was  going  to  pass  the  work  to  engage  the 
attention  of  the  men  in  the  fort,  while  from  the  other  boats  a force  of 
about  oOO  men  was  landed.  It  ajipears  to  me  that  if  the  garrison  was 
mrprised,  they  were  negligent ; if  not  surprised,  they  did  not  offer  a 
sufficient  resistance.

counted  the  number  of  shots  per  minute.  In  no  instance  did  they  exceed 
thirteen  to  the  minute;  the  average,  I think,  was  about  eight. " Of  the 
thirteen  shots  that  could  have  been  fired  at  a command  charging  across 
the  field  after  night  it  is  not  likely  that  more  than  four  could  have  taken 
effect,  and  those  ought  not  to  be  expected  to  destroy  more  than  2 men 
per  shot.  So  1 think  it  reasonable  to  conclude  that  the  fort  and  battery 
could  have  been  recaptured  Vvith  the  loss  of  75  men.  Many  of  the  offi- 
cers were  of  limited  experience,  however,  and  I have  no  doubt  acted  as 
they  thought  best.  1 do  not  know  that  any  of  them  deserve  particular 
censure.  This  lesson,  it  is  hoped,  will  be  of  service  to  us  all.  The  com- 
mand at  the  fort  seems  to  have  been  completely  surx)rised,  and  is  prob- 
ably less  excusable  than  other  parties  in  the  affair.

I.  Col.  J.  K.  Connally,  commanding  Fifty-fifth  North  Carolina  Troops,

will  furnish  a party  to  assist  in  loading  the  wagons  with  forage  and 
lu'ovisions  from  Riddick’s  farm.  In  case  of  attack  Colonel  Connally 
will  hold  his  regiment  in  readiness  to  suiiport  the  artillery  and  will

Rqwrt  of  Maj.  L.  M.  Shumalcer,  C.  8.  Artilley^  Chief  of  Artillery^  of  the 
capture  of  Battery  Huger ^ April  19. 

Headquarters, 

Near  Elfs^  Fa.,  April  21,  1863. 

General  : In  obedience  to  your  order  I have  the  honor  to  report  that 
on  the  morning  of  the  19th  I directed  Major  Boggs  to  send  Capt.  [D.  L.] 
Smoot,  [Alexandria  Light  Artillery,  or  Company  E,  Eighteenth  Battal- 
ion Virginia  Artillery],  with  his  two  30-pounder  Parrott  guns,  into  the 
works  constructed  for  him  to  the  west  of  Hill’s  Point  Battery,  occupied 
by  Captain  Stribling.  Captain  Smoot  got  into  position  just  before  day- 
light, and  I directed  Major  Boggs  to  order  him  not  to  unmask  or  fire 
until  the  boats  above  Hill’s  Point  attempted  to  come  down  or  those  be- 
low attempted  to  pass  up.  I also  directed  him  to  send  Captain  Brad- 
ford, with  his  four  heavy  12-pounders,  to  relieve  Capt.  [S.  T.]  Martin, 
[Battery  B,  Twelfth  Virginia  Battalion],  then  occupying  Major  Henry’s 
position  with  four  12-pounder  howitzers',  and  to  instruct  him  not  to  fire 
at  anything  but  a gunboat,  and  only  then  when  they  came  within  short 
range,  stating  that  your  orders  to  me  were  to  sink  the  boats  if  possible. 
Captain  Stribling’s  battery  was  placed  in  the  work  at  Hill’s  Point  after 
1 had  explained  the  position  and  character  of  the  work  to  both  General 
Longstreet  and  yourself. 

On  Thursday  night,  the  16th,  I had  thoroughly  inspected  the  work, 
and,  finding  the  platforms  burned  away,  took  the  heavy  siding  from  a 
corn-crib  on  the  Eiddick  farm  to  make  floors  for  the  carriages.  These 
floors  did  not  raise  the  guns  sufficiently  to  fire  over  the  parapet,  con- 
structed originally  for  guns  of  heavy  caliber,  mounted  on  barbette  car- 
riages. I ordered  Captain  Stribling  to  cut  embrasures  for  all  his  pieces, 
which  was  done  as  far  as  could  be  that  night  and  finished  the  succeeding 
night,  so  that  on  the  morning  of  the  19th  I had  three  batteries  in  posi- 
tion on  the  Nansemond  Eiver,  to  wit : Bradford’s  at  Norfleet’s  Landing, 
Major  Henry’s  position ; Captain  Stribling’s,  consisting  of  two  24-pounder 
howitzers  and  three  12-pounder  Napoleons,  at  Hill’s  Point,  in  a very 
strong  earthwork;  and  Captain  Smoot,  with  two  30-pounder  Parrott 
rifles,  to  the  west  of  and  about  two-thirds  of  a mile  from  Hill’s  Point, 
where  the  river  widens  and  a semicircular  bluff  bounds  a large  marsh. 

On  the  morning  of  the  17th  there  were  three  gunboats  above  Hill’s 
Point  and  below  Norfleet’s  Landing,  and  five  below  Hill’s  Point  lying 
below  the  mouth  of  the  West  Branch  of  the  Nansemond  Eiver.  About 
10  o’clock  three  of  these  attempted  to  pass  up  by  the  battery  at  Hill’s 
Point,  and  one  of  them  succeeded  in  passing;  the  others  were  driven 
back,  one  of  them  severely  damaged,  as  she  was  towed  down  the  river 
afterward,  disabled,  and  thought  by  the  citizens  to  be  sinking. 

Thus,  on  the  morning  of  the  19tli  there  were  four  gunboats  above 
Hill’s  Point  and  three  below.  About  10  o’clock  Colonel  Cunningham 
came  down  from  headquarters  (as  I understood  from  himself  and  Lieu- 
tenant Etting)  to  relieve  me,  and  he  at  once  took  charge  and  went  around 
to  Smoot’s  position.  Shortly  afterward  the  30-pounder  guns  opened, 
and  tlien  commenced  a general  firing  from  all  the  gunboats  and  two  of 
the  enemy’s  land  batteries,  four  of  the  boats  and  two  batteries  firing  upon 
Hill’s  Point,  the  others  directing  their  fire  upon  Smoot’s  position  and 
Occasionally  shelling  the  woods  where  our  sharpshooters  were.  About 
i o’clock  there  was  a general  cessation  of  firing,  and  I sent  a messenger 


332 


NORTH  CAROLINA  AND  S.  B.  VIRGINIA. 


[Chap.  XXX  j 


to  Captain  Stribling  with  a note  inquiring  into  the  casualties,  a copy 
of  which  is  herewith  inclosed,  with  Captain  Stribling’s  indorsement 
thereon.*  About  1 o’clock  Major  Boggs  informed  me  that  the  gun- 
boats above  Hill’s  Point  had  moved  farther  up  the  river,  their  decks 
covered  with  troops,  and  Captain  Martin  also  reported  to  me  that  a large 
body  of  infantry  (he  thought  a regiment,  if  not  more)  had  passed  bis 
position  (Norfleet’s  Landing)  the  day  before,  moving  down  the  river. 
These  facts  I mentioned  to  General  Law  immediately  after  being  in- 
formed of  them,  he  having  come  to  Moore’s  house  where  I then  was. 

Shortly  after  receiving  Stribling’s  reply  to  my  note  I received  a note 
from  yon  giving  me  general  directions,  and  I determined  not  to  return 
to  camp.  About  sunset  I saw  the  boats  in  motion  above  Hill’s  Point, 
and  from  the  signal  whistles  I judged  that  one  or  more  of  them  intended 
to  try  to  pass  the  batteries.  I dispatched  a messenger  to  Captain  Smoot 
to  hold  himself  ready,  and  held  Coit’s  two  3-inch  rifled  guns  to  dash 
out  whenever  I could  make  them  available  in  sinking  any  boat  that  we 
might  disable.  In  a short  time  I heard  a volley  of  musketry,  then  a 
few  scattering  shots,  and  then  loud  and  continued  cheering.  In  a few 
moments  a messenger  informed  me  that  the  enemy  had  landed  a large 
body  of  infantry  from  three  boats  above  Hill’s  Point,  and  had  charged 
and  taken  the  position.  I immediately  sent  Major  Boggs  to  inform 
Colonel  Connallj^,  who  at  once  moved  his  regiment  down.  I then  sent 
a courier  to  General  Law,  one  to  General  Hood,  and  one  to  yourself. 
The  courier  to  General  Law  returned,  bringing  me  word  from  him  that 
he  could  not  send  us  assistance,  and  I at  once  directed  Major  Boggs  to 
order  Captain  Bradford  out  from  his  position  and  sent  Captain  Smoot 
an  order  to  get  his  guns  and  ammunition  out  into  the  road  as  soon  as 
possible.  I then  ordered  Coit’s  two  light  guns  forward  and  went  to- 
ward the  fort  or  work  as  far  as  the  farm-houses  to  ascertain  the  position 
of  affairs.  I soon  became  satisfied  that  any  attempt  to  retake  the  guns 
with  the  force  we  had  must  fail,  and  that  neither  infantry  nor  artillery 
could  cross  the  plateau  under  the  cross-fire  of  seven  gunboats  and  two 
land  batteries,  with  an  unknown  body  of  infantry  filling  the  work  and 
lining  the  river  bank.  I therefore  returned  to  the  Eeed’s  Perry  road 
to  await  your  coming  and  to  direct  the  movements  of  the  remaining 
batteries.  Your  note  directing  me  to  have  Connally  post  his  regiment 
to  support  Stribling’s  battery  and  to  prevent  the  landing  of  troops  was 
not  received  until  8 o’clock,  an  hour  or  more  after  the  position  had  been 

I herewith  inclose  Major  Boggs’  and  Lieutenant  Carroll’s  t reiiorts,  and 
cojiies  of  the  various  notes,  directions,  &c.,  referred  to  above. 

In  conclusion,  general,  I have  the  honor  to  ask  tor  a court  of  iiiquir} 
as  well  to  verify  the  facts  stated  in  the  foregoing  report  as  to  have  a 
record  answer  to  any  charge  of  neglect  of  duty,  either  exxiressed  or  im 


plied. 

Very  respectfully. 


L.  M.  SHUMAKER, 
Major  and  Chief  of  Artillery.

Report  of  Capt.  Robert  M.  Stribling,  Fauquier  Artillery,  of  the  capture 
of  Battery  Huger,  April  19. 

Petersburg,  Ya.,  AFay  G,  1863. 

General  : In  reply  to  your  request  of  this  morning  I have  the  honor 
of  making  the  following  report  of  the  capture  of  my  battery  on  tlie  Nan- 
semond  Eiver  on  the  evening  of  April  19  : . . . 

About  11  p.  m.,  Anril  IG,  my  battery  was  placed  in  position  m tlie 
old  fort  on  Hill’s  Point  by  Major  Shumaker,  chief  of  artillery,  with 
orders  from  him  to  fire  upon  any  boats  running  up  or  down  the  river 
that  might  attempt  to  pass  the  fort,  and  to  fire  under  no  other  circum- 
stances except  when  the  fire  would  bo  undoubtedly  with  effect,  but  to 
keep  the  men  under  cover  as  well  as  possible.  Lieutenant-Colonel 
Coleman,  of  General  Law’s  brigade,  was  in  the  fort  with  some  infantry 
wlien  I went  into  position.  The  next  morning  the  enemy  opened  upon 
the  fort  from  gunboats  below  and  above,  and  also  from  a land  bat- 
tery upon  the  opposite  shore.  About  11  a.  m.  three  boats  attempted 
to  run  by  the  fort — one  ran  aground  about  600  yards  below,  and  only 
one  succeeded  then  in  passing ; we  fired  upon  it  and  made  several  holes 
through  it.  Toward  sunset  the  boat  which  had  been  aground  got  oil 
and  passed  by ; we  made  seven  holes  through  her,  and  I understood 
permanently  disabled  her.  Saturday  was  a day  of  comparative  quiet, 
no  shots  of  any  consequence  being  fired  at  the  fort  and  we  not  firing 

at  all.  1^1 

Early  Sunday  morning  firing  commenced  from  the  gunboats  and 
about  1 p.  m.  became  quite  furious  and  continued  so  until  between  sun- 
down and  dark,  when,  upon  a signal,  all  firing  ceased,  and  immediate!, \ 
one  of  the  boats  above  ran  near  the  shore  and  rapidly  landed  two  oi 
more  regiments  about  400  yards  abpve  the  fort.  They  double-quicked 
by  the  flank  across  the'  neck  of  land,  thereby  cutting  oft  all  cominuni^ 
cation.  They  then  faced  to  the  front,  discharged  their  pieces,  and 
charged  upon  the  fort.  The  pieces  which  had  been  turned  toward  tbj 
land  and  the  infantry  supports  (two  companies,  numbering  about 
men,  and  commanded  by  Captain  Bozeman,  of  Forty-fourth  Alabama 
Begiment,  General  Law’s  brigade)  opened  upon  them  and  held  then 
in  check.  They  soon,  however,  flanked  the  fort  on  either  side  an( 
entered  it  through  a swamp  and  over  the  parapets  on  the  river  side  am 
in  rear  of  the  guns.  We  were  hastened  offi  with  the  greatest  rapidiu 
and  put  on  board  the  boat.  . i 

About  2 o’clock  on  the  night  of  the  16th  the  pickets  stationed  up  th( 
river  fell  back  to  the  fort,  reporting  that  the  enemy  had  landed  in  larg< 
force  above.  Notice  was  immediately  sent  through  one  of  my  sergeant! 
to  General  Law.  In  the  mean  time  Lieutenant-Colonel  Coleman  art 
vanced  his  skirmishers  ui)  the  river  and  found  no  enemy  at  the  point 


j»AF.  XXX.]  SIEGE  OF  SUFFOLK,  VA.  337 

iidicated.  They  bad  re-embarked,  as  I learned  after  my  capture.  My 
sergeant  returned  and  reported  that  a regiment  was  in  the  woods,  about 
hree-qnarters  of  a mile  distant,  having  been  sent  down  to  our  support. 
A’ hen  the  enemy  landed  on  the  evening  of  the  19th  there  was  no  picket 
)r  lookout  ui)  the  river;  no  gun  was  fired  or  no  notice  whatever  served 
)f  their  approach,  and  as  the  shore  was  heavily  wooded  we  could  see 
lothing  from  the  fort.  1 had  been  led  to  suppose  that  the  banks  of  the 
iver  were  picketed  and  that  I would  receive  notice  of  the  approach  of 
b land  force,  and  also  that  there  was  a regiment  in  supporting  distance, 
die  construction  of  the  fort  was  of  such  a nature  that  I could  not  use 
ay  guns  with  full  elfect  against  a land  force,  though  it  was  admirably 
idapted  to  resist  an  attack  from  the  gunboats  and  to  blockade  the  river 
.t  that  point. 

I neglected  to  state  that  while  the  gunboat  was  aground  during  the 
Horning  of  the  17th  no  gun  in  the  fort  could  be  brought  to  bear  upon 
t on  account  of  the  narrowness  of  the  embrasure  which  had  been  hastily 
lit  out  the  night  before.  That  night  they  were  widened  sufficiently  to 
;ive  command  of  the  point. 

I am,  general,  with  great  respect,  your  obedient  servant, 

E.  M.  STRIBLING, 
Captain  Fauquier  Artillery.

TRIL  12,  1863. — Reconnaissance  from  Gloucester  Point  to  the  vicinity  of 

Hickory  Forks,  Va. 

Report  of  Lieut.  Col.  Charles  C.  Tevis,  Fourth  Delaware  Infantry. 

Camp  Gilpin,  Gloucester  Point,  Va., 

April  12,  18G3. 

Colonel  : In  pursuance  of  your  orders  I marched  a detachment  of  150 
len  (infantry),  taken  from  the  Fourth  Delaware  Regiment,  to  the  points 
idicated  in  your  instructions  to  me.  I felt  all  the  woods  between  York 
hver  and  the  main  county  road  as  far  up  as  Timber  Neck  Creek,  and 
lien  took  what  is  called  the  Pine  Swamp  road  until  its  intersection  with 
he  Bell  Roy  road,  about  IJ  miles  above  Hickory  Fork. 

All  the  country  was  carefully  examined  by  my  line  of  skirmishers, 
nd  indications  of  the  recent  presence  of  the  enemy  were  found,  iiarticu- 
irly  at  a small  Methodist  cbapel  called  Providence  Chapel,  about  5 
dies  beyond  our  lines.  All  the  inhabitants  concurred  in  stating  that 
bout  200  cavalry  (Captains  Littleton’s,  Clopton’s,  and  Allen’s  compa- 
ies),  under  Colonel  Godwin  and  Major  Vaughan,  had  been  down  since 
Tiday  morning,  and  had  returned  about  0 j).  m.  to-day  to  King  and 
hieen’s  Court-House,  where  they  are  encamped.  I found  a consider- 
ble  quantity  of  grain  in  the  mill  belonging  to  Coleman  Roberts,  on  the 
>ell  Roy  road,  and  as  the  rebels  are  in  the  habit  of  picketing  there  to 
uit  their  horses,  and  as  the  owner  confessed  to  correspondence  with 
h(‘ir  leaders,  I burned  the  mill.  My  detachment  returned  by  the  main 
ounty  road,  only  halting  to  destroy  a grist  and  saw  mill  belonging  to 
Tosser  Tabb,  near  Hickory  Fork,  in  which  large  quantities  of  flour  have 
*een  lately  ground  for  the  use  of  the  Richmond  army.  I would  esi)e- 
ially  call  attention  to  Charles  Curtis,  at  Wilson’s  Creek,  who  receives 
lores  for  the  rebels  and  who  had  rented  the  last-mentioned  mill. 

I have  the  honor  to  forward,  too,  the  papers  taken  from  two  cavalry 
oldiers  belonging  to  the  Fifth  Virginia  Cavalry,  whom  I captured,  and 
viio  were  empowered  by  the  rebel  general,  Stuart,  to  collect  horses  for 
iiis  regiments.  The  men  and  officers  of  my  command  did  their  duty  well. 

would  speak  x)articularly  of  the  services  of  Lieut.  John  J.  Toner,  regi- 
inontal  quartermaster,  and  of  Dr.  Hopkins,  regimental  surgeon,  who 
vere  of  material  assistance  to  me  in  the  cai)ture  of  the  prisoners. 

Very  respectfully, 

CHARLES  CARROLL  TEVJS, 
IJeutenant-Colonel  Fourth  Delaivare  Volunteers. 

Col.  A.  11.  Grimsiiaw,

uarters  of  April  2G,  18G3,  on  the  morning  of  the  27th  instant  I embarked 
) 3' division  upon  the  cars,  and  at  3 p.  m.  all  the  command  were  at  Batch- 
lller’s  Creek.  The  First  Brigade,  Colonel  Amory  commanding,  was 
0ut  forward  on  the  railroad  to  Core  Creek.  In  accordance  with  my 
rders  he  took  possession  of  the  bridge  at  that  point  and  sent  a force 
n mediately  across  the  creek  to  the  switch  but  found  nothing.  His 
omraand  bivouacked  on  the  railroad  immediately  behind  the  creek, 
'hile  the  remainder  of  the  command,  consisting  of  the  brigade  of  Colonel

Lie  command  posted  on  two  different  roads,  some  2J  miles  apart,  with 
good  cross-road  connecting. 

Immediately  after  my  arrival  at  the  Dover-road  Crossing  I sent  a force 
cross  the  creek  and  beyond  to  feel  the  enemy ^s  pickets,  but  the  party 
)und  nothing. 

At  midnight  it  commenced  to  rain  very  heavily  and  continued  until 
oon  of  Tuesday,  the  28th  instant.  At  the  conclusion  of  the  storm  the 
'hole  country  seemed  flooded — the  roads  in  a horrible  condition ; still 
determined  to  make  a movement  on  Sandy  Eidge  so  that  the  enemy 
light  at  least  be  kept  on  the  alert,  even  if  we  effected  no  captures  or 
lught  no  fight.  I felt  confident,  however,  that  we  should  find  some  of 
lie  enemy’s  troops  at  the  crossing  of  the  Dover  road  with  the  railroad, 
nd  perhaps  some  few  in  the  intrenchments  at  the  easterly  portion  of 
iaiidy  Eidge.  I therefore  ordered  the  following  movements : 

Colonel  Amory,  with  two  regiments  (the  Seventeenth  Massachusetts 
7'olunteers  and  the  Forty-fifth  Massachusetts  Volunteer  Militia),  was 
rdered  to  march  up  the  railroad  as  rapidly  as  possible  to  the  point 
t'here  the  railroad  and  Dover  road  cross.  I will  here  say  that  Colonel 
^mory,  who  has  been  ill  for  some  time,  was  not  able  to  go  with  the 
•rigade,  inasmuch  as  it  was  impossible  to  march  horses  on  the  railroad, 
le  therefore  returned  to  the  bivouac,  leaving  Colonel  Codman,  of  the 
'Yrty-fifth  Massachusetts  Volunteer  Militia,  in  command.

nd  tlie  Twenty-seventh  Massachusetts  Volunteers,  Lieutenant-Colonel

itia,  and  two  companies  of  the  Third  New  York  Cavalr^^  was  ordered 
orwnrd  on  the  Dover  road,  the  understanding  being  that  the  two  col- 
iinns  should  join  hands  at  the  above-mentioned  crossing.  In  accord- 
uce  with  orders  from  the  commanding  general  the  artillery  was  not 
aken  beyond  Core  Creek.  All  the  other  troops  were  held  in  readiness 
0 move  in  any  direction.  Colonel  Jones  moved  cautiously,  and  finding 
lie  intrenchments  on  Sandy  Eidge  abandoned  he  pushed  on  with  his 
oluinn  be^mnd  the  ridge,  seeing  nothing  of  the  enemy  until  the  head 
I*  the  column  arrived  within  ioo  yards  of  the  crossing,  when  he  was

No.  5. 

Report  of  Col.  Charles^R.  Codman^  Forty-fifth  Massachusetts  Infantry. 

Hdqrs.  Forty-fifth  Massachusetts  Vol.  Militia, 

Camp  Massachusetts,  near  Neiv  Berne,  N.  .0.,  May  1,  1863. 

Lieutenant  : In  compliance  with  orders  from  brigade  headquarters 
[ have*  the  honor  to  submit  a report  of  the  i)art  taken  by  the  troops 
inder  my  command  on  the  expedition  up  the  railroad  on  A])ril  28: 

On  the  evening  of  April  27,  the  brigade  being  then  at  Core  Creek, 
ni  the  railroad,  I received  orders  from  Colonel  Amory,  commanding  the 
irigade,  to  send  two  companies  of  this  regiment,  under  a held  ofhc(‘r,  to 
iroceed  up  the  railroad  the  next  morning  early  and  endeavor  to  ascer- 
tain the  strength  of  the  enemy,  with  orders,  however,  not  to  drive  in  the 
memy’s  pickets  or  to  engage  in  any  action. 

Early  on  the  morning  of  the  28th  the  com])anies  of  Caj)rains  Minot 
and  Tappan  were  placed  under  the  orders  of  Major  Sturgis,  and  that, 
ohicer  was  directed  to  carry  out  the  above  instructions.  The  companies 
■eft  camp  before  7 o’clock  and  proceeded  upon  their  destination.  At 
ilie  same  time,  in  compliance  with  orders  from  Colonel  Amory,  Caiitain 
Bumstead’s  company  was  directed  to  proceed  to  the  cross-roads  leading 
:o  the  Dover  road,  with  instructions  to  explore  that  road  and  to  commu- 
nicate with  Brigadier-General  Palmer,  whose  column  was  on  the  Dover 
coad. 

At  about  12  o’clock  I received  orders  from  (h)lonel  Amory  to  proceed 
with  the  rest  of  the  regiment  and  the  Seventeenth  Massacliusetts  Vol- 
inteers  (Lieutenant-Colonel  Fellows  commanding)  up  the  railroad  to 
>vertake  Major  Sturgis,  and  to  push  on  to  the  cross-roads  nearest  to  the 
lunction  of  the  Dover  road  with  the  railroad,  with  discretionary  orders 
to  proceed  to  the  junction.  I was  instructed  to  intercept  any  parties 


350

of  the  enemy  tliat  might  be  driven  down  this  cross-road  by  General 
Palmer’s  column. 

The  troops  immediately  started  upon  the  expedition,  and  upon  reacli- 
ing  the  cross-roads  I found  Major  Sturgis  who  reported  the  enemy  in 
some  force  in  the  neighborhood  of  the  junction.  That  officer  had  carried 
out  his  instructions  with  the  most  scrupulous  fidelity,  having  carefully 
concealed  his  force  from  the  enemy,  so  as  to  give  them  no  warning  of 
our  approach,  and  thus  preventing  them  from  receiving  re-enforcements, 
the  presence  of  which  at  a later  period  of  the  day  might  have  been  em- 
barrassing. As  his  men  were  much  exhausted  I directed  him  to  leave- 
one  comi)any  at  the  point  at  which  I overtook  him  and  to  order  the 
others  to  follow  the  column  slowly.  The  column  then  proceeded,  driv- 
ing in  the  enemy’s  vedettes  and  pickets.  This  duty  was  performed  by 
Company  B,  Forty-fifth  Eegiment,  Captain  Churchill,  the  pickets  being 
uniformly  posted  behind  log  barricades  and  uniformly  driven  out  by 
fianking  parties  from  Company  B. 

Upon  arriving  at  the  cross-roads  and  learning  that  General  Palmer’s 
column,  under  Colonel  Jones,  Fifty-eighth  Pennsylvania  Volunteers, 
was  pushing  up  the  Dover  road,  I determined  to  proceed  to  the  junc- 
tion. Company  F,  Captain  Daland,  was  ordered  to  relieve  Company  B, 
in  the  advance,  and  the  column  then  pushed  forward,  one  company  of 
the  Seventeenth  Massachusetts  Volunteers  being  left  at  the  cross-roads. 
As  we  approached  the  junction  Lieutenant-Colonel  Peabody,  in  charge 
of  the  advance,  sent  me  word  that  there  was  an  earthwork  across  the 
railroad.  I immediately  ordered  a halt  and  determined  to  make  no  at- 
tack until  Colonel  Jones  arrived,  not  knowing  what  might  be  the  wisli 
of  the  brigadier-general  commanding.  The  breastwork  had  no  ditch 
in  front,  and  I inferred  that  the  enemy  had  no  artillery,  as  they  migiit 
have  used  it  with  effect  before  this  time  if  they  had  had  any  in  position. 
In  a few  moments  the  enemy  fired  a volley  from  the  breastwork  upon  the 
advance  of  Colonel  Jones,  which  was  immediately  returned,  and  T then 
made  dispositions  for  an  attack.  The  breastwork  was  thrown  ui)  across 
the  track  and  extended  some  distance  to  our  left.  It  also  ran  along  the 
track,  crossing  the  Dover  road.  I immediately  ordered  Captain  Daland 
to  open  fire  with  his  company,  stationed  on  the  railroad  and  deployed 
as  skirmishers  on  the  right  and  left,  which  was  done  very  vigorously. 
I then  deployed  the  companies  of  Captains  Wales  and  Homans  of  the 
Forty-fifth,  and  subsequently  two  companies  of  the  Seventeenth,  as  skir- 
mishers on  the  left  of  the  railroad,  with  orders  to  advance,  firing.  The 
firing  of  these  companies  was  rapid  and  energetic,  and  that  of  the 
enemy,  which  was  sharp  for  a time,  soon  slackened. 

A favorable  opportunity  was  then  presented  for  a charge,  and  as 
'night  Avas  approaching  it  was  necessary  to  decide  the  affair  at  once. 
Company  A,  Captain  Denny,  of  the  Forty-fifth,  having  the  colors  of  the 
regiment,  had  been  held  in  reserve,  and  was  iio^v  ordered  to  fix  bayonets 
and  prepare  to  advance.  It  came  up  gallantly  along  the  railroad  in 
column  of  platoons,  supported  by  a company  of  the  Seventeenth,  ami 
as  it  approached  the  work  the  first  platoon  fired  a volley,  and  then, 
stooping  down,  the  second  fired  over  the  heads  of  the  first.  The  com- 
pany then  rushed  forward  with  the  bayonet,  the  whole  line  of  skir- 
mishers charging  at  the  same  time,  and  the  colors  of  the  regiment  were 
})lanted  upon  the  work,  the  enemy  giving  waj'.  I then  communicated 
with  Colonel  Jones,  and  in  accordance  with  orders  the  w hole  command 
marched  back  to  camp. 

In  this  affair  the  trooi)s  under  my  commaiHrsustained  a loss  of  1 man

:nAr.  XXX.]  SKIRMISH  AT  WISE^S  CROSS-ROADS,  N.  C.  353 

Hdqrs.  Fifty-eighth  Kegt.  Pennsylvania  Yols., 
Cam])  at  Batchelderh  Creelc,  N.  (7.,  May  1,  isfe. 

Sir  : In  reference  to  the  reconnaissance  ordered  by  General  Palmer 
resterday  on  the  Neuse  road  in  front  of  Core  Creek  I have  the  honor  to 
’eport : 

I proceeded  with  Companies  — and  G,  Third  New  York  Cavalry,  com- 
nanded  by  Captain  Pond,  in  the  aggregate  about  90  men,  toward  the 
S’euse,  making  a long  detour  in  order  to  get  into  the  rear  of  and  sur- 
prise the  cavalry  picket  at  Biddle’s,  about  6 miles  beyond  Core  Creek. 
iChe  picket  was  not  there,  having  been  withdrawn  on  Tuesday  evening 
)n  the  news  of  the  fight  on  the  Dover  road.  Being  unsuccessful  in  this 
collateral  affair,  I moved  forward  on  the  Neuse  road  toward  Moseley’s 
3reek.  According  to  the  information  obtained  at  Biddle’s  there  was  a 
)rigade  of  infantry,  with  artillery,  at  Moseley’s  Creek,  but  as  I advanced 
he  number  reported  continually  decreased  until,  about  a mile  this  side, 

was  told  that  the  enemy  had  retired  entirely  after  the  fight  of  Tues- 
lay.  Advancing  cautiously,  with  part  of  the  cavalry  dismounted  and 
leployed  as  skirmishers,  I verified  the  report  and  found  the  position 
ibandoned.  The  position  at  Moseley’s  Creek  is  naturally  strong,  there 
)eing  two  branches  of  the  creek,  about  50  yards  apart,  and  the  works 
vhich  I found  there  are  two  lines  of  breastworks,  one  behind  each 
)ranch.  The  first  line,  about  400  feet  long,  is  in  part  a heavy  earth- 
york  with  an  embrasure,  covering  the  road,  but  principally  a lighter 
ivork,  good  only  against  musketry,  but  with  a deep  rifle-pit  in  the  rearj 
t has  also  flanking  and  enfilading  faces.  The  second  work  is  much 
leavier  j has  two  embrasures ; more  flanking  fire  5 broad  and  deeper 
vater  in  front,  and  is  altogether  a formidable  defense.  In  the  rear  of 
he  works  I found  three  separate  camps,  which  I burned  and  destroyed, 
^rom  the  information  I received  it  seems  that  the  enemy  (a  brigade  of 
nfantry  without  artillery)  retired  precipitately  on  Wednesday  evening, 
^s  iny  apangements  to  return  the  same  day  did  not  allow  me  to  follow 
he  fugitives,  I was  obliged  to  rest  satisfied  with  the  reports  of  the  people 
n the  neighborhood  that  there  were  no  regular  posts  of  the'  enemy 
hort  of  Kinston,  and  that  Kinston  itself  was  7 or  8 miles  distant. 
Yom  the  trepidation  everywhere  apparent  I have  no  doubt  of  my  hav- 
ng  been  able  to  advance  within  sight  of  that  place  without  oppoktion, 
.nd  I would  have  done  so  if  other  circumstances  had  allowed.  On  my 
oute  the  inhabitants  expressed  their  opinion  freely  that  the  Southern 
roops  had  abandoned  them,  and  generally  they  asked  me  for  written 
)rotection. 

Having  accomplished  fully  the  object  of  the  reconnaissance  I re- 
urned  and  reached  the  bivouac,  behind  Core  Creek,  about  9 p.  m. 

The  cavalry  are  entitled  to  great  praise  for  this  arduous  march  of  36 
idles  through  a country  supposed  to  be  filled  with  enemies  and  afford- 
ng  continual  opportunities  for  ambuscade,  and  with  the  prospect  of 
[Itimately  confronting  a brigade.  They  did  their  duty  unflinchingly, 
nd  the  admirable  arrangements  made  by  Captain  Pond  prevented  the 
cattered  guerrillas  whom  we  saw  occasionally  from  using  the  advan- 
ages  of  the  swamps  and  thickets  against  us. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  EICHTEB  JONES, 

Colonel  Fifty -eighth  Pennsylvania  Volunteers. 

Captain  Judson, 

Assistant  Adjutant- General.

MAY  15, 1863. — Expedition  from  West  Point  to  Eobinson’s  Plantation,  King 

and  Queen  County,  Va. 

Report  of  Bruj.  Gen.  George  11.  Gordon^  U.  >9.  Army. 

Headquarters  United  States  Forces, 

West  Point,  Va.,  May  16,  1863. 

General  : Last  night  I sent  out  a small  expedition  to  capture  if  pos- 
sible— if  not,  destroy — nany  hundred  bushels  of  grain  which  a negro 
iT.ported  to  be  in  a barn.  Kunning  up  the  left  bank  of  the  Y^ork  Eiver, 
about  2 miles  below  the  month  of  the  Mattapony,  Captain  Babcock,  of 
the  gunboat  IMorse,  carried  my  infantry  to  its  destination  and  co-oper- 
ated with  his  men  and  boats.  The  grain  was  found  stored  in  a large 
granary  ; it  was  in  bulk.  The  distance  inland  was  about  1 mile.  It  was 
found  impossible  to  carry  the  grain  away  j therefore  the  building,  with 
'its  contents,  was  destroyed.  Captain  Motley,  of  my  staff,  who  accom- 
panied the  ex])edition,  estimates  the  amount  of  grain  destroyed  at  over 
'JOO  bushels.  The  barn  was  very  large  and  a very  fine  one,  securely 
locked  and  barred.  The  negro,  who  proved  a faithful  guide,  says  the 
proprietor,  Mr.  Eobinson,  has  been  in  the  habit  of  shipping  grain  to 
Richmond  ; that  he  sent  a schooner  load  just  before  my  arrival. 

I am  satisfied  that  the  occupation  of  this  Point  by  our  forces  and  the 
•iver  by  the  gunboats  will  compel  rebels  to  resort  to  land  travel,  if  that 
36  possible,  to  transport  the  large  amounts  of  grain  now  on  the  river 
lank  awaiting  transportation  to  Eichmond. 

i The  company  of  infantry  I sent  out  was  Captain  Wheeler’s,  of  the  One 
lundred  and  forty-second  Eegiment  Eew  York  Volunteers,  Colonel 
Curtis. 

I am  indebted  to  Captain  Babcock,  of  the  Morse,  for  information  that 
ed  to  the  capture  of  this  grain. 

I am,  general,  very  truly,  your  obedient  servant, 

GEO.  n.  GOEDOll, 

Brigadier-General,  Comdg.  U.  S.  Forces,  West  Point,  Va. 

Maj.  Gen.  John  A.  Dix, 

Fort  Monroe,  Ya.

! Headquarters  Eiohteenth  Army  Corps, 

New  Berne,  N.  C.,  June  2,  1863. 

General  ; Eeferring  to  my  brief  report  of  May  22, 1 have  the  honor 
to  report  that,  Jearning  from  Col.  J.  Eichter  Jones,  commanding  outpost, 
that  he  deemed  it  possible  to  capture  the  enemy^s  outpost  regiments  at 
Gum  Swamp,  8 miles  from  Kinston,  I ordered  Colonel  Lee^s  brigade,  con- 
sisting of  the  Fifth,  Twenty-fifth,  Twenty-seventh,  and  Forty-sixth 
Massachusetts  Eegimeuts,  three  pieces  of  Eiggs’  battery,  and  a bat- 
talion of  cavalry,  to  report  to  him. 

Colonel  Jones  ordered  the  Fifth,  Twenty-fifth,  and  Forty-sixth,  with 
the  artillery  and  cavalry,  under  command  of  Colonel  Peirson,  Fiftli 
Massachusetts,  to  advance  up  the  railroad  and  Dover  roads  to  attack 
the  enemy’s  works  in  the  front,  while  the  Fifty-eighth  Pennsylvania 
Volunteers  and  the  Twenty-seventh  Massachusetts  Volunteers,  under 
the  immediate  command  of  Colonel  Jones,  took  a path  through  the 
swamp  to  reach  the  rear  of  the  enemy’s  position. 

The  main  column,  under  Colonel  Peirson,  met  the  enemy’s  pickets  at 
daylight  of  the  22d,  and,  driving  them  in,  commenced  an  ktack  on  the 
front.  Colonel  Jones,  with  his  command,  owing  to  the  character  of  the 
road  they  had  taken  (the  men  having  to  go  by  single  file),  did  not  arrive 
at  the  desired  place  until  9 a.  m.  On  arriving  in  rear  of  the  enemy’s 
position  Colonel  Jones  deployed  such  portions  of  his  command  as  could 
be  used  to  advantage,  opened  fire,  and  advanced.  The  enemy  fired  a 
few  desultory  volleys,  then  broke  and  fled  in  great  confusion,  taking  to 
the  swamps,  and  escaping  by  paths  known  only  to  themselves.  On 
hearing  the  firing  of  Colonel  Jones’  command  Colonel  Peirson  advanced 
his  command  and  entered  the  works  in  front.  After  securing  the  pris- 
oners (165)  and  spoils,  demolishing  the  enemy’s  works  and  resting  his 
iien.  Colonel  Jones  made  a demonstration  and  show  of  advance  on  Kin- 
don.  At  dusk  the  same  evening  his  pickets  were  driven  in  and  he 
oiind  himself  attacked  by  the  enemy  in  force  and  with  artillery.  He, 
n obedience  to  orders,  at  once  retired,  followed  by  the  enemy,  and 
‘cached  our  outpost  line  without  loss.  Colonel  Fee’s  brigade  was  put 
)n  cars  in  waiting  and  returned  to  their  camps. 

The  enemy,  mortified  at  the  success  of  Colonel  Jones,  and  being 
strongly  re-enforced  from  Goldsborough,  attacked  pur  outpost  line  on 
he  p.  m*  of  the  23d.  I sent  out  a supporting  force  to  Colonel  Jones  and 
,he  enemy  were  repulsed  at  every  point,  but  with  great  loss  to  us  and 
ihe  service  in  the  death  of  Colonel  Jones,  who  was  shot  through  the 
leart  as  he  was  leading  on  two  companies  of  his  regiment  to  dislodge  the 
hnemy  from  a position  he  had  taken  up.  By  the  death  of  Colonel  Jones 
[b  most  brave,  zealous,  and  able  ofiicer  has  been  lost  to  the  service  and 
0 this  department. 

I have  the  honor  to  inclose  a list  of  casualties  and  a list  of  prisoners 
imd  articles  captured. 

I have  tlie  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  G.  FOSTEE, 

^ Major-General,  Gommandinq.

Sir  : I have  the  honor  to  report  that  my  attempt  to  cut  off  the  en- 
emy’s troops  at  Gum  Swamp  has  partially  succeeded. 

1 made  the  detour  successfully  with  the  Fifty-eighth  Pennsylvania 
and  Twenty-seventh  Massachusetts,  and  attacked  the  enemy  in  the  rear; 
but,  owiug*^  to  my  defective  knowledge  of  the  ground,  he  was  able  to  de- 
fend himself  some  time  under  cover  of  a swamp,  and  when  hnally  broken 

his  men  mostly  escaped.  ^ 

However,  we  captured  165  firisoners,  and  almost  took  General  Han- 
som himself,  who  was  accidentally  at  the  post.  T|ie  enemy’s  regiments 
engaged  were  the  Fifty-sixth  North  Carolina  and  Twenty-fifth  North 
Carolina,  and  on  our  part  the  Fifty-eighth  Pennsylvania  and  -Cwerdy- 
seventh  Massachusetts.  Our  loss  is  small — 2 wounded,  oi  the  hitty- 
eighth.  Of  the  enemy,  I have  6 wounded  reported  to  me. 

Our  [II  propose  recounoitering  Wise’s  Cross-E-oads  this  afternoon, 
and  to-morrow  returning  to  our  old  lines.  A particular  report  here- 
after. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  se-an*- 

Commanding  Outposts.

Massacliusetts  Volunteers  and  the  FiftJi  Massachusetts  Volunteer 
Militia,  was  transported  by  railroad  to  White’s  house,  about  1 mile  frbm 
Core  Creek,  where  they  were  afterward  joined  by  the  remainder  pf  the 
brigade  and  the  Fifty-eighth  Pennsylvania,  with  some  cavalry  and  ar- 
tillery. At  dusk  the  Twenty- seventh  was  sent,  with  the  Fifty-eighth 
Pennsylvania,  both  under  the  immediate  command  of  Colonel  Jones,  of 
the  Fifty-eighth  Pennsylvania,  by  an  unfrequented  path  to  the  rear  of 
the  enemy’s  outpost,  at  Gum  Swamp,  some  8 miles  from  Kinston,  K.  0. 
At  midnight  the  remainder  of  the  column  moved  up  the  Dover  road  (to 
which  they  had  previously  marched  from  the  railroad)  to  attack  the 
enemy  in  front. 

May  22.— At  daybreak  the  advance  of  the  United  States  troops  on  the 
Dover  road  encountered  the  enemy’s  pickets  and  drove  them  in.  The 
main  body  then  came  up  and  annoyed  the  enemy  with  desultory  skir- 
mish firing  until  about  10  a.  m.,  when  Colonel  Jones  (who  had  succeeded 
in  reaching  the  enemy’s  rear)  made  a dash  upon  their  position,  and,  in 
conjunction  with  the  troops  in  front,  succeeded  in  capturing  165  prison- 
( rs.  Our  column  now  slowly  retired,  closely  follow^ed  by  the'enemy  with 
cavalry  and  artillery.  He  shelled  our  rear  for  some  time,  but  without 
eliect,  and  about  9 p.  m.  our  troops  bivouacked  behind  Core  Creek. 

May  23.— At  daylight  our  pickets  were  attacked,  but  the  enemy’s  ad- 
vance was  driven  back  by  a few  well-directed  shell.  A move  was  then 
made  toward  the  railroad,  but  it  was  soon  discovered  that  the  enemy 
had  crossed  Core  Creek,  on  the  line  of  the  railroad,  and  were  reoccu- 
pying in  force.  Accordingly  Colonel  Jones,  wishing  to  avoid  another 
action,  made  his  way  through  a dense  swamp,  striking  the  railroad 
several  miles  below  White’s  house,  and,  taking  the  cars  awaiting  there, 
returned  to  Kew  Berne  about  5 p.  m.  The  prisoners  on  their  arrival 
were  paroled  by  the  following  staff  officers  of  this  division : Captain 
Judson,  assistant  adjutant-general;  Lieutenant  Horton,  acting  commis- 
sary of  musters;  Lieutenant  Allen,  acting  aide-de-camp.  The  pickets 
at  Batchelder’s  Creek  were  shortly  after  attacked,  and  the  Forty-fifth 
Regiment  Massachusetts  Volunteer  Militia,  of  the  First  Brigade,  was 
sent  out.  ’

Creek  at  daybreak  on  the  morning  of  the  21st. 

The  Twenty-seventh  and  Fifth  Eegiments  arrived  at  Batchelder’s 
Creek  by  rail  at  8 o’clock  on  the  21st,  and  soon  after  the  cavalry  re- 
ported near  the  creek,  on  the  Neuse  road.  Colonel  Jones  then  took 
command,  sent  forward  by  rail  the  Twenty-seventh  and  Fifth  Eegiments 
to  White’s  house,  in  the  vicinity  of  a mile  from  Core  Creek  ; the  cav- 
alry and  artillery  by  the  Dover  road,  and  subsequently,  on  the  return  of 
the  train,  transported  the  remaining  infantry  to  White’s  house.  From 
there,  about  5 o’clock,  the  Twenty-seventh  Eegiment  was  sent  up  the 
railroad  to  a depot  on  Core  Creek,  there  to  halt  and  await  further  or- 
ders. The  remaining  regiments  marched  to  Core  Creek,  on  the  Dover 
road,  where  we  joined  the  Fifty-eighth  Pennsylvania,  previously  sent 
forward  by  Colonel  Jones. 

The  object  of  the  expedition  was  to  surround  and  capture  a rebel 
regiment  at  Gum  Swamp,  the  outpost  of  the  enemy,  8 miles  from  Kins- 
ton. I have  now  the  honor  to  state  in  detail,  so  far  as  I am  able,  the 
means  taken  to  accomplish  it. 

It  was  decided  to  send  two  regiments  by  an  unfrequented  and  cir- 
cuitous path  to  the  enemy’s  rear,  while  the  main  column  moved  up  and 
occupied  the  enemy’s  attention  and  prevented  his  escape  in  front;  both 
columns  were  to  arrive  at  the  enemy’s  intreuchments  as  near  daybreak 
as  possible  on  the  morning  of  the  22d,  and  thus  .make  a joint  attack 
front  and  rear.  Accordingly,  at  dusk  on  the  21st,  Colonel  Jones 
moved  at  the  head  of  his  column,  consisting  of  the  Fifty-eighth  Penn- 
sylvania and  Twenty-seventh  Massachusetts,  which  he  subsequently 
joined  at  the  depot,  and  stealthily  proceeded,  under  cover  of  tbe  night 
and  by  direction  of  a faithful  guide,  to  gain  the  enemy’s  rear. 

Not  being  able  to  state  from  personal  knowledge  the  movements  and 
doings  of  this  column  I quote  so  much  of  the  reports  of  Lieutenant- 
Colonels  Lyman  and  Curtiss  as  appertains  to  this:

no  harm,  to  which  Lieutenant  Clark  replied  with  a few  shots.  Another 
column,  apparently  of  considerable  strength,  moved  down  the  railroad 
on  the  right.  At  10  o’clock  p.  m.  we  crossed  Core  Creek  and  encamped 
for  the  night,  being  undisturbed  by  the  enemy.  A little  after  daybreak 
on  the  morning  of  the  23d  the  enemy’s  skirmishers  engaged  ours  at  the 
creek,  but  a few  shell  from  our  artillery  silenced  their  skirmish  firing 
altogether. 

Colonel  Jones  had  previously  determined  to  move  his  command  i*ii 
two  columns  from  Core  Creek,  the  one  on  the  Dover  road  to  Batchel- 
der’s  Creek  and  the  other  by  the  cross-roads  to  the  railroad  and  thence 
by  cars  to  hTew  Berne.  In  the  opinion  of  Colonel  Jones  the  enemy  were 
not  posted  in  any  very  considerable  strength  at  this  creek,  and  hence 
he  did  not  deem  it  necessary  to  vary  from  his  previous  plans.  Accord- 
ingly Colonel  Jones,  with  the  artillery,  cavalry,  and  Fifty-eighth  Penn- 
sylvania, guarding  the  prisoners  and  baggage  train,  moved  leisurely 
down  the  Dover  road  to  Batchelder’s  Creek  without  the  least  molesta- 
tion from  the  enemy.  The  main  column  (Lee’s  brigade),  under  my  im- 
mediate command,  took  the  cross-road  leading  to  the  railroad,  distant 
some  3 miles.  Colonel  Pickett,  being  at  the  head,  sent  forward  one 
company  as  an  advance  guard,  with  orders  to  proceed  to  the  railroad 
and  report  the  condition  of  things  there.  In  a few  moments  messengers 
came  back  from  Lieutenant  Hunt,  Twenty- seventh  Eegiment,  who  had 
been  left  with  20  men  at  the  Core  Creek  railroad  bridge,  with  the  in- 
formation that  the  enemy  had  driven  in  his  pickets  and  that  three  reg 
iments  were  coming  down  the  railroad  track  with  the  very  evident 
intention  of  commanding  the  road,  or,  at  all  events,  of  attacking  our  left 
and  rear  before  we  could  reach  the  cars.  Judging  that  it  was  most 
wise  under  the  circumstances  to  avoid  a collision  with  the  enem5^  inas 
much  as  a victory  even  would  have  been  a sacrifice  of  men  and  barrel 
of  any  substantial  benefits,  and  the  more  certainly  to  prevent  theii 
getting  between  our  column  and  the  cars,  then  in  waiting  in  the  vicinity 
of  White’s  house,  on  consultation  with  Colonel  Pickett,  Twenty-fiffl 
Massachusetts,  and  my  staff  officers.  Captain  Bartlett  and  Lieutenani 
Myrick,  I determined  to  strike  in  a diagonal  direction  through  tin 
woods  to  the  left  and  thus  reach  the  cars  in  the  shortest  time.  Uiifor 
tunately  we  were  obliged  to  pass  through  a dense,  briery-tangled,  am

country.  Our  progress  was  thus  somewhat  delayed,  but  in  due  tinn 
the  whole  column  safely  crossed  and  took  the  cars  for  Xew  Berne.

we  could  reach  the  cars.  In  order  to  prevent  this  movement,  which 
would  have  proved  very  disastrous  to  us,  by  order  of  Colonel  Peirson 
I filed  the  head  of  the  column  to  the  left  into  the  woods,  intendino-  to 
run  parallel  with  the  railroad  for  some  distance  and  then  to  strilfe  it 
lar  enough  down  as  to  enable  us  to  bring  our  whole  force  into  position 
and  pve  them  battle.  The  head  of  the  column  struck  into  a swamp, 
which  at  first  seemed  but  little  likely  to  impede  our  march,  but  ere  long 
It  became  almost  impenetrable  and  seemed  interminable:  without  guides 
and  in  endeavoring  to  reach  the  railroad,  we  lost  our  way.  Finally  a 
liocket-compass  was  obtained,  and  in  a short  time  we  struck  the  rail- 
road some  distance  below  where  we  intended  to  and  about  2 miles  above 
inscarora  Depot.  Here  we  met  the  cars,  and  the  men  were  picked  ui) 
p they  came  out  of  the  woods,  and  without  any  further  occurrence  of 
importance  were  conveyed  to  New  Berne.  I reached  my  camp  between 
3 and  4 p.  m.  Saturday,  the  23d.=^ 

I have  the  honor  to  be,  respectfully,  yours, 

^ ^ JOSIAH  PICKETT, 

Colonel,  Comdg,  Twenty-fifth  Eegt  Massachusetts  Vols. 

Capt.  George  W.  Bartlett, 

A.  A,  A,  G.,  Second  Brig.,  First  Biv.,  Eighteenth  A.  G.

Itinerary  of  the  Second  Division,  Fourth  Army  Corps,  May  4.-0 une  1.* 

May  4. — At  Suffolk,  Ya.,  Brig.  Gen.  George  H.  Gordon  assumed  com 
mand  of  the  division  [formerly  Abercrombie’s]. 

May  5. — Broke  up  camp  and  moved  by  rail  to  Norfolk  the  sanx 
night. 

May  G. — Embarked  on  transports  for  Port  Monroe. 

May  7. — Sailed  for  West  Point,  and  on  arriving  there  immediatcl.' 
commenced  throwing  up  fortifications  for  defense,  consisting  of  a line  o 
intrenchment  extending  from  the  Mattapony  to  the  Pamunkey.  Tlx 
Fortieth  Massachusetts  was  thrown  out  to  the  front  on  picket  wliib 
the  rest  of  the  division  worked  constantly  and  well  on  the  intrencb 
ments.  Six  earthworks,  mounting  fifteen  guns,  and  having  embrasure:

Headquarters  Army  of  the  Potomac, 

August  22,  1862. 

Maj.  Gen.  E.  D.  Keyes, 

Commanding  Fourth  Army  Corps  : 

The  duty  intrusted  to  your  corps,  while  it  is  no  doubt  disagreeable, 
is  of  the  utmost  importance.  1 fully  realize  how  severe  a tax  it  is  upon 
men  who  have  fought  so  gallantly  and  worked  so  hard  as  your  corps  to 
require  them  now  to  go  upon  fatigue  duty.  1 feel  sure,  however,  tuat 
if  they  know  that  the  work  1 now  call  upon  them  to  perform  is  neces 
sary  they  will  perform  it  cheerfully.  You  will  please  detail  as  large

375 


working  i^arties  as  tlie  tools  available  will  permit  to  perform  the  work 
laid  out  by  the  engineer  officers. 

It  is  a matter  of  vital  importance  that  the  details  should  be  furnished 
and  the  work  done  in  the  shortest  possible  time. 

I have  taken  all  the  necessary  steps  to  have  your  command  relieved 
by  new  troops  at  the  earliest  practicable  moment. 

It  is  imperatively  necessary  that  the  work  required  should  be  pushed 
with  the  utmost  vigor.  You  will  be  held  responsible  that  this  work 
is  pushed  with  all  the  rapidity  possible  with  the  means  at  your  com- 
mand, and  hold  your  command  in  readiness  to  move  at  the  shortest 
notice. 

If  you  judge  it  necessary,  send  two  regiments  or  an  entire  brigade  of 
infantry  to  Williamsburg  to  cover  your  operations. 

Please  push  as  far  as  possible  the  instruction  of  the  old  garrison  in 
heavy  artillery  practice,  and  give  me  in  full  your  views  as  to  the  best 
method  of  holding  Williamsburg  and  the  force  necessary  for  that  pur- 
pose. 

Send  a couple  of  squadrons  of  cavalry  to  Goucester  to  patrol  and  ex- 
amine the  country  on  the  left  bank  of  the  York. 

If  you  think  it  advisable,  send  a much  larger  force  of  cavalry  there 
for  temporary  duty.  While  we  have  a large  cavalry  force  compara- 
tively idle  it  may  be  well  to  occupy  a large  i)ortion  of  it  in  clearing  out 
the  country  on  that  side  of  the  York  Eiver. 

If  you  think  it  best  to  occupy  a point  near  Williamsburg  by  infantry, 
hold  Port  Magruder  and  destroy  the  adjacent  works. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

GEO.  B.  McClellan, 

Major- General^  Commandinr/.

Of  what  is  necessary. 

The  plan  of  the  board  of  engineers,  a copy  of  which  is  in  possession 
of  Major-General  Peck,  a member  of  this  board,  and  which  has  been 
approved  by  General  McClellan  and  herewith  submitted,  contains,  in 
the  opinion  of  the  board,  all  the  suggestions  necessary  to  place  York- 
town  in  a state  of  defense.  But  in  the  opinion  of  the  board  the  force 
now  left  here  is  wholly  inadequate  to  accomplish  this  work  within  the 
time  when  the  enemy  is  likely  to  attack  this  work,  it  it  is  attacked  at 
all ; and  of  the  armament  suggested  in  that  plan  of  defense,  none  has 
been  sent. 

The  board  recommend  that  armament  be  at  once  sent,  and  urgently 
recommend  that  an  ordnance  officer  be  sent  to  mount  that  armament 
and  direct  the  readjustment  of  the  pieces  now  here. 

The  board  is  of  the  opinion  that  when  the  work  is  in  a state  of  defense 
contemplated  by  the  engineers,  the  garrison  necessary  to  hold  it  and  the 
approaches  should  consist  of  one  regiment  of  cavalry,  one  regiment  of 
artillery,  and  4,000  infantry,  if  of  old  troops ; if  of  new  levies,  from  6,000 

to  8,000  infantry.  ; . 

There  is  at  present  but  one  gunboat  at  this  place,  in  the  opinion  ot 
the  board  two  more  are  necessary — one  on  each  of  the  flanks  of  the  work, 
and  the  third  to  pass  up  and  down  the  river  and  break  up  the  trade  be- 
tween Bichmond  and  the  rich  counties  of  Gloucester  and  Matthews,  on 
the  eastern  side  of  the  river.  , . , . , 

In  this  connection  it  is  proper  to  state  that  the  height  and  abruptness 
of  the  bank  of  the  river  at  Yorktown  will  diminish  the  aid  that  might 
otherwise  be  expected  from  their  co-operation  in  the  defense  of  the 

There  is  with  the  garrison  at  Gloucester  Point  a field  battery  of  four 
pieces,  and  in  this  fort  two  field  batteries  of  four  guns  each,  but  it  is  not 
known  whether  the  two  batteries  at  this  place  are  a part  of  the  garrison.

Hon.  E.  M.  Stanton, 

Secretary  of  War : 

Sir  : Immediately  after  I was  placed  in  command  of  the  troops  a 
this  post  and  in  the  vicinity  I called  the  attention  of  the  GovernmcTi 
to  the  destitute  condition  of  the.20,000  people  of  Norfolk,  arising  Iron 
the  interruption  of  their  commercial  intercourse  while  the  rebels  wta* 
in  possession  of  the  city,  and  the  system  of  exclusion  which  was  adopw 
after  it  was  captured  by  us  and  which  I found  in  force.  I recoin 
mended  a total  change  of  regimen  on  grounds  of  humanity  Js  well  a 
policy.  I thought  it  due  to  ourselves  as  generous  conquerors  to  pn 
an  end  to  the  restrictions,  which  under  the  insurgents  were  a matter o 
constraint  but  which  we  continued  as  a matter  of  choice,  and  to  affon 
a free  ingress  to  the  necessaries  and  comforts  of  life  of  which  the  in 
habitants  were  in  extreme  need.  My  recommendations  were  adopte< 
only  to  a limited  extent.  Eight  vessels  were  permitted  by  the  Secretar; 
of  the  Treasury  to  proceed  there  with  cargoes.  Nearly  three  montu 
have  elapsed,  and  the  people  are  even  more  destitute  than  they  wer 
when  they  came  under  our  dominion.  The  suspension  of  business  to  ; 
great  extmit  necessarily  com])els  them  to  live  on  what  they  have  savci 
instead  of  their  daily  earnings,  which  are  for  the  mostiiart  cut  off,  am 
they  are  constantly  becoming  by  the  consumption  of  their  savings  les

able  to  pay  liigli  prices.  Besides,  the  nou-iutercourse  we  are  keeping 
up  bas,  by  exeliidiiig  supplies,  reudered  the  city  entirely  destitute  of 
many  of  the  essential  articles  of  subsistence } they  are  not  to  be  had 
at  any  price.  This  infliction,  and  it  is  a serious  one,  falls  on  the  loyal 
as  well  as  the  disloyal,  and  it  is  certainly  not  calculated  to  add  to  the 
number  of  our  friends  or  diminish  the  number  of  our  enemies.  I ad- 
vised a liberal  treatment  for  all,  punishing  where  any  open  hostility  to 
the  Government  was  -shown. 

• I do  not  understand  that  this  view  of  the  subject  was  disapproved  by 
the  Government;  but  from  a communication  recently  received  from  the 
Treasury  Department  a difficulty  is  supposed  to  exist  in  the  fact  that 
Norfolk  is  within  the  section  of  the  country  affected  by  the  blockade. 

It  is  respectfully  suggested  that  ^ince  the  capture  and  occupation  of 
Norfolk  by  the  military  forces  of  the  United  States  the  principles  of 
public  law  applicable  to  blockaded  2)orts  are  no  longer  in  force  there. 
It  is  not  a case  of  complete  conquest,  in  which  we  must  look  to  our 
Constitution  and  laws  for  the  authority  which  we  exercise,  but  it  is  a 
case  in  which  the  iflace  is  held  by  the  right  of  military  occupation,  in 
which  we  are  exercising  the  powers  given  by  the  laws  of  war,  and  in 
which  we  may  further  accord  to  the  inhabitants  privileges  not  strictly 
conferred  by  those  laws.  Bear- Admiral  Goldsborough,  who  lies  in  the 
harbor  in  the  Minnesota,  is  not  there  to  enforce  the  blockade,  but  to 
enforce  the  military  occupation. 

That  this  is  the  view  taken  by  the  Government  I cannot  doubt,  for 
certainly  the  right  to  grant  the  permits  given  by  the  Secretary  of  the 
Treasury  to  introduce  eight  cargoes  of  merchandise  for  general  traffic 
is  not  to  be  found  in  the  laws  of  blockade,  which  imply  a naval  force 
on  the  part  of  one  belligerent  and  a closed  port  on  the  part  of  another. 

I do  not  overlook  the  fact  that  Norfolk  is  a recovered  possession,  and 
that  we  hold  it  theoretically  to  be  now,  and  alwmys  to  have  been,  a part 
ot  the  United  States.  But  we  do  not  act  on  this  assumption,  for  if  we 
did  we  should  extend  our  civil  jurisdiction  over  it  and  set  in  motion 
the  customary  machinery  of  administration.  On  the  contrary,  we  gov- 
ern it  by  military  force  and  treat  it  for  all  practical  purposes  as  a 
conquest. 

Under  the  rule  of  military  occupation,  therefore,  we  may,  without  being 
questioned  by  neutrals,  admit  any  intercourse  with  our  own  citizens,  or 
any  portion  of  them,  essential  to  the  maintenance  of  our  authoritv  or 
to  the  preservation  and  comfortable  support  of  those  whom  we  have 
subjected  by  our  power.  It  is  on  this  principle,  I suppose,  that  the 
limited  right  to  trade  has  been  conferred  in  a ffiw  instances  on  partic- 
ular individuals. 

I beg  leave  further  to  suggest  whether  permits  of  this  description, 
gianted'to  afford  to  the  inhabitants  of  the  town  or  district  thus  sub- 
Ijected  and  held  by  force  the  means  of  subsistence,  should  not  be  given 
h.v  the  military  commander;  whether  they  can  with  propriety  come 
uom  the  Secretary  of  the  Treasury,  who  is  at  the  head  of  a civil  de- 
liaitment  and  whose  functions  in  respect  to  revenue  and  commerce  are 
wholly  inap])licable  to  conquerednerritories  governed  by  the  laws  of 
war.  It  seems  to  me  that  the  other  function  is  incident  to  the  right  of 
aiilitarv  occujiation  and  not  to  be  defended  on  anv  other  grounds. 

^ IShould  this  view  of  the  subject  be  concurred  in  I respectfully  request 
aat  1 may  be  authorized  to  grant  permits  to  vessels  to  go  to  Norfolk 
Aith  such  supplies  as  I deem  indispensable  to  save  the  inhabitants  from 
uitienug  by  hunger  and  cold,  and  that  Bear- Admiral  Goldsborough  be 
nrected  to  respect  the  permits  thus  granted  by  me. 


384  NORTH  CAROLINA  AND  S.  E.  VIRGINIA.  [Cii^p.  XXX. 

Id  regard  to  tbe  justice  of  this  measure  there  are  consideratious, . 
already  briefly  alluded  to,  which  address  themselves  to  us  with  great 
force.  The  people  of  Norfolk  are  cut  off  by  our  occupation  of  the  place 
from  their  former  sources  of  supplies.  We  have  surrounded  them  by  a 
chain  of  sentinels  and  have  interdicted  trade  with  the  insurgent  States 
from  which  they  could  always  draw  at  some  price  the  necessaries  they 
needed.  They  are  in  worse  condition  in  this  respect  now  than  they  v^ere 
under  the  Confederates ; and  it  is  submitted  whether,  on  every  prin- 
ciple of  justice  to  them  and  to  ourselves,  we  should  not  allow  theiii  th*e 
privilege  of  obtaining  what  they  need  from  the  loyal  portions  of  the 
Union.  It  seems  to  me  that  we  are  bound  to  do  this  or  to  let  them  pass 
through  our  lines  into  the  insurgent  States. 

The  inclosed  letter  from  Brigadier-General  Yiele,  the  military  gov- 
ernor of  Norfolk,  states  the  case  with  great  brevity  and  force,  and  I 
commend  it  to  the  attention  of  the  Government. 

I have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

JOHN  A.  DIX, 

Major-General.

General  : There  are  two  questions  connected  with  the  administray 
tion  of  affairs  in  this  city  and  Portsmouth  which  have  become  a source 
of  embarrassment  to  me.  The  one  is  the  procurement  ot  supplies  foi 
those  who  have  the  means,  and  the  other  the  supplying  of  those  wlio' 
have  not  the  means.  | 

We  are,  in  point  of  fact,  holding  here  in  custody  about  20,000  people: 
we  must  either  let  them  feed  themselves  or  we  must  feed  them.  [ 

The  opening  of  the  port  for  a restricted  trade  seems  to  me  to  be  a 
measure  of  necessity  to  save  the  Government  from  great  annoyance' 
Food  must  be  allowed  to  come  in  or  the  people  will  starve.  If  food  is 
allowed  to  come  in  the  products  of  the  surrounding  country  must  he, 
allowed  to  go  out  to  pay  for  it.  Again,  there  is  a large  class  of  persoiiH 
here  who  have  no  means  whatever  to  purchase  food  if  it  were  herc:'i 
these  are  mostly  willing  to  go  away  to  the  neighboring  counties  and  tc  . 
North  Carolina  if  allowed  to  do  so.  They  are  helpless  women  aiub 
children,  who  are  begging  daily  at  my  headquarters  for  food.  ThosC 
who  are  too  poor  to  go  or  who  have  no  friends  may  be  supported  hv 
levying  contributions  upon  those  who  have  the  means. 

1 have  always  considered  that  the  only’  point  to  be  attained  here  wiiL 
])erfect  tranquillity.  This  has  been  secured  so  far;  in  order  to  contimiM 
it  the  steps  I have  referred  to  appear  to  be  necessary.

Major-General  Halle CK : 

Major-General  Keyes  is  very  desirous  of  leaving  Yorktown  with  his 
reserve  artillery  to  resume  the  command  of  CoucKs  division,  and  is 
villing  to  take  and  train  another  division  from  the  new  forces  now 
coming  into  the  field.  I should  be  very  glad  to  retain  him,  but  cheer- 
fully consent  to  the  arrangement  if  it  meets  with  your  approval,  as  it 
will  obviate  the  necessity  of  sending  new  troops  here  and  enable  me  to 
retain  Major-General  Peck,  a very  good  officer,  and  his  division,  which

Headquarters  Seventh  Army  Corps, 

Fort  Monroe,  Va.,  September  7,  1862. 

Brig.  Gen.  O.  S.  Ferry, 

Commanding  at  Suffollc,  Va. : 

I wish  to  complete  a reconnaissance  in  the  vicinity  of  the  Dismal 
Swamp.  It  will  be  under  the  direction  of  Oapt.  William  Heine,  who  is 
engaged  in  constructing  military  maps  of  the  district  south  and  west  of 
Suffolk.  It  will  be  necessary  to  send  with  him  two  companies  of  infantry, 
a company  of  cavalry  or  mounted  riflemen,  and  a section  of  artillery, 
with  two  mountain  howitzers,  under  a discreet  and  efficient  field  officer. 
It  will  probably  be  necessary  to  pass  around  the  Dismal  Swamp,  return- 
ing on  the  east  side.  The  men  must  have  rations  for  eight  days,  and 
they  must  take  with  them  their  tents  and  the  smallest  practicable  amount 
of  camp  equipage.  During  the  first  two  or  three  days  it  will  be  well  to 
send  two  or  three  companies  of  cavalry  out  on  the  road  nearest  to  the 
Black  water,  in  the  direction  of  Somerton  and  Winton,  as  a cover  to  the 
movement.  A ijumber  of  wagons,  sufficient  to  carry  the  provisions, 
forage,  and  tents,  will  be  sent  with  them,  and  an  ambulance  for  the  use 
of  the  engineers.  At  this  season  the  men  should  be  covered  at  night, 
and  if  possible  their  tents  should  be  pitched  under  the  shelter  of  trees 
and  their  march  should  be  suspended  during  the  heat. 

The  movement  will  conform  to  the  requirements  of  Captain  Heine, 
who  is  charged  with  the  reconnaissance ; but  the  command  of  the  escort, 
and  all  that  relates  to  the  control  of  the  men,  will  be  under  the  direction 
of  the  senior  officer,  who  will  be  enjoined  to  enforce  the  strictest  disci- 
pline. The  inhabitants  of  the  country  will  be  protected  against  all  dis- 
turbance, and  the  least  violation  of  their  property  will  be  visited  with 
the  most  extreme  rigor  of  the  law.  Should  it  be  necessary  to  procure 
supplies  from  the  district  through  which  the  movement  is  made  the  com- 
manding officer  will  endeavor  to  obtain  them  by  agreement  with  the 
parties,  or,  if  compelled  to  take  them,  he  will  give  receipts  on  public 
account  and  render  a return  to  me  of  the  articles  taken,  with  the  names 
of  the  owners. 

Everything  will  be  in  readiness  on  Monday,  so  that  the  party  will 
move  early  on  Tuesday  morning,  and  I trust  to  you  to  make  such  ar- 
rangements as  to  insure  the  object  of  the  expedition,  and  at  the  same 
time  to  carry  out  my  wishes,  which  will  be  creditable  to  those  who  are 
engaged  in  it. 

If  you  have  not  mountain  howitzers  we  can  send  them  from  here. 

Answer  immediately. 

JOHN  A.  DIX, 

Major-General.

Capt.  Southard  Hoffman, 

Assistant  Adjutant- General : 

Dear  Hoffman  : Captain  Jocknick  made  a reconnaissance  yester- 
day to  Tranter’s  Creek.  Upon  reaching  the  bridge  he  discovered  that 
it  was  undergoing  repairs,  and  going  on  it  to  examine  more  close  y 
was  fired  on  by  a concealed  force.  Only  two  of  his  men  were  slightly 
wounded.  There  is  good  reason  to  believe  that  the  enemy  are  collected 
. in  considerable  numbers,  and  that  they  are  repairing  the  bridge  lor  a 
speedy  attack  on  this  place.  Their  force,  according  to  negro  and  se- 
cesh”  authority,  is  set  down  at  from  2,000  to  G,000.  I have  4o  of  the 
Marine  Artillery  in  the  fort  and  Captain  Wall’s  company  of  the  iliiid, 
New  York,  some  30  men.  The  block-house  at  the  east  end  of  the  town 
is  finished  but  there  is  no  gun  for  it.  The  one  on  the  Greenville  road  is 
going  up  rapidly.  Two  guns  are  immediately  needed  for  these  hoiises< 

Please  send  them  at  once.  i i . 

Private  Hahn,  of  Captain  Jocknick’s  company  of  cavalry,  o^^ored  to 
New  Belne,  was  detailed  by  General  Poster  to  act  as  editor  of  the  JNew 
Era.  Colonel  Mix’s  order  is  for  Captain  Jocknick  to  take  all  his  men 
detached  or  otherwise;  so  Hahn  will  go.  I told  him  he  would  have  t( 
make  application  to  you  or  the  general  if  he  is  to  return  here. 

Lieutenant  McLane,  of  the  First  North  Carolina,  went  to  New  Beru(| 
on  sick  leave.  His  brother  writes  that  he  is  just  recovering  and  tha^ 
the  surgeon  says  that  a short  visit  to  a Northern  climate  is  necessan 
for  his  recovery.  I mention  the  case  for  the  general’s  consideration. 

Yours,  very  truly,  eDWAED  E.  POTTEE,

Fort  Monroe,  Va.,  September  13,  1862. 
Hon.  E.  M.  Stanton,  ? ? ^ ? 

Seeretary  of  War : 


Sir:  The  contraband  negroes  who  have  been  permitted  to  collect  in 
great  numbers  at  this  fort  and  in  this  vicinity  have  always  been  and  are 
now  a very  great  source  of  embarrassment  to  the  troops  in  this  garrison 
and  in  the  camps  hereabouts  and  to  the  wLite  population  in  this  neigh- 
borhood. In  case  the  fort  should  be  invested  or  approached  by  the 
enemy^s  forces  I should  feel  obliged  to  ship  them  all  to  the  Xorth. 

This  disposition,  it  seems  to  me,  ought  to  be  made  of  them  without 
needless  delay,  and,  if  possible,  with  the  concurrence  of  the  authorities 
of  the  State  or  States  to  which  they  may  be  sent.  To  this  end  I respect- 
fully ask  permission  and  authority  from  the  War  Department  to  com-

by  the  enemy’s  forces  you  should  be  obliged  to  ship  them  all  North.

communicate  and  make  arrangements  with  the  Governors  of  Massachu- 
setts and  other  Northern  States  with  a view  to  a transfer  to  those

tendence of  Mr.  0.  B.  Wilder  at  Old  Point  Comfort  and  its  vicinity
