against  attack.  I have  ordered  a reconnaissance  in  force  to  be  made 
to-day  in  the  direction  of  the  Blackwater. 

Yorlitown. — The  armament  is  now  in  progress.  General  Peck  is  super- 
intending it.  I have  no  one  who  can  do  it  so  well.  Indeed,  I have  for 
duty  but  one  engineer  under  my  command;  only  one  ordnance  officer, 
who  has  charge  of  the  arsenal  here,  and  only  one  artillery  officer,  who 
has  been  until  recently  the  commanding  officer  of  this  post.  The  scien- 
tific corps  of  the  army  have  been  absorbed  by  other  commands.  I may 
be  obliged  to  send  General  Peck  to  Suffolk  if  an  advance  is  made  by  the 
enemy. 

The  intrenchments  constructed  by  the  Confederates  at  Yorktown  are 
very  strong,  but  were  intended  for  a large  force.  It  is  not  proposed  to 
bold  the  place  with  more  than  4,000  men,  and  therefore  some  out- works 
not  intended  to  be  occupied  are  in  progress  of  demolition.  The  arma- 
ment will  be  completed  as  rapidly  as  possible,  and  with  the  present 
force  and  the  guns  already  in  position  the  place  could  hold  out  against 
greatly  superior  numbers. 

Gloucester,— McClellan,  before  he  left  here,  ordered  Glouces- 
ter to  be  armed.  I do  not  propose  to  execute  the  order  until  we  have 
completed  the  armament  of  Yorktown  and  until  I have  20,000  effective 
men,  for  I do  not  think  a smaller  number  sufficient  to  protect  my  ex- 
tended lines. 

This  position  is  auxiliary  to  Yorktown  in  controlling  the  navigation  of 
the  York  Eiver.  It  is  commanded  by  Yorktown  Heights,  but  it  might, 
nevertheless,  in  the  hands  of  an  enemy,  be  a source  of  annoyance. 

Neicport  Yexcs.— This  post  was  abandoned  in  June  last  by  order  of 
General  McClellan.  Everything  was  removed  except  the  sick  and  a 
company  of  cavalry,  as  a guard.  Since  then  the  sick  have  been  increased 
and  I have  added  a very  small  regiment  of  infantry. 

The  Secretary  of  the  Yavy  requested  that  we  would  mount  two  or 
three  200-pounder  guns  to  aid  the  gunboats  in  defending  themselves 
against  the  new  Merrimac,  but  we  have  no  200-pounders,  and  unless  I 
have  a competent  force  there  the  enemy  might,  if  we  were  to  obtain 
them,  use  them  against  us.  There  are  some  earthworks,  a good  deal 
dilapidated,  for  defense  against  an  inland  attack,  but  they  require  about 
3,000  men  to  man  them.  All  the  guns  were  removed. 

Yewport  Yews  as  a station  defends  nothing.  The  channel  of  the 
James  Eiver  is  wide.  A vessel  drawing  from  17  to  18  feet  can  pass 
out  at  a distance  of  IJ  miles,  although  the  deeper  part  of  the  channel 
IS  near  the  land.  Its  occupation  as  a post  was  always  of  questionable 
utility. 

Williamshurg  I consider  of  no  importance,  except  as  an  advance  post 
or  watching  a movement  of  the  enemy  from  the  Chickahominy.  By 
holding  it  we  are  able  to  push  our  vedettes  farther  out.  It  is  too  dis- 
tant from  Yorktown  (13  miles),  but  I have  only  a small  cavalry  force 
there.  It  is  under  a brave  and  vigilant  officer,  who  I think  will  take 
wire  of  himself.  I need  for —

Fort  Monroe.,  Va.,  September  21,  1802. 

Hon.  Salmon  P.  Chase, 

Secretary  of  the  Treasury : * 

Sir:  Captain  Slicer,  of  the  revenue  service,  has  written  to  you  in 
re«-ard  to  some  shipments  by  the  schooner  Geranium  from  Baltimore  to 
tins  post,  under  a regular  clearance  from  the  custom-house.  I gave  a 
permit  to  the  shippers  to  bring  certain  enumerated  articles  for  the  peo- 
ple at  Back  Diver  and  the  vicinity.  But  a quantity  of  other  articles 
not  embraced  in  my  permit  were  allowed  to  be  shipped  by  the  collector; 
among  them  are  3,000  percussion  caps.  These  articles  were  intended 
for  a neighborhood  where  there  is  at  this  season  a good  deal  of  game, 
and  the  inhabitants  ought  not  to  be  deprived  of  the  privilege  of  shoot- 
ing. I propose  to  detain  them  to  be  sold  here  to  individuals,  for  their 
personal  use,  under  special  permits  and  in  such  small  quantities  as  to 
make  it  clear  that  thej^  are  not  intended  for  traffic.  Back  Diver  is  about 
7 miles  from  the  fort. 

There  are  also,  not  embraced  in  my  permit,  84  gross  of  inatches— 
12,096  boxes.  In  Baltimore  they  may  have  cost  875.  In  Dichmond 
they  would  bring  75  cents  a box— $9,072.  Such  a quantity  imported 
for  a small  neighborhood,  taken  in  connection  with  the  difference  of 
price,  shows  that  they  were  intended  for  sale  vrhere  the  enormous  profit 
is  to  be  obtained.  These  I propose  also  to  detain. 

As  the  custom-house  officers  liave  cleared  these  articles,  and  as  there 
is  no  irregularity,  there  seems  to  be  no  reason  for  holding  the  vessel  or 
the  residue  of  the  cargo.  She  has  been  detained  by  Caiitain  Sheer,  and 
the  only  question  is  whether  the  articles  referred  to  shall  be  stopped 
here.  This  question  I suppose  need  not  embarrass  me,  as  the  clearance

was  for  this  post,  and  there  is  no  reason  why  the  articles  not  included

I think  it  very  important  that  the  trade  with  NTorfolk  and  Portsmouth 
and  the  district  immediately  adjoining  my  command  should  be  regulated 
by  permits  given  by  me  as  the  commander  of  the  military  department 
Through  my  provost-marshals  and  other  subordinates  I can  ascertain 
the  wants  of  every  neighborhood,  and  indeed  of  every  family,  and  thus 
be  able  to  limit  the  supply  to  their  reasonable  wants.  Collectors  at  a 
distance  have  no  such  knowledge,  and  a privilege  intended  to  meet 
rea  necessities  may  be  perverted,  as  it  often  is,  to  purposes  of  traffic 
with  disloyal  districts  and  individuals.

Maj.  Gen.  John  J.  Peciv,  Commanding  at  Suffolk  : 

General  : I have  ordered  Captain  Davis’  battery  to  you  from  York- 
town.  I will  direct  General  Yiele,  in  ease  of  any  sudden  emergency, 
to  execute  any  order  yon  may  give  him.  His  force  is  small,  and  I do 
not  wish  it  disturbed  except  in  an  exigency  so  pressing  as  to  render 


consultation  with  me  dangerous. 

The  Morse  draws  so  much  water  that  she  cannot  safely  go  higher  up 
the  Nansemond.  Admiral  Lee  has  promised  me  another  gunboat  of 
less  draught,  and  I will  ask  him  to  put  her  under  your  orders  so  that 
she  can  take  the  place  of  the  West  End  in  case  of  need. 

1 trust  the  telegraph  line  will  be  completed  to-day  so  that  our  com- 
munications may  be  more  regular. 

I am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

’ JOHN  A.  DIX,

Maj.  Gen.  H.  W.  Halleck:  ’ 

General:  In  my  letter  of  the  27th  instant  I stated  that  permits  to 
trade  in  Norfolk  had  been  given  to  improper  persons.  Yesterday  Mr. 
Noyes,  the  person  I alluded  to  as  having  been  turned  out  of  the  quar- 
inaster’s  department  for  fraud  and  having  been  found  with  a large 
quantity  of  quinine  in  Norfolk  sent  to  him  surreptitiously,  arrived  here, 
^vith  a permit  from  General  Wadsworth  to  trade,  with  a very  heavy 
nvoice  of  merchandise— among  other  items  2,000  tons  of  coal.  I am 
irery  happy  to  know  that  such  a supply  of  necessaries  is  to  go  to  Nor* 
blk  for  the  relief  of  the  people,  but  I greatly  regret  that  it  is  in  such 
lands.  At  the  same  time  the  quartermaster  has  received  for  examina- 
;ion  from  Mr.  Tucker,  Assistant  Secretary  of  War,  a fraudulent  claim 
igainstthe  Government  from  this  same  man. 

There  also  arrived  here  yesterday  a man  named  Ward  with  supplies 
’or  the  Marine  Corps,  purchased  by  him  on  a permit  from  the  Secretary 
)f  the  Navy.  He  refused  to  take  the  oath  of  allegiance,  and  I stopped 
he  goods.  I sent  him  with  the  assistant  provost-marshal  to  General 
nele,  who  reports  as  follows  : 

“This  man  Ward  is  a rebel  scoundrel,  who  was  imposed  upon  the 
irovost-marshal  by  Captain  McCawley  (Marines),  who  is  certainly  very 
Quch  in  fault  in  the  matter.  The  mafrs  antecedents  are  bad.  He  has 
□ade  a fortune  in  contracts  for  the  insurgents.  I think  a man  named 
iirby,  a renegade  Englishman,  is  the  agent  in  the  matter.’^ 

If  there  had  been  a proper  system  of  supervision  here  in  regard  to 
hermits  to  trade  these  cases  would  not  have  occurred. 

I think  this  will  show  the  importance  of  trusting  the  matter  of  grant- 
Qg  permits  to  the  commander  of  the  military  department  or  of  having 
» spmal  agent  of  the  War  or  Treasury  Departments  here.  In  that 
ase  Capt.  James  Millward,  jr.,  the  captain  of  the  port  here,  would  be 
I proper  person,  and  his  duties  would  be  jierformed  under  my  super- 
ision.  He  keeps  an  account  of  all  supplies  received  for  the  inhab- 
.ants  around  here,  and  is  thus  able  to  tell  at  any  moment  what  any 
imily  needs.  The  same  system  through  subordinates  might  be  ex- 
ended  to  Norfolk. 

I am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

JOHN  A.  DIX, 

Major-General.

Admiral  : We  had  advices  yesterday  from  the  Blackwater.  The 
^emy  iiave  not  crossed,  nor  can  I ascertain  that  they  have  been  re-

enforced.  I tliiuk  there  is  not  an  armed  insurgent  within  40  miles  of 
Norfolk,  unless  it  be  some  lurking  squads,  or  perhaps  companies,  in  the 
Dismal  Swamp.  In  the  mean  time  we  have  strengthened  Suffolk  so 
as  to  feel  confident  of  resisting  any  force  the  enemy  can  have  on. the 
Blackwater. 

I have  fully  considered  the  matter  of  the  proposed  notice  to  the  people 
of  Norfolk  and  the  foreign  consuls  residing  there,  and  regret  to  differ 
in  opinion  with  you  in  regard  to  the  policy  of  giving  it  at  the  present 
time.  I am  not  sure  that  we  can  say  that  Suffolk  is  threatened  until 
there  is  an  advance  of  the  enemy^s  forces,  and  I do  not  think  the  people 
of  Norfolk  should  be  disturbed  unnecessarily.  The  hostile  attack 
should  be  imminent.  A notice  of  twenty-four  hours  is  all  that  is  needed 
in  case  of  an  attack  or  intended  bombardment,  and  where  we  ^re  merely 
acting  on  the  defensive  a longer  one  cannot  be  expected  of  us. 

I have  express  orders  not  to  allow  any  one  to  pass  through  our  lines 
without  the  permission  of  the  Secretary  of  War.  If  the  proj)osed 
notice  is  to  have  any  effect  at  all  it  will  be  to  induce  the  wealthier 
portions  of  the  people  to  leave,  and  they  are  in  general  opposed  to  us. 
The  poor,  among  whom  are  all  the  loyal  part  of  the  population,  have 
not  the  means  of  leaving.  The  result  would  therefore  be  to  drive  off 
those  who  sympathize  with  the  insurgents  and  diminish  the  objection 
on  the  part  of  their  forces  to  attack  the  place.  I should,  moreover,  feel 
greatly  embarrassed  by  applications  to  pass  our  lines.  I am  constantly 
refusing  them  now  to  parties  who  wish  to  go  to  Bichmond.  The  pro- 
posed notice  would  insure  a renewal  of  these  applications  and  im])ose 
on  me  the  obligation  to  grant  them  as  well  as  others  which  might  he 
made,  while  I am  i)rohibited  from  doing  so. 

There  is  another  consideration : I do  not  like  at  this  time  to  acknowl- 
edge that  we  are  acting  on  the  defensive.  The  enemy,  as  I see  from 
the  Richmond  papers,  have  been  expecting  an  attack  on  Petersburg, 
and  they  think  we  have  been  very  heavily  re-enforced  at  Suffolk.  The 
notice  would  be  an  acknowledgment  that  we  have  not  the  means  of 
making  an  aggressive  movement,  and  it  might  encourage  such  a move- 
ment against  us. 

These  objections,  as  you  see,  relate  chiefly  to  time.  The  form  of  the 
notice  you  inclosed  to  me  is  entirely  unobjectionable.  The  only  sug- 
gestion that  occurs  to  me  is  the  addition  of  the  following  words  at  the 
close,  viz : ‘‘In  case  these  places  shall  be  assailed.” 

If  you  will,  as  you  proposed  in  your  letter  of  the  2Gth,  send  me  such 
a notice,  signed  by  yourself,  I will  use  it  when  I think  it  necessary. 

I am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

/ JOHN  A.  UIX, 

Major-General.

Hdqrs.  Dept,  of  Virginia,  Seventh  Army  Corps,

Actg.  Rear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Commanding  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron : 

Admiral  : I have  the  honor  to  inclose  a copy  of  the  notice  you  sent 
me. 

I also  inclose  a copy  of  a letter  from  the  Secretary  of  the  Treasury  in 
regard  to  a vessel  detained  at  Norfolk.  You  will  observe  that  the  right 
of  the  military  commander  to  clear  a vessel  from  a blockaded  port — the 
vessel  having  arrived  there  under  a proper  clearance — is  distinctly  ad- 
mitted. This  will  relieve  the  question  of  supplies  for  Norfolk  of  a good 
deal  of  difficulty.  The  Secretary  of  the  Treasury  has  just  granted  a 
permit  for  a very  large  quantity  of  necessaries — among  other  items,  2,000 
tons  of  coal.  The  inhabitants  have  no  money,  or  at  least  none  which 
the  importers  will  take.  They  must  therefore  pay  in  the  products  of 
their  labor — tobacco,  shingles,  sweet  potatoes,  &c.  Under  the  decision 
of  the  Secretary  of  the  Treasury  they  may  do  so ; and  I trust,  as  the 
right  to  regulate  commerce  resides  in  the  Treasury  Department,  that 
you  will  not  consider  your  instructions  from  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy 
as  conflicting  with  this  decision.  This  rule  has  always  been  recognized 
heretofore.  On  the  return  of  a vessel  entering  Norfolk  under  the  au- 
thority of  the  Treasury  Department,  with  merchandise,  I have  author- 
ized her  to  be  cleared,  with  a cargo  of  agricultural  products,  to  auj"  port 
of  entry  in  a loyal  State.  Were  it  otherwise  the  permit  to  carry  neces- 
saries there  would  be  a moclvery.  The  case  of  the  Marblehead  is  pre- 
cisely in  point,  for  she  was  regularly  cleared  for  Norfolk,  and  is  laden 
with  staves,  &c.,  for  a return  cargo.  The  Secretary,  you  will  notice,

does  not  decide  her  case  as  a special  one  but  states  the  rule  which 
covers  it. 

The  Delaware,  which  has  taken  the  place  of  the  Morse,  is  precisely 
what  we  want.  With  the  West  End,  a heavy  tug  which  I have  armed, 
we  shall  have  an  efficient  river  defense.  I do  not  know  what  instruc- 
tions you  have  given  the  commander  of  the  Delaware,  and  I will  be 
much  obliged  to  you  if  you  will  request  him  to  act  in  conjunction  with 
the  West  End,  under  the  direction  of  Major-General  Peck,  who  will  be 
advised  of  all  exigencies  as  they  arise  and  know  how  to  meet  them. 

I am,  admiral,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

JOHN  A.  DIX,

The  honorable  Secretary  of  the  Navy  says ; 

That  there  is  distress  in  Norfolk  and  the  whole  insurrectionary  region  I doubt  not. 
The  object  of  the  blockade  is  to  destroy  their  traffic  while  in  rebellion.  The  relief  is 
in  the  hands  of  the  people  who  have  only  to  be  loyal  to  be  relieVed.  The  case  is 
not  one  of  sympathy  but  of  duty. 

The  honorable  Secretary,  under  date  of  October  13,  also  says  : 

The  rule  which  General  Dix  applies  to  Norfolk,  denying  that  it  is  a blockaded  port, 
would  exempt  any  port  and  the  whole  coast,  with  the  exception  of  Wilmington  and 
Charleston,  from  blockade,  for  all  are  held  by  military  occupation. 

I have  the  honor  to  be,  general,  very  respectfully,  yours, 

. ^ . S.  P.  LEE,

Secretary  of  the  Treasury : 

Dear  Sir  : I respectfully  call  your  attention  to  certain  facts  which 
mve  come  to  my  notice,  and  which  as  an  officer  of  the  United  States 
jovernment  I feel  my  duty  to  make  known  to  you.  Flags-of-truce 
loats  are  now  and  have  been  to  a great  extent  used,  in  addition  to  their 
awful  mission,  to  pass  contraband  goods  and  other  articles  through 
lie  lines  at  Aikeffis  Landing  on  James  Eiver.  I predicate  my  belief 
ipon  this : First,  a trunk  was  placed  on  board  of  the  John  A.  Warner, 
)urporting  to  pass  upon  the  permission  of  a lady  going  South  and 
)laced  by  accident  on  board  of  said  boat,  then  under  my  command. 
Jpon  examination  I found  no  single  article  of  woman’s  apparel,  but 
cloths,  quinine,  mathematical  instruments,  a large  quantity  of  silk, 
iiread,  needles,  &c.  I retained  and  will  turn  it  over  to  the  proper

Ion.  Salmon  P.  Chase, 

Secretary  of  the  Treasury : 

Sir:  I have  received  this  evening  your  letter  and  the  papers  prepared 
)y  you  concerning  trade  with  Korfolk,  and  I feel  a good  deal  of  embar- 
assment  in  regard  to  the  certificate.  Tliere  are  in  Korft)lk,  Princess 
Vnne,  and  Kansemond  Counties,  which  we  have  taken  possession  of  and 
lit  oif  from  Southern  sources  of  supply,  40,000  inhabitants.  We  must 
eed  them,  and  they  can  only  be  fed  from  the  Korth.  Can  I certify  that 
he  supplies  they  need^food,  fuel,  clothing  (for  they  must  be  warmed 
iid  clothed  as  well  as  fed)— are  “required  for  military  purposes  ! ” Will 
lot  this  extended  traffic  be  complained  of  as  a violation  of  the  law  of 
►lockade  if  we  admit  that  Korfolk  is  blockaded? 

I regret  that  the  Government  has  taken  this  view  or  the  subject,  for 
feel  with  you  the  exceeding  embarrassment  to  which  it  subjects  ns. 

I have  insisted  that  it  was  a case  of  military  occupatton  and  not  of 
tlockade;  that  you  cannot  blockade  your  own  ports  or  a port  you  have 
aken  from  an  enemy  j that  the  act  of  capture  ipso  facto  terminates  the 
•lockade  and  puts  you  in  military  possession  with  a totally  difierent 
ode  of  law  for  yourself  as  well  as  neutrals.  You  may  make  it  as  to 
hem  a closed,  but  it  is  no  longer  a blockaded,  port.  In  most  modern 
reaties,  I believe,  certainly  in  some,  there  is  a chapter  on  military  oc- 
upation,  stating  the  consequences  that  flow  from  it.  I conversed  with 
lajor-General  Halleck  on  the  subject,  in  Washington,  ten  days  ago, 
lid  he  concurred  with  me  fully.  I also  conferred  with  the  President, 
ecretary  of  State,  and  Secretary  of  War,  and  understood  the  latter  to 
ssent  to  my  positions,  and  the  two  former  to  be  at  least  impressed  by 
ly  suggestions.  I was  very  anxious  to  see  you  and  called  both  at  your 
nice  and  your  house,  but  was  disappointed* 

My  reasoning  is  briefly  this : 

1st.  Norfolk  is  not  a blockaded  port,  as  it  lacks  the  fundamental  con- 
ition  of  a blockade — hostile  possession. 

■3d.  if  it  is  a blockaded  port,  the  traffic  allowed  under  the  regulations 
oncerning  “ coastwise  intercourse”  is  in  violation  of  the  laws  of  blockade 
•^cognized  by  all  civilized  States.  A government  cannot  shut  out  neu- 
rals  from  trade  with  a blockaded  port  and  allow  intercourse  with  such 
ort  to  its  own  people. 

3d.  Norfolk  not  being  an  enemy’s  port,  but  held  by  military  occupa- 
011,  Ave  are  free  to  allow  such  traffic  as  is  necessary  to  maintain  the 
ossession  and  to  prevent  those  whom  we  have  subjected  to  our  power 
■om  suflering  by  hunger  and  cold,  a duty  enjoined  by  every  considera- 
011  of  humanity.  It  is  on  these  conditions  only  tliat  the  traffic  pro^ 
osed  to  be  allowed  can  be  justified,  ^

the  introduction  of  such  supplies  as  are  indispensable  for  the  troops  and:

authority  he  may  in  his  discretion  grant  permits  to  others  than  our  own 
citizens:  it  is  a matter  over  which,  as  the  military  commander,  he  bas; 
the  entire  control,  subject  to  the  interposition  of  the  Government  for  thel 


correction  of  abuse.  ^ i i

essary to  the  sustenance  of  40,000  people  are  required  for  military  piir-

General:  I have  the  honor  to  report  that  1 am  about  to  start  on  an

Information  was  sent  me  from  Plymouth  by  the  navy  that  three  regi-

dning  conscripts.  These  counties  form  a bag,  the  mouth  of  which  is 
3tween  Washington  and  Plymouth.  If  I am  not  too  late  (as  the  in- 
rmation  was  forty  hours  in  reaching  me)  I hope  to  engage  and  cap- 
irc  this  force.  Should  I accomplish  that  I shall  push  on  for  Hamilton, 
1 the  Eoanoke  Diver,  and  endeavor  to  take  that  place.  Should  the 
rces  in  the  counties  above  named  have  escaped  I will  push  on  at  once

eceived  from  the  Havy)  that  two  iron-clad  gunboats  were  being  con-

Is  Excellency  Abraham  Lincoln, 

President  of  the  United  States : 

Sir  : I feel  a strong  sympathy  in  behalf  of  the  people  of  the  Eastern 
bore  of  V irginia— Accomack  and  Northampton  Counties.  When  I sent 
I armed  force  against  them,  giving  them  assurances  of  protection  and 
remising  them  the  enjoyment  of  all  the  rights  of  loyal  citizens,  they 
id  down  their  arms.  They  have  at  no  time  since  been  in  rebellion 
?^st  the  United  States  j on  the  contrary,  they  have  united  themselves 
> Western  Virginia  j they  have  had  two  elections,  and  they  have  sent 
rong  Union  men  to  the  Legislature  and  Congress.  In  all  things  they 
ive  fulfilled  the  conditions  on  which  I pledged  to  them  equality  iii 
ghts  and  privileges  with  the  people  of  the  loyal  States.  When ’you 
sued  your  proclamation  in  July  last,  designating  the  States  and  parts 
States  that  were  to  be  deemed  loyal  and  omitting  these  two  counties, 
thought  to  write  to  you  begging  that  they  should  be  added  to  the 
amber  thus  designated.  I write  now  to  make  the  request  in  order 
lat  they  may  be  relieved  from  the  penalties  of  disloyalty,  and  that  the 
imt  of  disaffection  may  not  rest  upon  a community  in  which  no  such 
leling  exists  excepting  in  individual  cases  which  may  unfortunately 
3tound  evpywhere.  They  are  entitled  to  exemption  by  their  loyal 
>u  uct  during  the  last  year,  and  the  efiect  of  such  a declaration  from 
^u  at  tins  time  could  not  fail  to  have  a beneficial  efiect  in  other  quar- 
I'rs.  But  it  is  chiefly  as  an  act  of  justice  to  them  that  I urge  it,  and  I 
.D  sure  you  will  appreciate  the  earnestness  with  which  I ])ress  it  when 
pu  consider  the  relation  in  which  I stand  to  them. 

1 have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

JOIIX  A.  DIX,

Headquarters  Department  of  Virginia, 

November  22,  1862. 


Hon.  E.  M.  Stanton: 


Sir  : I have  received  your  order  appointing  Dr.  Le  Grand  Eussell 
^‘special  commissioner  to  take  charge  of  the  colored  refugees  from  the 
enemy  at  Fortress  Monroe  and  its  vicinity,”  and  shall  do  all  in  my  power 
to  aid  him  in  the  proper  discharge  of  his  duties. 

The  peculiar  phraseology  of  the  order  suggests  the  propriety  of  stat- 
ing that  all  the  negroes  here  are  not  refugees  from,  the  enemy."  On  the 
contrary,  there  are  a number  who  are  fugitives  from  the  service  of 
Union  men,  who  have  been  persecuted  by  the  secessionists  for  their 
lidelity  to  the  Government  of  the  United  States,  and  a few  who  belong 
to  pmsons  residing  in  districts  which  have  never  been  in  possession  of 
the  insurgents.  Some  Union  families  in  this  neighborhood  have  lost 
all  their  negroes,  whom  I have,  in  obedience  to  the  act  of  Congress, 
refused  to  giVe  up.  It  will  be  troublesome  to  separate  one  class  liouj 
the  other,  and  assuming  that  the  order  was  not  intended  to  make  any 
distinction,  1 shall,  unless  otherwise  directed,  put  Dr.  Eussell  in  eliarge 
of  both. 

I avail  myself  of  the  opportunity  of  stating  'that  under  vour  au- 
thority I opened  negotiations  with  the  Governors  of  the  States  of 
Maine,  Massachusetts,  and  Ehode  Island,  with  a view  to  provide  a tem- 
porary asylum  for  the  contrabands  here  until  the  Government  could 
make  some  permanent  provision  for  them.  The  proposition  was  re- 
ceived with  such  marked  disfavor  by  Governor  Andrew,  of  Massachu- 
setts, that  I decided,  notwithstanding  a very  kind  and  prompt  response 
from  Governor  Sprague,  of  Ehode  Island,  to  retain  them  here  and  make 
suitable  iirovision  for  them  for  the  winter.  Accordingly  I withdrew 
the  sick  from  the  hospital  at  E^ewport  Eews  and  sent  over  a thousand 
of  the  colored  fugitives  there.  But  the  very  day  they  were  removed 
from  their  encampment,  where  they  were  dying  rapidly,  I was  advised 
that  the  Irish  Legion,  under  General  Corcoran,  would  arrive  on  the 
following  day.  Their  tents  had  been  so  injured  in  New  York  by  a 
storm  on  the  eve  of  their  departure  that  they  were  obliged  to  be  put 
under  cover,  and,  having  no  place  for  them  but  Newport  News,  I was 
compelled  to  remove  the  colored  people  again.  They  were  sent  to  Cra- 
iiey  Island,  and  the  quartermaster  is,  -under  my  instructions,  erecting 
barracks  for  them.  They  will  all  be  covered  in  the  course  of  the  coming 
week. 

I am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

JOHN  A.  DIX, 

Major- 'General.

Headquarters  Department  of  Virginia, 

Fort  Monroe,  Ya,,  November  24,  1862. 

His  Excellency  Abraham  Lincoln, 

President  of  the  United  States  : 

Sir  : I have  had  the  honor  to  receive  your  letter  of  the  20th  instant* 
in  regard  to  the  counties  of  Accomack  and  Northampton,  or  what  is 
usually  called  the  Eastern  Shore  of  Virginia,  and  am  gratified  to  learn 
from  you  that  there  is  no  objection  to  a recognition  of  their  loyal  condi- 
tion. The  reasons  which  make  them  so  anxious  on  the  subject  are  two : 

1st.  An  unwillingness  to  be  classed  with  the  insurrectionary  districts, 
considering  it  a stain  upon  their  character  and  unjust  to  them,  as  they 
have  given  repeated  evidences  of  their  loyalty ; and 

2d.  A desire  to  be  exempt,  as  they  claim  they  are  entitled  to  be,  from 
the  penalty  of  50  per  cent,  in  addition  to  the  taxes  to  be  raised  to  sup 
port  the  Government,  &c.  This  penalty  is  imposed  by  the  concluding! 
clause  of  section  1 of  the  act  of  June  7,  1862,  chapter  98^  of  the  laws  ol 
1862.  This  is  a “ practical  difficulty  ” from  which  they  ask  to  be  relieved 
They  are  perfectly  willing  to  pay  their  share  of  the  taxes  like  otliei 
loyal  districts. 

I am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

’ JOHN  A.  DIX, 

Major-General.

Dear  Sir  : During  tlie  march  of  the  army  under  your  command  u 
the  valley  of  the  Eoanoke  Eiver,  in  the  early  part  of  this  month,  man 
wanton  acts  of  destruction  of  private  property  and  many  depredation! 
were  committed  by  the  troops  under  your  command. 

Negroes  were  forcibly  abducted  from  their  owners ; many  isolate 
houses  in  the  villages  of  Hamilton  and  Williamston  were  willfull 
burned : ])aiiors  of  private  residences  were  used  for  stables ; family  ca 
riages  were  taken  to  your  camps,  abandoned,  and  destro^^ed  houses  ( 
peaceful  citizens  were  forcibly  entered,  doors  and  windows  broken  an 
all  the  furniture  destroyed  ; bedding  was  carried  into  the  streets  an 
burned  : women  were  insulted  by  your  soldiers  and  robbed  of  all  tl 
money  and  valuables  on  their  persons,  and  all  their  clothing  and  tin 
of  their  children,  except  what  they  had  on,  was  cast  into  the  fire  or  toi 

to  pieces.  , , . 

In  general  terms,  your  soldiers  committed  many  robberies  and  pra 
ticed  a wanton  and  malicious  destruction  of  private  property. 

Having  been  over  a portion  of  your  line  of  march  and  examined  the, 
evidences  of  destruction  I reported  them  to  my  Government,  and  I a. 
instructed  to  address  you  and  inform  you  that  such  outrages  are  co 
sidered  as  forfeiting  the  right  of  yourself  and  officers  to  be  treated 
prisoners  of  war,  and  to  inquire  of  you  whether  these  outrages  we 
committed  with  your  knowledge  and  sanction. 

The  action  to  be  taken  in  the  case  will  depend  on  the  answer  you  mi 
make,  and  if  no  answer  be  returned  in  ten  days  after  the  delivery 
this  letter  it  will  be  considered  by  the  Government  that  you  admit  ai 
hold  yourself  responsible  for  the  acts  charged. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  G.  FEENOH, 
Major- General,  Commanding.

Headquarters  Department  of  North  Carolina,- 
New  Berne,  N.  G.,  December  4,  1862. 

Maj.  Gen.  S.  G.  French, 

Comdg.  Department  of  North  Carolina,  Petersburg,  Va.: 

General  : Your  favor  of  November  27  1 have  the  honor  to  acknowl 
edge.  I had  previously  received  from  General  Martin  a letter  on  tb( 
same  subject,  and  as  my  answer  to  him  covers  most  of  the  ground  ii 
yours  I beg  leave  to  inclose  a copy.  I beg  to  say  in  relation  to  • post 
script  of  your  letter  that  not  a negro,  to  the  best  of  my  belief,  wa: 
forcibly  abducted  from  his  owner,  and  indeed  I only  suffered  thos< 
to  follow  who  insisted  upon  so  doing.  There  were  fifteen  houses  (say: 
General  Martin)  burned  at  Hamilton ; the  fact  I deplore.  At  Williams 
ton  two  were  burned  from  a defect  in  the  flue  of  the  chimney,  as  showi 
by  investigation,  and  one  small  house  pulled  down  to  prevent  tin 
spread  of  the  fire.  Members  of  my  staff  were  in  each  house  and  non* 
of  them  saw  horses  in  the  parlors,  though  in  one  or  two  instances  oi 
piazzas ; family  carriages  (not  over  three)  may  have  been  taken  to  trans 
port  sick  meu,*not  to  destroy  or  abandon.  That  houses  of  peaceful  cit 
izens  with  the  families  in  occupancy  were  entered,  women  and  childrei 
insulted  and  robbed,  I do  not  believe,  as  the  provost-marshal  hean 
nothing  of  the  kind  so  gross  as  you  report.  In  respect  to  that  part  o 
your  letter  as  to  the  treatment  of  any  officers  not  as  prisoners  of  war, 
would  say  that  if  after  my  letter  your  Government  proposes  to  act  or 
that  principle  I beg  that  you  will  have  me  informed  for  the  regulatioi 
of  my  own  course. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  G.  FOSTER, 
Major-General,  Commanding.

Commanding,  &c. : 

General  : Your  letter  -of  November  25,*  inclosing  an  extract  from 
he  Boston  Traveller,  describing  the  alleged  depredations  of  the  army 
inder  m^  command  in  their  late  march  up  the  country,  I have  received 
u reply  to  your  request  to  know  whether  these  things  were  done  by  my 
>rdei  I have  to  state  that  draught  animals,  and  in  some  cases  carriages 
0 be  used  as  ambulances,  beeves  and  pigs  to  subsist  ‘my  men  when 
hort  ot  provisions,  and  forage  to  subsist  cavalry  horses  and  draught 
uimals  were  taken  by  my  order.  Every  other  species  of  depredation 
pas  not  only  not  done  by  my  orders  but  against  them  and  against  the 
trongest  efforts  to  prevent  them.  On  the  march  we  found  all  the 
owns  almost  entirely  abandoned  by  their  inhabitants,  the  houses  in 
ome  cases  cleared  of  their  furniture,  in  others  partly,  and  in  some  not 
t all.  1 quartered  my  troops  in  the  abandoned  houses  only.  The 
rincipal^  cause  of  the  depredations  which  I know  were  committed 
'as,  I think,  that  so  many  houses  contained  apple  brandy,  and  which 
scaped  the  eye  of  the  provost-marshal.  I trust  sincerely  that  in  the 
ituie  marches  in  this  State  you  will  be  pleased  to  find  a marked  im- 
rovemeut  in  all  these  respects,  and  I earnestly  recommend  that  you 
rge  all  peaceable  citizens  to  remain  on  their  estates,  as  that  course 
'ill  aid  me  greatly  in  protecting  their  property. 

I have  the  honor  to  remain,  general,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  G.  FOSTEE, 
Major-General,  Commanding.

:;ate  with  General  Foster  and  to  co-operate  with  him  in  harassing  the 
memy.  I wrote  to  him,  but  he  being  absent  did  not  receive  my  letter 
for  some  time  and  his  answer  did  not  reach  me  till  November  27.  I 
idvised  you  of  these  circumstances  by  letter  of  the  29th  ultimo  and 
Fat  I had  sent  an  officer  to  him.  He  came  here  immediately,  and  on 
3onferring  with  him  I agreed  to  let  him  have  a brigade  for  ten  days  ta 
ittack  Goldsborough  and  cut  the  railroad  at  that  place.  I directed

Beaufort^  JST,  0.,  December  8,  1862. 

Maj.  Gen.  J.  G.  Foster, 

Comdg.  JJ.  tS.  Army  Forces,  Dept,  of  North  Carolina  : 

General:  I glean  the  following  information  from  the  masters  of  the 
ately  seized  schooners  Brilliant  and  J.  C.  Roker,  to  wit : There  is  at 
S^assaii  intending  to  run  the  blockade  a small  screw  steamer,  the  Lizzie, 
jelonging  to  Wilmington.  Said  steamer  would  be  ready  about  the  last 
)f  November  or  soon  after. 

Fort  Fisher,  at  New  Inlet,  is  considered  the  stronger  fort  compared 
vith  Caswell.  There  are  forty  guns  mounted,  including  one  8-inch 
Jolumbiad  (rifled)  and  two  Whitworth  guns.  The  fort  is  built  of  cab- 
lage-wood,  filled  in  with  sand  14  feet  thick.  At  Brunswick,  up  Cape 
?ear  River,  there  is  a strong  work,  and  some  5 miles  below  Wilmington 
here  is  a stronger  fortification  in  process  of  building. 

The  channels  are  all  obstructed,  with  only  a narrow  passage,  which 
s reported  easily  stopped  when  necessity  requires,  being  defended  by 
latteries  on  either  side. 

The  irou-clads  are  to  be  perfected  whenever  iron  is  landed,  intended 
oainly  for  river  defense. 

In  my  opinion  the  present  moment  is  the  best  time  to  attack  Wil- 
Qington  and  the  adjacent  forts.  The  longer  the  enterprise  is  delayed 
be  more  difficult  it  will  prove  to  be,  as  a large  number  of  men  are  kept 
,t  work  strengthening  the  fortifications.  I believe  the  troops  should 
te  landed  in  the  vicinity  of  Fort  Caswell,  although  Masonborough 
Diet  should  be  examined  in  this  connection,  but  a military  reconnais- 
ance  will  determine  the  relative  advantages  of  the  two  places. 

At  the  last  accounts  there  were  about  4,000  troops  in  the  vicinity  of 
Vilmington.  The  yellow  fever  has  entirely  disappeared. 

Salt  is  selling  at  $150  (Confederate  money)  per  sack,  or  about  $60  per 
•ushel,  and  everything  else  in  proportion,  which  is  a proof  that  the 
lockade  has  been  effectual.  Gold  is  exchanged  at  the  rate  of  $2.25 
!oufederate  scrip  for  $1  in  gold. 

Let  me  repeat  that  the  golden  moment  for  action  has  arrived. 

About  700  persons  died  from  yellow  fever  in  October  and  November 
ut  of  a population  of  about  2,500. 

The  impression  is  that  if  Fort  Caswell  is  taken  Fort  Fisher  will  be 
baudoned. 

I am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

WM.  A.  PARKER, 

Commander,

1 sincerely  trust  that  the  re-enforcements  asked  for  in  my  letter  of

My  present  force  of  infantry,  consisting  of  9,000  men  capable  of 
marching  and  fighting,  6,000  of  whom  are  new — nine  months’  men — is 
too  weak  to  give  a good  support  to  my  forty  pieces  of  artillery  and  to 
afibrd  a fair  chance  of  success  against  the  older  troops  of  the  enemy  in 
front  of  us.  I have  therefore  found  it  necessary  to  borrow  from  General 
Dix  the  services  for  a time  of  General  Wessells’  brigade,  consisting  of 
six  regiments  (2,200  men).  These  regiments  were  kindly  iiromised  me

to  this  place,  arriving  yesterday. 

General  Peck  has  agreed  to  make  a simultaneous  attack  on  the 
Blackwater,  from  Suffolk,  in  which  our  gunboats  are  to  co-operate. 

Even  if  I do  not  succeed  in  my  expectations  I hope  ray  movement

Sir:  Complaints  have  been  made  by  those  who  take  a strong  interest 
in  the  condition  of  fugitives  from  service  here,  usually  denominated 
^‘contrabands,”  that  their  labor  since  they  have  been  employed  by  tue 
United  States  has  not  been  fully  paid  for.  There  are  other  grounds  ol 
complaint  also,  and  with  a view^  to  remove  them  1 desire  to  make  the 

following  suggestions,  viz : i i 

1st.  The  labor  of  these  persons  was  not  paid  for  until  iSovember  l.: 
1861,  at  which  time  a system  of  compensation  was  adopted  under  Major 
General  Wool.  Before  that  time  a large  number  of  them  had  been  em 
ployed  and  supplied  with  food  and  clothing.  If  the  x^ayment  of  wages 
was  right  after  November  1 it  would  have  been  equally  right  befon

ever,  some  data  for  an  estimate.  The  numbers  employed  July  4 anc 
November  1 are  known,  and  by  assuming  a mean  number  a proxima

to  the  sum  of  $2,450.  Both  these  sums  should  be  paid.  Many  of  tii

Commanding.,  &c. : 

General  : I have  been  informed  that  a i)ortion  of  the  forces  of  tl 
enemies  of  the  United  States  recently  invaded  the  county  of  Washin 
ton  and,  among  other  deiiredations  committed  upon  innocent  citizen 
they  seized  and  carried  away  against  their  consent  and  against  tl 
consent  of  their  owners  a large  number  of  slaves.  From  the  home 
Mr.  M.  Bowen  they  took  away  several  of  his  negroes  who  had  be( 
faithful  to  him,  and  whom  he  protected  and  humanely  supported.  Tli 
outrage  has  not  the  defense  attempted  for  the  African  slave  trade,  ‘-tli 
it  brought  uncivilized  beings  under  the  influence  of  Christianity  ai 
civilization.”  This  robbery  takes  civilized  beings  from  their  fainili 
and  homes;  it  deprives  a kind  master  of  his  property  and  puuisli 
slaves  for  their  fidelity  to  him.  I cannot  believe  the  good  people  ' 
North  Carolina  will  justify  such  conduct.  To  the  barbarous  and  wi 
ful  burning  of  the  town  of  Plymouth  by  the  enemy  your  attention  li 
already  been  called,  and  of  that  nothing  more  need  be  said.  As  t 
voice  of  civil  authority  outside  of  our  lines  has  no  longer  any  poteiic 
I solicit  your  intervention  with  those  commanding  the  forces  of  t 
so-called  Confederate  States,  that  we  may  ascertain  by  what  rules  tl 
war  is  to  be  conducted,  and  whether  those  negroes  to  wbom  I lia 
referred  are  to  be  delivered  uj)  to  those  to  whom  their  services  may 
due. 

I have  the  honor  to  be,  &c.,

eut.  Col.  H.  T.  Yan  Buren,  Fortress  Monroe  : 

Colonel  : I would  respectfully  report  the  arrival  at  this  port  of  the 
earner  Cahawba,  with  the  Eleventh  Maine  and  Ninety-eighth  New 
ork.  We  found  entering  the  harbor  just  before  us  the  Kennebec 
ith  the  Eighty-first  New  York,  and  that  the  Belvidere  had  discharged 
lO  One  himdredth  New  York.  Off  Hatteras  we  parted  our  hawser  and 
ft  the  ship  Montebello.  Soon  thereafter  the  wind  shifted  to  the  west 
jid  afterward  to  the  northwest,  whicli  will  insure  her  prompt  arrival 
le  two  monitors  behaved  admirably,  and  although  we  had  quite  a

olina.  In  relation  to  prisoners  of  war  when  they  have  been  paroled  1

Washington  and,  among  other  depredations  committed  upon  innocent 
citizens,  we  seized,  carried  away,  against  the  consent  of  their  owners,  a 
large  number  of  slaves ; that  from  the  house  of  Mr.  M.  Bowen  we  took 
away  several  of  his  negroes  who  had  been  faithful  to  him  and  whom  he 
protected  and  humanely  supported  5 that  this  outrage  has  not  the  de- 
fense attempted  for  the  African  slave  trade — “ that  it  brought  uncivilized 
beings  under  the  influence  of  Christianity  and  civilization  ; that  this 
robbery  takes  civilized  beings  from  their  families  and  homes ; it  de- 
jirives  a kind  master  of  his  property  and  punishes  slaves  for  their 
fidelity  to  him.  It  is  true  our  forces  did  invade  the  county  of  Wash- 
ington, and  the  officer  in  command  did  report  to  me  that  he  brought 
out  with  him  some  negroes.  Mr.  Stauly  is  a representative  of  the 
United  States  Government,  and  I take  it  for  granted  speaks  by  au- 
thority, and  if  it  be  the  determination  of  your  Government  to  deliver 
uj)  to  their  owmers  the  100,000  slaves  you  have  stolen  from  their  kind

communication  and  Mr.  Stanly’s  letter. 

As  it  is  an  acknowledged  principle  among  Christian  nations  to  re- 
spect private  property  on  land  I am  sure  my  Government  will  hail  this 
as  an  evidence  that  hereafter  you  will  cease  to  deprive  private  citizens

Camp  Batelielder'’s  Station^  January  13,  1803. 

Lieut.  Col.  Southard  Hoffman, 

Assistant  Adjutant- General : 

Sir  : I have  the  honor  to  report  that  while  examining  in  person  yes 
terday  the  position  at  Tuscarora  ’Station  I discovered  a small  party  o 
rebel  guerrilias  in  the  neighborhood.  As  soon  as  practicable  I sen 
one  of  my  companies  (K,  under  Lieutenant  Clay)  with  orders  to  movt; 
in  the  woods  to  the  rear  of  the  enemy  and  punish  them  for  their  i\x\ 
dacity.  Unfortunately  my  men  were  discovered  too  soon,  upon  whicll 
the  guerrillas  formed  (to  the  number  of  about  50),  but  broke  and  rai 
before  Lieutenant  Olay  could  approach  nearer  than  a quarter  of  a uiilti 
It  being  almost  dusk,  pursuit  through  the  woods  was  impracticable. 

On  the  facts  being  reported  to  me  1 ordered  two  companies  to  b 
ready  to  move  at  2 a.  m.  ^(when  the  moon  would  be  up)  and  a third  con 
pauy  at  4 a.  m.  The  former  (Companies  B and  I,  Captains  Mtdcif 
and  Buyers)  were  directed  to  move  through  the  woods,  a half  mile  0i 
the  hank  of  the  railroad,  some  5 or  G miles,  until  in  the  rear  of  the  pos 
tion  where  the  rebels  were  probably  bivouacked,  then  to  sweep  tli 
woods  backwards  to  that  position.  The  other  company  (A,  Captai 
Brown)  was  directed  to  take  post  near  the  station,  so  as  to  intercjei 
fugitives  seeking  the  Tuscarora  road.  The  officers  were  also  directe 
in  case  the  guerrillas  should  be  seen  anywhere  to  follow  them  rapidJi 
as  far  as  Core  Creek. 

My  men  have  not  yet  returned,  but  haying  no  guide  and  bein 
obliged  to  move  by  the  compass,  their  success  in  catching  those  pc 
fectly  acquainted  with  the  country  is  doubtful. 

At  dusk  and  until  about  10  p.  m.  there  was  a large  fire  on  the  ral 
road  at  some  miles  distance  beyond  Tuscarora  ; whether  a signal  or  tl 
burning  of  a culvert  I have  no  means  as  yet  of  detecting. 

In  connection  with  my  duties  here  I also  report  that  on  examinatic 
and  inquiry  I find  the  Trent  road  good  now  and  likely  to  contiiii 
practicable  for  transportation.  Also  that  I could  post  another  infanti 
regiment  advantageously  on  that  line,  not  o<dy  on  account  of  the  ii 
portance  of  the  line  itself  but  also  in  order  to  allow  me  gradually  : 
cover  the  country  in  my  front  and  encourage  and  protect  the  traiispo 
tation  of  turpentine  to  and  within  our  lines.  With  the  same  view 
propose  as  soon  as  practicable  to  rebuild  the  bridge  on  the  Neuse  roa 
over  Batchelder^s  Creek,  stationing  there  a strong  infantry  ])icket. 

On  the  whole  I think  a few  days  will  suffice  to  teach  the  enemy  tli. 
they  have  no  business  east  of  Core  Creek,  and  cannot  safely  ventu 
across. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  BICHTEB  JONES, 

Col.  Fifty -eighth  Regiment  Pa.  Vols.^  Comdg.  Fichet  Line,  A,e.

General  Orders,  ) Hdqrs.  Eighteenth  Army  Corps, 

22.  1 Few  Berne ^ January  15,  1863. 

The  commanding  general  learns  with  deep  regret  of  the  insubordi- 
nate conduct  of  the  Ninety-sixth  New  York  Volunteers  on  the  night 
of  the  13th  instant.  It  is  the  duty  of  commanding  officers  to  use  every 
effort  to  promote  the  comfort  of  the  troops,  their  prompt  payment,  &('. 
This  has  been  done.  The  commanding  general  has  asked  for,  and  is  in 
hourly  expectation  of  receiving,  funds  to  pay  those  who  have  not  been 
paid  for  a long  time.  The  course  of  the  soldier,  if  any  neglect  is  shown 
in  his  case,  is  to  make  a respectful  petition  or  remonstrance  on  the 
matter,  but  to  obey.  The  recent  acts  of  the  Ninety-sixth  were  muti- 
nous, and  such  as  all  good  soldiers  should  be  ashamed  to  have  shared 
in.  The  only  effect  can  be  to  lay  the  men  open  to  trial  for  mutiny  and 
consequent  punishment,  aud  cannot  hasten,  certainly,  their  desires. 
The  duty  of  a regimental  officer  is  to  use  his  efforts  to  put  down  any 
attempt  at  insubordination,  mildly  if  he  can,  by  force  and  arms  if  he 
must.  The  officers  of  the  Ninety-sixth  and  those  regiments  to  which 
the  mutineers  Avent  lamentably  tailed  in  their  duties  as  commanders, 
or  the  breach  of  discipline  referred  to  would  have  been  promptly  pun- 

The  commanding  general  hopes  that  no  officer  or  soldier  will  again 
so  fail  in  his  duty.  Another  offense  will  surely  meet  its  punishment. 

Bv  command  of  Major-General  Foster: 

[SOUTHARD  HOFFMAN,] 

Assistant  Adjutant- General.

Actg.  Eear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Commanding  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron  : 

Admiral  : There  are  indications  of  activity  on  the  part  of  the  en- 
emy above  Yorktown  and  also  on  the  Blackwater.  General  Pryor  has 
crossed  the  river  and  is  7 miles  on  this  side.  I am  so  weakened  by  re- 
enforcing General  Foster  in  North  Carolina  that  I can  only  act  on  the 
defensive.  There  are  rumors  in  Norfolk  of  a raid  from  the  direction  of 
the  Dismal  Swamp,  and  General  Peck  telegraphs  me  this  evening  that 
our  pickets  have  been  fired  on  between  Suffolk  and  Deep  Creek.  Gen- 
eral Viele  is  very  anxious  to  have  a small  gunboat,  or,  as  he  says,  ‘‘an 
additional  small  gunboat  sent  up  to  remain  near  the  draw-bridge,”  that 
he  may  look  after  the  threatened  raid  in  other  directions.  You  will 
oblige  me  if  you  can  comply  with  'his  request.  Thp  secessionists  in 
Norfolk  have  been  in  high  spirits  for  several  days,  and  we  hear  in  many 
quarters  that  some  movement  against  us  is  intended. 

I am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

JOHN  A.  DIX, 

Major- General.

Major-General  Foster, 

Commanding  Eepartmefit  of  North  Carolina: 

Sir:  On  the  5th  of  January,  1863,  at  10.30  o’clock  p.  m.,  as  Lieutenant 
Sanders  was  walking  in  company  with  three  other-men  on  the  principal 
street  in  Elizabeth  City,  N.  C.,  they  were  fired  upon  by  a party  of  guer- 
rillas from  behind  some  brick  walls,  the  ruins  of  burnt  buildings.  One 
of  the  men  was  killed  instantly.  My  brother  walked  to  his  quarters 
and  died  in  half  an  hour  from  the  time  he  received  the  wounds.  Tbe 
company  immediately  turned  out  and  succeeded  in  capturing  two  of  tlie 
murderers  with  their  guns  in  their  hands.  We  captured  several  otliers, 
but  without  their  arms.  They  were  placed  in  prison  to  await  an  inves- 
tigation, which  was  held,  and  the  innocent  set  free. 


Some  details  omitted  from  this  dispatch.

The  murder  of  Lieutenant  Cox  and  family  occurred  on  the  morning 
f the  9th  of  February,  1863,  in  the  following  manner : He  being  a resi- 
ient  of  Pasquotank  County,  and  living  16  miles  from  town,  went  down 
OT  the  purpose  of  moving  his  family  to  the  city.  On  his  return  he  was 
,ttacked  by  a gang  of  guerrillas,  who  came  upon  him  from  a thicket  and 
red  a volley,  killing  him  and  a girl  of  four  years  old  instantly  and 
rounding  the  wife  so  that  she  died  on  the  13th  instant.  Three  other 
len  of  my  company  were  wounded,  1 mortally,  1 badly,  1 slightly. 

The  team  ran  to  the  city,  but  without  any  one  to  tell  what  had  be- 
ome  of  its  riders,  but  the  marks  of  blood  on  the  carriage  gave  evidence 
f foul  play.  I immediately  sent  out  an  expedition,  which  returned  in 
he  evening  with  the  bodies  of  Lieutenant  Cox  and  child.  This  caused 
reat  excitement  among  the  people,  both  civil  and  military,  who  urged 
bat  something  be  done  to  avenge,  if  possible,  or  at  least  to  set  an  ex- 
raple  to  prevent  the  committing  of  such  brutal  outrages.  I was  asked 
y many  to  take  all  of  those  prisoners  who  could  be  proven  guilty  of 
eing  guerrillas  and  have  them  shot.  I was  not  myself  in  favor  of 
oiug  so  5 but  when  I thought  the  matter  over  deliberately  I ordered 
oe  prisoner,  by  the  name  of  A.  White,  to  be  brought  ouib  and  shot, 
hich  was  done  by  a brother  of  Lieutenant  Cox,  for  which  I hold  my- 
ilf  personally  responsible. 

E.  C.  SANDERS, 

Captain^  Commanding  Post  at  Elizabeth  City,

Fort  Monroe,  Ya.,  March  2,  1863. 
aj.  Gen.  H.  W.  Halleck,  Chief  of  Staff : 

A demonstration  was  made  on  the  enemy’s  lines  yesterday  which 
ought  out  a considerable  force.  An  attack  was  to  have  been  made 
one  of  his  batteries  last  night,  but  was  probably  postponed  for  want 
boats,  to  be  brought  from  ^^orfolk.  Every  effort  will  be  made  to 
certain  promptly  his  strength.  I telegraphed  General  Peck  on  the 
bject  last  night,  after  my  return  from  Suffolk,  in  consequence  of  a 
spatch  from  General  Butterfield  stating  that  Hood’s  and  Pickett’s 
visions  were  reported  in  Hooker’s  front.  I have  just  received  a dis- 
tcli  from  General  Peck  in  which  he  says  deserters  from  Pickett’s 
rision  state  that  they  saw  Pickett  yesterday  and  that  no  brigades 
ve  gone  from  Longstreet’s  command.  They  received  orders  to  be 
idy  to  move  last  night,  but  the  orders  were  countermanded.  One  of 
e deserters,  a Texan,  says  that  Hood  was  there  yesterday.  Jenkins’ 

' nsion  is  before  Suffolk.  I will  direct  General  Peck  to  make  a recou- 
issance  in  force,  and  will  be  ready  to  make  the  movement  referred  to 
you  promptly. 

JOHN  A.  DIX, 

Major- General j Commanding.

*bject  had  not  been  thoroughly  accomplished,  I sent  a larger  force, 
mder  command  of  Colonel  Morris,  One  hundred  and  first  Pennsylvania 
Volunteers.  From  this  I have  not  yet  heard. 

The  information  derived  from  these  various  scouts  is,  briefly — 
Thirty-eight  thousand  rations  are  issued  daily  from  Goldsborough  to 
roops  within  drawing  distance.  This  in  all  probability  includes  the 
orces  at  Goldsborough,  Kinston,  Tarborough,  Kenansville  (west  of 
)nslow,  near  the  railroad),  and  possibly  the  force  on  the  Koanoke  Fiver, 
eaving  Weldon  and  Wilmington  as  separate  points  of  issue. 

The  information  given  in  mine  of  March  2,  as  to  the  force  on  Koanoke 
liver,  has  been  confirmed,  both  as  to  position  and  numbers.  The  iron- 
lad,  also  mentioned,  is  again  reported  as  being  now  read}^ 

Owing  to  the  dearth  of  transportation  in  this  department  at  present 
shall  have  to  await  the  return  of  the  expedition  to  Hyde  County  in 
rder  to  send  re-enforcements  to  Plymouth,  which  I propose  to  do,  and 
Iso  to  erect  a battery  there  capable  of  defending  the  town,  holding  the 
louth  of  the  river,  and  assisting  the  Havy  in  repelling  the  iron-clads. 
Owing  to  the  fact  that  so  large  a portion  of  my  light  artillery  is  now 
II  the  Department  of  the  South  (a  picked  force)  it  is  necessary  to  mount 
wo  companies  Third  Hew  York  Artillery,  and  I have  made  the  requisi- 
ions  (to  day’s  mail)  for  two  batteries  of  Hapoleon  guns,  complete,  and 
3r  the  requisite  number  of  horses.  I trust  this  will  meet  j^our  api)roval, 
nd  that  the  guns  and  horses  will  be  at  once  ordered. 

I omitted  to  mention  that  General  Dix  having  kindly  offered  to  scout 
rom  Horfolk  and  Suflblk,  with  his  cavalry,  in  the  direction  of  Edenton, 
llizabeth  City,  and  Winfield,  1 have  embraced  the  offer,  and  shall  con- 
entrate  the  forces  at  these  small  posts,  Plymouth,  and  Koanoke.  The 
mall  posts  above-named  were  difficult  to  re-enforce  or  support,  and 
et  some  force  should  be  in  this  direction,  and  this  relieves  me  of  the 
weight. 

Your  favor  of  the  4th  of  March,  on  the  subject  of  the  Maine  artillery, 
as  just  come  to  hand,  and  in  obedience  thereto  1 am  taking  the  neces- 
ary  steps  to  muster  out  such  members  of  that  organization  as  do  not 
oluntarily  join  some  other  arm  of  the  service. 

I am,  general,  with  great  respect,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  G.  FOSTEK, 

Major- General,  Comma^iding.

General-in-Chief  U.  S.  Army,  Washington,  D.  C. : 

General:  I have  the  honor  to  most  respectfully  and  earnestly  reque: 
that  the  detachment  of  the  Eighteeenth  Army  Corps  now  in  the  Depar 
ment  of  the  South  be  ordered  to  return  here.  My  reasons  for  this  reque: 
are  the  accounts  from  PortEoyal  show  that  there  is  no  immediate  prospe< 
of  a movement  from  that  place,  and  the  withdrawal  of  troops  thereto] 
would  not  be  detrimental  to  the  service;  also  the  enemy  ^e  in  lar^ 
force  in  this  State  and  becoming  aggressive.  General  D.  H.  Hill  is  i 
immediate  command,  and  the  expressed  determination  of 
Longstreet  is  to  ‘‘  clean  out  the  Yankees  from  the  State  of  North  Car 
lina.^>  Again,  with  the  detachment  of  my  troops  returned  I would  I 
able  to  make  some  important  movements  in  this  State,  cutting  the  rai 
road  again,  and,  if  a movement  on  the  Blackwater  were  made  simult 
neously,  perhaps  reaching  Weldon.  , i 

The  enemy  have  a moving  column  30,000  strong  and  with  abundain 
of  artillery.  They  should  be  met,  and  my  picked  troops  and  best  art 
lery  being  absent  I am  utterly  unable  to  do  so. 

I trust,  general,  that  the  above  reasons  given  will  be  favorably  r 
ceived  bv  you,  and  that  in  my  request  you  will  see  a desire  for  the  go( 
of  the  service.  I consider  that  we  are  perfectly  able  to  act  on  the  a 
fensive  here,  but  with  the  return  of  my  detachment,  from  the  lack 
spirit  displayed  by  the  enemy  in  their  recent  demonstration,  I leel  co 
fident  that  I can  overpower  the  enemy  here. 

I have  the  honor  to  be,  general,  with  great  respect,  your  obedie

Maj.  Gen.  AmRosE  B.  Burnside,  Commanding: 

One  brigade  of  Willcox’s  division  is  embarked  and  part  of  the  second; 
also  a battery  of  artillery;  but  it  is  not  proper  that  they  should  start. 
A severe  snow-storm  set  in  this  morning  and  still  continues,  and  as  the 
steamers  will  have  to  wait  until  it  is  over  I have  ordered  the  embar- 
kation to  be  postponed.  Shall  the  ammunition  and  ambulance  train  of 
the  First  Division  follow  the  division,  or  wait  until  the  Second  Division 
IS  embarked  ? General  Smith  is  still  absent.  The  chief  quartermaster 
has  not  yet  reported  for  duty;  went  west  with  General  Burns.  Cap- 
tain Van  Ness,  acting,  absent  on  leave.  Dr.  McDonald  is  absent  with 
leave;  all  others  present.  Bowen,  Coale,  and  Chambloss  were  assigned 
to  the  Ninth  Corps,  and  Babcock  to  the  Sixth,  by  orders  from  the  War 
Department  of  March  1.  It  appears  that  these  assignments  are  ordered 
by  the  President.  Should  not  therefore  those  remain  that  are  assigned 
to  the  Ninth  Corps  ? The  following  list  of  officers  composing  the  staffi 
Df  the  Ninth  Corps  was  furnished  me  by  Colonel  Bowen,  assistant  ad-

P.  A.  O’Connell,  acting  medical  director;  Dr.  J.  E.  McDonald,  medical 
nspector;  First  Lieut.  O.  M.  Dearborn,  ordnance  officer;  First  Lieut.

Hdqrs.  Forty-fourth  Eegt.  Mass.  Yol.  Militia, 
Washington^  N.  C.,  March  20,  1863. 
Lieut.  Col.  Southard  Hoffman, 

Assistant  Adjutant- Oeneraly  Eighteenth  Army  Corps : 

Colonel  : Since  my  note  of  March  16  I have  deemed  it  prudent  to 
keep  the  lines  here  closed.  The  cavalry  have  made  daily  scouts  upon 
the  Jamestown  and  Greenville  roads,  and  we  have  gathered  only  this : 
That  it  seems  to  be  a general  impression  upon  the  minds  of  all  the  in- 
habitants, white  and  black,  outside  the  rebel  lines,  that  we  are  likely  to 
be  attacked  at  any  time,  and  that  the  enemy  have  considerable  forces 
in  motion  in  this  vicinity. 

Lieutenant-Colonel  Lyman  does  not  seem  to  think  there  is  much 
chance  of  an  attack ; still  I have  thought  best  to  make  every  preparation 
in  my  power,  and  we  will  try  to  give  them  a warm  reception  if  they  come. 

The  last  news  we  have  heard  of  the  enemy’s  movements  was  that 
Pryor’s  brigade  was  at  Greenville  on  Monday  and  that  Pettigrew’s 
brigade  was  between  Swift  Creek  and  Greenville  on  Tuesday,  moving 
slowly  up  toward  that  place,  stripping  the  country  of  provisions  of  every 
description. 

To-day  we  have  a report  of  the  supposed  presence  of  a force  (“right 
smart,”  be  that  large  or  small)  at  Tranter’s  Creek.  I will  venture  to 
suggest  that  if  you  have  any  reason  to  apprehend  any  immediate  attack 
here  a battery  of  artillery,  say  Belger’s,  and  a company  of  cavalry 
would  greatly  strengthen  the  defense.  The  rain  has  been  heavy  here 
to-day  and  yesterday,  which  it  is  thought  may  delay  their  attack  if  they 
still  contemplate  one. 

I am,  your  obedient  servant, 

FRANCIS  L.  LEE, 
Colonely  Commanding  Fost.

Hdqrs.  Forty-fourth  Regt.  Mass.  Vol.  Militia., 
Washington^  N,  0.,  March  23, 1863. 

ieutenant-Colonel  Hoffman, 

Assistant  Adjutant- General : 

Colonel  ; On  Saturday  Lieutenant-Colonel  Lyman  notified  me  that 
3 had  received  intelligence  from  what  he  considered  ‘^good  authority” 
lat  the  enemy  had  “ moved  away  from  our  front  ” ; that  a large  force 
as  10  miles  from  us  last  Monday,  but  had  disappeared. 

Of  course  that  may  or  may  not  be  correct,  but  I should  judge  by  all 
e can  learn  that  it  is  true.  Yesterday  Colonel  Lyman  learned  at  old 
r.  Griert’s  that  the  Army  of  the  Potomac,  under  Hooker,  had  crossed 
e Rappahannock;  but  we  can  get  no  papers,  as  the  rebels  allow  no 
le  to  pass  through  their  lines  and  no  mail  matter  to  pass  out. 

I would  remind  you  that  we  left  New  Berne  at  two, hours’  notice  and 
ith  no  idea  of  a longer  stay  than  ten  days’  rations  implied.  You  told 
e that  you  should  probably  send  a boat  up  to  bring  us  back  on  Sun- 
ly,  the  22d.  We  not  only  had  no  time  to  pack  up  our  property  which 
3 left  behind,  but  we  brought  nothing  but  a spare  under-suit  and  the 
3n  not  even  that,  as  they  were  ordered  to  take  only  blankets.  In 
is  condition  we  are  extremely  uncomfortable,  and  the  men  will  soon 
come  sick  on  account  of  unavoidable  filth.  I would  therefore  venture 
suggest  that  to  avoid  sickness  the  regiment  should  be  recalled  when- 
er  it  may  be  thought  that  this  place  is  safe  from  attack. 

I am,  your  obedient  servant, 

FRANCIS  L.  LEE, 

Colonel j Commanding  Post, 

I send  by  this  boat  the  men  detailed  for  the  census  business. 

LEE,

lajor-General  Dix: 


Suffolk,  Va.,  March  31,  1863. 


‘ Yesterday  the  enemy  came  over  to  the  vicinity  of  Carrsville  with  one 
r two  regiments  of  infantry  for  the  purpose  of  ambuscading  our  patroll- 
ig  parties.  They  were  secreted  in  woods  on  both  roads,  about  2 miles 
'iis  side  the  place.  Major  Cornog,  with  some  160  men,  was  on  his  way 
) Carrsville  to  return  by  the  Deserted  House.  His  advance  of  20  men, 
Oder  a lieutenant,  passed  the  center  of  the  lines,  when  the  enemy  show^ed 
lemselves ; singular  to  say,  all  escaped  save  one. 

' Our  cavalry  pickets  expected  an  attack  last  night,  but  all  passed  in 
uiet. 

JOHN  J.  PECK, 

Major- General. 


Headquarters  Fourth  Corps, 

Yorktoicn,  March  31,  1863. 
olonel  Lewis,  Commanding  at  Williamshurg : 

Let  me  hear  at  once  all  you  know  of  the  enemy’s  present  force  and 
58ition. 

In  case  of  an  attack  in  force  send  down  the  public  property.  Hold 
ort  Magruder  and  shell  the  town  the  moment  an  armed  enemy  is 
^lown  to  be  within  it. 

Let  me  hear  from  you  frequently  so  long  as  the  enemy  remains  in 
^ur  neighborhood. 

E.  D.  KEYES, 

Major-General.

and  that  place  is  estimated  at  something  more  than  20,000,  under  the 
command  of  Generals  D.  H.  Hill,  Pettigrew,  and  Garnett.  There  are 
roads  leading  into  the  route  from  here  to  Washington,  down  which  the 
enemy  can  pour  any  number  of  troops,  and  several  points  on  the  route 
are  fortified.  A great  portion  of  the  country  is  swamp  and  exceedingly 

difficult  to  get  over.  _ i o • i / i i 

111  a dispatch  received  this  morning  trom  General  Spinola  (who  has 
proved  himself,  I think,  an  officer  of  energy,  discretion,  and  good  judg- 
ment) he  informed  me  that  from  all  the  information  he  can  get  he  con- 
cludes it  impossible  to  force  his  way  through  to  Washington  without 
first  taking  the  battery  at  Hill’s  Point,  and  he  proposes  to  try  that  to- 
day. A success  will  place  him  in  a better  position,  as  he  can  then 
communicate  with  the  gunboats  on  the  river.  Should  he  not  liave 
sufficient  force,  however,  to  take  that  position  he  will  return  here  if  he 
can.  I have  not  given  him  orders  to  that  effect,  as  I have  only  directed 
him*  to  carry  out"  the  instructions  of  General  Poster  to  tbe  letter,  if 
possible.  Hew  Berne,  which  should  be  held  at  all  hazards,  is  threat- 
ened, and  I have  scarcely  3,000  men  here. 

There  is  no  general  officer  with  me,  and  the  troops  are  mostly  new— 

nine-months’  men.  i 

Of  General  Poster’s  policy  in  abandoning  everything  to  the  saving  ot 
Washington  1 have  nothing  to  say,  except  that  it  meets  with  no  favor 
from  the  military  and  naval  officers  who  consider  themselves  privileged 
to  speak  of  the  matter.  I obey  General  Poster’s  orders  implicitly,  trust- 
ing to  holding  this  place.  _ 1 

Should  the  forces  now  en  route  get  to  Washington  they  will  be  there 
without  supplies.  It  will  take  a large  army  to  keep  the  road  between 
that  place  and  this.  The  river  is  lined  with  batteries,  and  the  senior 
naval  officer  at  the  lower  batteries,  who  has  some  of  the  finest  gunboats 
iu  these  waters  under  his  control,  informed  me  that  he  can  make  no  im- 
pression on  them.  n • 1 1 • 1 

I informed  General  Hix  of  the  condition  of  affairs  here  by  a siiecial 
messenger,  requesting  a re-enforcement.  I have  only  heard  by  the  re- 
turn of  the  officer  sent  that  we  could  expect  no  re-enforcements  here 
from  the  Army  of  Virginia,  as  they  are  now  fully  occupied  there. 

Admiral  Lee  has  sent  a small  re-enforcement  of  gunboats,  winch  iii 
the  absence  of  the  troops  make  this  place,  of  course,  more  secure. 

I am,  general,  very  respectfully,  your

Commanding  Forces,  New  Berne  : 

General  : Your  dispatches  arrived  this  morning  at  2 a.  m.  by  the 
hands  of  Lieutenant-Colonel  McOhesney,  who  will  return  to-night. 

I am  directed  by  the  major-general  commanding  to  say  that  he  could 
have  wished  that  you  had  yourself  come  in  command  of  the  forces  which 
moved  yesterday  from  New  Berne  under  General  Spinola,  notwith- 
standing the  confidence  you  express  in  his  activity  and  intelligence. 

If  General  Wessells  has  arrived  General  Foster  wishes  you  to  take 
command  in  person  of  the  advancing  forces.  Should  General  Naglee 
arrive  he  will  be  sent  forward  at  once  to  take  command. 

In  case  you  are  not  sufficiently  strong  at  New  Berne  you  will  send: 
for  tlie  regiment  at  Plymouth,  leaving  at  that  post  three  companies 
with  three  pieces  of  artillery  as  garrison  for  the  fort  if  it  be  suflaciently 

completed.  , ...  . , 

The  general  wishes  that  a light-draught  steamer,  with  her  sides  pro- 
tected by  hay-bales,  should  be  sent  here  at  once  loaded  with  ammiini 
tion  and  provisions.  Send  also  several  schooners  of  light  draught,  pro 

tected  and  loaded  in  the  same  way.  , 

The  enemy  have  opened  fire  to-day  from  five  batteries  on  the  crest 
of  the  rising  ground  in  rear  of  town.  Their  fire  for  a short  time  was 
very  sharp,  but  no  damage  has  yet  been  done.  , . , , . ^ 

The  general  expects,  even  if  the  expedition  which  has  started  b( 
successful,  that  you  will  continue  to  make  persistent  efforts  to  send  £ 
force  across  to  our  relief. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

^ EDWARD  E.  POTTER,

General-in-  Chief: 

The  enemy  approached  our  lines  at  Suffolk  to-day  and  exchanged 
some  cannon-shots  and  retired.  The  force  of  the  enemy  is  great  and  1 
think  they  will  make  a serious  attack.  General  Peck  has  just  tele- 
graphed that  he  has  reason  to  believe  Longstreet  is  receiving  re-enforce-

The  proximity  of  the  Confederate  forces  renders  it  proper,  by  virtue 
of  the  military  and  naval  authority  of  the  United  States,  to  give  the 
following  notice : 

All  foreign  consuls  and  their  families,  all  women  and  children,  and 
all  other  persons  not  in  the  service  of  the  United  States  who  prefer 
safety  to  the  conflicts  of  war,  are  notified  that  on  the  approach  of  the 
enemy  to  any  town  or  village  within  this  department  and  the  range  of 
the  Union  guns,  such  town  or  .village  will  be  fired  on  without  further 
consideration.

Via  Fort  Monroe,  Ya.,  April  13, 1863. 

(Eeceived  2.50  p.  m.) 

Maj.  Gen.  H.  W.  Halleck, 

General  in-  Chief: 

I am  now  in  consultation  with  Major-General  Peck.  The  enemy  is  in 
sight,  and  not  far  off.  Artillery  firing  is  going  on  slowly.  Peekes  po- 
sition is  strong,  and  will  be  vigilantly  guarded.  The  only  fear  is  that 
the  enemy  mayoress  the  Nansemond.  To  prevent  that,  gunboats  must 
be  freely  used.  I will  try  to  examine  the  riv^er  to-day.  It  is  my  opinion 
that  the  enemy^s  campaign  is  the  recovery  of  the  whole  James  Biver, 
and  re-enforcements  are  arriving  from  various  points,  many  of  them 
from  before  Fredericksburg.  The  enemy’s  batteries  have  been  open  for 
some  time.  It  is  an  imperative  necessity  that  the  Navy  keep  the  Nanse- 
mond Biver  open. 


E.  D.  KEYES, 

Major-General,

Suffolk,  Va.,  April  13, 1863—5  p.  m. 

(Eeceived  6 p.  m.) 

Maj.  Gen.  H.  W.  Halleck, 

General-in-  Chief : 

I have  now  completed  a thorough  examination  of  Major-General 
Peck’s  position  except  the  river,  which  I am  now  going  to  examine  to 
its  mouth.  I have  been  up  and  down  both  railroads  to  Norfolk  and 
made  the  circuit  of  the  lines.  From  every  source  it  is  made  certain 
that  upward  of  40,000  rebels  are  in  front  and  on  the  flanks  of  this  posi- 
tion. The  easiest  way  for  the  enemy  to  take  it  is  to  invest  and  starve 
us  out.  To  prevent  that  I shall  be  able  to  give  an  opinion  after  going 
down  the  river.  As  most  of  the  enemy  are  from  the  Eappahannock 
my  present  impression  is  that  two  divisions  of  Major-General  Hooker’s 
army  ought  to  be  sent  here  at  once. 


E.  H.  KEYES, 
Major-General^  Commanding, 


Fort  Monroe,  Va.,  April  13, 1863—11  p.  m. 

(Eeceived  14th,  12.10  a.  m.) 

Maj.  Gen.  H.  W.  Halleck, 

General-in-  Chief: 

I have  this  moment  returned  from  an  examination  of  the  Nansemond 
Eiver.  The  enemy’s  sharpshooters  line  the  left  bank  some  distance 
down  and  all  the  passing  steamers  have  been  pelted  to-day.  Our  pilot- 
house was  struck  seven  times.  The  gunboats  on  that  river  are  frail, 
wooden  structures,  which  the  enemy’s  fleld  batteries  can  soon  cripple  or 
burn  with  hot  shot.  He  can  then  without  much  exertion  cross  out  of 
range  of  any  of  our  works,  get  upon  Peck’s  rear,  and  seize  the  two  rail- 
roads, or  attack  his  weakest  side,  which  is  from  the  Seaboard  Eailroad 
to  the  river,  and  along  the  river  when  the  gunboats  are  out  of  the  way. 
Once  invested,  it  will  be  next  to  impossible  to  relieve  Peck,  and  he 
would  in  a short  time  be  starved  into  a surrender.  The  problem  is  a 
difficult  one  and  requires  the  most  able  attention.  Pickett’s,  Hood’s, 
and  Pryor’s  (now  Davis’)  divisions  are  there.  Pickett’s  left  the  Eappa- 
hannock February  15  and  Hood’s  shortly  after.  The  Southern  Army 
is  in  fine  health — soldiers  made  by  poverty  and  hardships — and  is  per- 
fectly armed.  They  have  about  fifty  pieces  of  artillery  and  some  cav- 
alry. All  or  nearly  all  the  horses  are  in  poor  condition.  Coming  down 
the  river  has  increased,  but  not  perfected,  my  knowledge  of  Peck’s  sib 
nation.  I will  need  to  observe  it  still  more  to-morrow.  I will  write 
more  fully. 

E.  D.  KEYES, 
Major-General^  Commanding,

ericksburg, the  condition  of  the  roads  rendering  an  attack  there  impos-

Fort  Monroe,  Va., 

Halleck, 

General-in-  Chief: 


April  13, 1863—8.30  p.  m. 

(Received  10  p.  m.) 


Longstreet’s  advance  division  arrived  in  my  front  on  Saturday  and 
was  followed  by  Pickett’s,  Hood’s,  and  Anderson’s  yesterday.  They 
advanced  on  my  front  and  right  flank  about  noon  on  the  12th,  within 
extreme  artillery  range,  and  after  much  skirmishing  fell  back  several 
miles.  Early  this  morning  they  advanced  on  my  front  and  rear  with 
one  division  on  the  right  flank.  More  or  less  artillery  Are  all  day  and 
much  skirmishing.  Colonel  Foster’s  Light  Troop  handled  the  enemy’s 
advance  roughly,  driving  them  back  and  retiring  the  picket  line  at  dark. 
Anderson’s  division  has  been  engaged  on  the  waterfront  with  our  gun- 
boats and  batteries.  The  firing  has  been  brisk,  and  the  enemy  suffered. 
The  command  is  in  good  spirits  and  will  do  its  duty. 


JOHN  J.  PECK, 

Major-General,

Suffolk,  Va.,  April  14, 1863 — 2.30  p.  m. 


Maj.  Gen.  H.  W.  Halleck, 

General-in-  Chief : 


I arrived  here  this  morning.  The  post  is  closely  invested  with  ovei 
30,000  men.  The  report  of  the  1st  instant,  in  the  Adjutant- General 
Office,  will  show  our  force.  Two  gunboats  in  the  Nansemond  are  dis 
abled : one  is  sunk.  Our  danger  is  that  the  enemy  will  cross  the  rivei 
and  cut  us  off  from  Norfolk.  I consider  it  necessary  that  an  army  corps 
or  at  least  two  divisions,  should  be  sent  to  Norfolk  at  once,  so  as  to  pro 
tect  the  Nansemond.  The  great  superiority  of  the  enemy  makes  it  im 
possible  to  divide  the  force  here  with  safety,*  and  we  cannot  retreat  on 
Norfolk  without  great  sacrifice  of  property  and  life.  This  place  mus 


be  held  if  possible. 


JOHN  A.  DIX, 


Major-General*

Headquarters  Fourth  Army  Corps, 

YorMoicn,  Va..  April  14,  1863. 

Maj.  Gen.  H.  W.  Halleck, 

Commanding  U.  S.  Army  : 

Sir  : Major-General  Dix  arrived  this  morning  and  resumed  command 
of  tlie  Department  of  Virginia. 

During  the  nine  days  I was  in  temporary  command  of  the  depart- 
j ment  the  approach  of  the  enemy  in  great  force  down  the  Peninsula  and 
upon  Suffolk  gave  a serious  aspect  to  affairs,  and  this  paper  is  respect- 
fully submitted  as  the  result  of  my  examinations  and  consequent  con- 
clusions while  I was  in  command. 

Of  Peekes  position  and  the  surrounding  country  beyond  Norfolk  I 
had  no  ocular  knowledge  until  the  6th  instant,  when  I made  a hasty 
visit  to  Suffolk  by  rail.  Since  that  date  I have  made  a careful  exami- 
uation  of  his  defenses  and  passed  over  the  other  railroad  from  Norfolk 
and  down  the  Nansemond  Eiver  to  Hampton  Eoads. 

As  I stated  before  in  telegrams  I consider  our  troops  at  Suffolk  in  a 
very  critical  situation,  and  it  may  be  the  rebels^  boast  that  they  have 
another  HarpePs  Ferry  affair  on  hand  will  be  made  good, 
j I have  reflected  on  the  following  points  : 

I 1st.  Is  Peck  secure  against  an  attack,  or  is  he  able  to  resist  an  attack 
I in  his  position  ? 

I 2d.  Can  the  enemy  cut  his  communication  and  invest  him  ? 
i 3d.  If  the  enemy  should  invest  him  have  we  the  means  to  relieve 

1 him  before  he  would  be  starved  out? 

4th.  Can  he  retreat  and  take  away  his  material  ? 

; On  the  above  points  I conclude  as  follows : 

1st.  He  is  secure  against  an  attack  on  any  front  now  accessible  to  the 
enemy,  and  he  will  not  be  seriously  attacked  (feints  will  be  made)  until 
ilie  is  invested.  After  he  is  invested  he  is  not  secure  from  an  attack, 
f 2d.  The  enemy  can  cut  his  communications  and  invest  him  in  spite 
jif  anything  we  can  do  to  prevent  him  with  the  means  north  of  Albe- 
laiarle  Sound  and  south  of  Hampton  Eoads  and  James  Eiver. 

2 3d.  If  the  enemy  does  invest  him  we  could  not  break  the  investment 
ffter  it  had  existed  three  days  and  relieve  Peck  with  any  available 
neans  within  the  command  of  the  Government. 

4th.  I cannot  give  a positive  opinion  on  this  point.  I have  had  no 
ime  to  examine  the  line  of  retreat.  The  railroads  are  through  the  Dis- 
iial  Swamp  and  are  perfectly  straight  and  the  roadway  narrow,  and 
)u  either  side,  an  impracticable  morass.  ’ 

I assume  that  the  Government  knows  Peck’s  strength  and  the  amount 
>f  his  supplies  of  provisions  and  ammunition.  It  is  certain  he  has  but 
I few  days’  supply  of  forage. 

, I have  assumed  all  those  facts  of  the  last  paragraph,  and  I have  kept 
Napoleon’s  maxims  in  view  (you  called  my  attention  to  those  maxims) 
u coming  to  my  conclusions. 

In  regard  to  the  Peninsula : If  the  line  of  Fort  Magruder  below  Will- 
amsburg  is  given  up  the  enemy  can  go  to  Fort  Monroe  at  once  and 
mssess  everything  outside  the  sand-spit  on  which  the  fort  stands, 
orktown,  owing  to  the  ravines  around  it,  would  be  nearly  as  uncom- 
ortable  as  Fort  Magruder  now  is,  and  of  no  great  value  to  the  Govern - 
Qent.  If  the  upper  line  is  abandoned  I trust  this  most  sickly  place 
, Aorktown)  may  be  also  abandoned.  I recommended  its  abandonment 
a Allgust  last  when  called  on  for  my  views. 

, With  one  gunboat  on  James  Eiver,  stationed  opposite  Williamsburg,

Suffolk,  Ya.,  April  15, 1863 — 9 a.  m. 


Maj.  Gen.  H.  W.  Halleck, 

General-in-  Chief : 

On  Monday,  with  the  aid  of  the  gunboats,  I was  enabled  to  hold  the 
line  of  the  Nansemond,  and  things  looked  well,  as  I advised  you,  buti 
yesterday  10,000  or  11,000  attacked  the  line  of  the  river  some  miles 
down,  and,  with  the  aid  of  earthworks  thrown  up,  cut  off  the  water 
communication.  All  the  gunboats  except  one  were  crippled  and  cut 
off  many  miles  below.  The  enemy  attempted  to  cross  during  the  night; 
but  has  not  succeeded  yet.  I hope  to  hold  him,  although  the  river,  by 
the  curves,  is  some  12  miles  in  length  before  you  reach  the  wide  water, 
with  an  average  width  of  100  feet.  At  daylight  I opened  the  Jericho 
Canal  into  the  river  and  hope  to  fill  up  the  marshes  so  as  to  impede 
their  operations.  A few  troops  at  this  time  will  make  all  secure.  A 
large  force  in  reserve  is  necessary,  say  10,000,  to  take  the  initiative.  li 
General  Hill  co-operates,  more  will  be  necessary.  Prisoners  state 
Washington  has  been  taken.  ^ 

Major-General
