7 a signal  officer)  safely  at  the  wharf  in  Washington  yesterday.

y,  Macon,  and  the  railroad.  This,  I think,  is  only  to  prevent 
sending  too  many  of  our  forces  from  here  toward  Washington. 
weutenant-Oommander  Flusser,  a bold,  energetic  naval  officer,  has

Suffolk,  Ya.,  April  16,  1863—9.30  a.  m. 
Major-General  Halleok,  General-in- Chief : 

My  lines,  which  extend  along  the  Nansemond  from  mouth  of  West 
Branch  to  swamp  on  the  left,  are  occupied,  and  are  about  16  miles  in 
eagth.  The  enemy  has  failed  to  turn  either  flank  and  has  not  dared 
in  assault.  Longstreet  is  resolved  upon  getting  in  if  possible.  He  is 
cutting  out  extensive  roads,  destroyed  and  blocked.  Parties  were 
lent  to  blow  up  culverts,  but  failed.  My  roads  are  well  guarded.  If 
hold  my  flanks,  he  will  be  compelled  to  assault  after  shelling  from 
nmmanding  ^ound.  He  has  a great  preponderance  of  artillery  as 
v^ell  as  other  branches. 

JOHH  J.  PECK, 

Major-General.

Fort  Washington,  N.  C.,  April  12, 1863. 

Maj.  Gen.  H.  W.  Halleck: 

General:  I have  the  honor  to  report  that  no  very  material  change  in  the  position 
of  opposing  forces  around  this  town  has  taken  place  since  the  date  of  my  letter  of  the 
5th  instant.  The  enemy  has  been  constantly  at  work  erecting  batteries,  and  now  has 
in  full  operation  six  batteries,  mounting  seven  guns,  on  this  side  of  the  river,  north 
side  of  the  town,  and  three  batteries,  mounting  six  gnns,  on  the  south  side  of  the 
river  opposite  the  town.  Added  to  these  are  the  batteries  erected  to  prevent  boatt 
coming  up  the  river,  some  miles  down.  The  guns  are,  however,  mostly  rifled,  ot 
small  caliber,  none  being  larger  than  20-pounder  Parrotts,  except  one  32-ponndei 
smooth-bore.  The  works  of  the  defensive  have  kept  pace  with  the  offensive,  being 
always  a little  ahead,  and  the  result  of  each  day’s  firing  has  been  the  silencing  of  the 
enemy’s  batteries,  forcing  them  to  withdraw  their  guns  from  sight.  The  firing  on 
both  sides  is  quite  sharp  for  a short  time  each  day.  No  killed  or  wounded  since  ni\ 
last  letter.  The  force  that  I directed  to  march  for  my  relief  from  New  Berne  has  nol 
as  yet  exhibited  any  result.  General  Palmer  reports  that  the  advance  guard  letl 
New  Berne  on  Wednesday  under  General  Spinola.  The  latter  general  was  under  tli6 
impression  that  the  whole  force  in  his  front  was  16,000  men,  double  his  own  torce.  J 
have  therefore  to  renew  my  application  for  re-enforcements,  and  that  the  number  of 
increased  to  10,000  men;  also  for  General  Naglee,  who  has  been  ordered  to  report  tf 
me.  He  hurried  off  as  soon  as  possible  to  take  command  of  the  operating  force.  i 
am’ confident  that  I can  hold  out  here  provided  I am  supplied  with  ammunition  ant 
provisions  from  below.  There  is  no  great  difficulty  in  supplying  us  by  means  of  ves 
sels  and  boats  running  the  gauntlet  of  the  batteries;  and  although  the  gunboats  ape 
our  transports  have  not  as  yet  fulfilled  our  expectations  in  this  respect,  yet  I am  in 
formed  by  General  Palmer  that  arrangements  are  now  made  to  send  me  supplies  o. 
men  and  ammunition.  I do  not  intend  to  yield  one  inch  on  any  point  if  I can  in  an> 
wav  prevent  it,  and  shall  therefore  contest  the  occupation  of  this  place  until  Genera. 
Hill  is  forced  to  withdraw.  I beg  that  you  will  look  favorably  upon  my  apphcatioi 
for  re-enforcements,  unless  the  necessities  of  the  service  forbid  it,  for  without  tnen 
some  disaster  to  our  arms  may  occur  in  this  department.  The  enemy’s  numbers  an 
fully  equal  to  the  representations  in  my  letters  of  last  month,  and  from  their  move, 
ments  I am  confirmed  in  my  opinion  that  as  soon  as  the  main  army  is  mreod  to  eyac 
uate  Virginia  the  field  of  operations  will  be  this  State;  hence  their  efforts  to  ootan 
possession  of  the  eastern  counties,  which  are  the  most  fertile  in  the  State. 

^ J.  G.  FOSTER, 

Major-General,  Commanding. 

JOHN  A.  DIX,

eral  Wise  and  the  consequent  abandoument  of  the  city  by  the  Union

Off  Weicport  Weivs,  Va.^  April  17,  1863. 

Major-General  Foster, 

Commanding  Military  Department  of  North  Carolina : 

My  Dear  General:  I am  glad  to  hear  by  the  steamer  Spaulding 
that  you  are  at  New  Berne.  The  experience  attending  your  escape 
will  give  you  a practical  idea  of  the  difference  between  the  endurance 
and  capabilities  of  frail,  improvised  wooden  gunboats  and  earthworks. 
I saw  in  the  papers  that  a brigade  hesitated  to  land  and  attack,  but 
waited  for  the  little  Lockwood  to  silence  a battery  of  field  artillery  oc- 
cupying earthworks  which  the  enemy  had  abandoned  last  spring. 

I mention  this  now  that  you  are  in  less  trouble,  as  in  your  private 
letter  from  Washington  you  speak  of  the  gunboats  as  having  too  much 
veneration  for  such  batteries.  The  Army  places  a complimentary  but 
exaggerated  opinion  upon  the  capabilities^  of  these  gunboats. 

In  the  Mississippi  a scattered  battery *of  six  small  field  pieces  did 
great  damage  to  two  regular  Navy  gunboats  commanded  by  gallant 
officers.  Here,  at  this  time,  on  the  narrow  Upper  Nansemond,  a miser- 
able creek,  our  frail,  light-armed,  light-draught  steam-cmft,  called  gun- 
boats, with  their  powder  and  steam  magazines  and  their  machinery  nil 
so  exposed  and  so  vulnerable,  are  fighting  the  enemy’s  artillery  and 
sharpshooters  with  great  gallantry  and  sustaining  much  loss  in  killed, 
wounded,  and  injury  to  the  vessels,  which  are  much  cut  up,  grounding, 
and  having  no  water  to  work  in. 

The  combat  would  be  much  more  equal  if  our  troops  fought  theirS; 
with  like  means,  as  they  should  do,  but  somehow  they  don’t  see  it. 

The  calls  so  numerous  and  so  constant  for  gunboats  to  defend  urniy 
posts  are  distressing,  because  so  earnest  and  so  much  bejmnd  my  means 
to  supply. 

This  important  point  (Newport  News),  upon  the  i)reservation  of  which 
the  public  interests  in  this  quarter,  the  seat  of  Government,  and  even 
the  communications  of  the  Army  of  the  Potomac  depend,  is  weakened 
in  its  movable  force  to  assist  the  army  in  its  occupation  of  its  many 
detached  and  assailable  positions  in  the  Sounds  and  here  j but  I will 
write  you  a brief  official  letter  on  this  subject. 

As  i have  before  proposed  to  you,  these  detached  and  weak  positions’ 
should  be  abandoned  and  our  forces  concentrated,  then  Ave  can  attack 
instead  of  being  attacked  in  detail.  This  concentration  cannot  be  ef- 
fected as  respects  the  naval  force  until  it  is  done  by  the  army,  as  the 
gunboats  are  required  at  the  principal  positions  occupied  by  the  army. 
Therefore  the  change  depends  upon  you  there  and  General  Dix  here.

;Wo  armed  steamers  are  to  remain  there.  I know  that  there  is  danger 
bat  they  will  be  fired  into,  injured,  perhaps  crippled;  but  this  hazard 
bust  be  incurred  to  prevent  the  rebels  from  crossing.  Yours  will  be 
exposed  to  no  more  danger  than  mine.  The  position  of  the  captured 
)attery,  though  a commanding  one,  gives  us  no  security  against  the 
Tossing  of  the  enemy  except  at  that  point.  It  would  have  been  no 
)bstacle  to  his  crossing  1,  2,  3,  4,  5,  or  6 miles  above,  and  the  troops  we 
nust  have  kept  there  to  hold  it  would  have  been  much  more  useful  on 
he  right  bank  of  the  river  as  a movable  force  to  oppose  him  whenever 
le  should  have  made  an  attemptto  cross.  Besides,  its  occupation  would 
lot  have  removed  your  objections  to  the  employment  of  your  gunboats 
u the  narrow  channel  above.  What  we  want  is  to  have  two  or  three 
puiboats  moving  up  and  down  the  Upper  Kansemond  for  several  miles 
0 watch  the  enemy’s  movements  and  to  aid  in  destroying  his  pontoon 
iriclge  if  he  should  attempt  to  throw  one  across  the  river.

ueutenants  Lamson  and  Cushing  (who  have  displayed  so  much  gal- 
autry)  discretionavv  power,  so  that  they  may  go  up  the  Upper  Kanse- 
uond  when  they  think  it  safe,  and  permit  them  to  act  in  conjunction

]d  I felt  assured  that  I could  get  them  to  him  by  the  way  of  the 
ver  while  the  demonstration  was  being  made  by  land.  I had  deter- 
ined  that  if  any  officer  should  arrive  to  take  command  of  New  Berne 
would  take  a steamer  loaded  with  men  and  supplies  and  go  to  the 
ockade  and  see  them  through.  General  Wessells  arrived  here  on  the 
jh  and  I left  with  the  Escort  on  the  next  day.  The  delay  in  getting 
ds  steamer  through  the  blockade  was  by  no  means  unavoidable,  but 
was  a delay  for  which  I was  in  no  way  responsible.  Three  times  the 
earner  was  ready  to  move  and  she  was  stopped.  The  first  time  on  the 
^ening  of  my  arrival  at  the  blockade  by  the  refusal  of  Lieutenant-Oom- 
ander  McCann  (the  senior  naval  officer  there)  to  assist,  at  night ; the 
cond  time,  on  the  next  morning,  by  the  fog,  which  was  so  dense  on  the 
^er  that  nothing  could  be  seen  at  the  proposed  hour  of  starting ; and 
e third  time,  the  next  night,  by  the  mist  and  rain,  that  prevented  any 
ovement  on  the  river. 

The  safe  arrival  eventually  of  the  steamer  at  Washington  accom- 
ished,  I was  satisfied,  more  than  could  have  been  attained  in  any  other 
ay,  and  I was  satisfied  that  my  judgment  was  correct  and  that  I had 
ted  wisely  in  the  matter. 

With  regard  to  the  third  interrogatory — 

Was  the  question  ever  raised  in  any  consultation  or  council  of  commanding  officers 
to  my  authority  to  give  orders  for  movement  of  troops;  if  so,  when,  by  whom,  and 
der  what  circumstances  ? — 

wWl  state  that  I never  presumed  to  call  any  council  or  consultation 
officers”  to  discuss  plain  orders  sent  to  me  by  the  commanding  gen- 
al.  His  orders  issued  from  Washington  were  just  as  much  obeyed 
d respected  by  me  as  they  would  have  been  had  they  been  issued  from 
is  place. 

It  is  true,  however,  that  I was  an  unwilling  listener  to  several  private 
nversationsjn  which  the  “propriety”  of  sending  too  many  troops 
^ay  from  this  place,  or  the  “policy”  of  abandoning  everything  to  the 
ving  of  Washington,  was  spoken  of,  and  doubts  expressed  as  to  who 
kler  the  circumstances  was  in  command  of  the  department.  I took  no 
rt  in  any  such  discussions  any  more  than  to  inform  every  person  that 
e orders  of  the  commanding  general  would  be  obeyed,  even  if  they 
3re  to  abandon  New  Berne  and  everything  in  it. 

I am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

I.  N.  PALMER, 
Brigadier- General,

The  history  of  the  occupation  of  Washington  and  Plymouth  is  tha 
they  were  first  held  by  gunboats  lying  opposite  the  towns.  Afterwar 
a picket  guard  of  one  company  was  sent  to  each  place,  as  a picket  guar 
for  the  gunboats  on  shore.  This  guard  was  afterward  increased  a 
demanded  by  circumstances  and  the  necessities  of  service.  Finally  tb 
importance  of  occupying  the  posts  permanently  was  seen  and  reco[ 
nized,  and  works  were  erected  for  this  purpose.  Some  of  the  reasor 
which  led  to  this  determination  were  as  follows : 

1st.  By  not  occupying  these  points — New  Berne,  Washington,  an 
Plymouth — we  permit  their  occupation  by  the  enemy  and  their  use  b 
them  as  yards  and  arsenals  in  which  to  prepare  rams  and  gunboats  t 
operate  against  our  gunboats  in  tbe  Sounds. 

2d.  To  permit  egress  of  any  lighter-draught  gunboat  that  may  I 
built  in  the  rivers  above;  and,  in  fine,  gives  our  gunboats  the  control  < 
those  rivers  for  ofiensive  operations  by  water. 

3d.  These  towns  afford  excellent  landing  places,  at  which  our  force 
could  be  quickly  and  safely  concentrated  for  offensive  operations  b 
land,  having  the  towns  as  bases.  This  advantage  is  the  more  sensibl 
felt  when  any  one  town  is  besieged. 

4th.  These  three  strategical  points  retain  within  their  power  all  tl 
counties  to  the  east  of  them,  which  is  a matter  of  some  importance,  t 
they  are  the  most  fertile  in  corn,  &c.,  of  any  in  the  State,  and  are  s 
considered  by  the  Confederate  Government,  as  shown  by  the  efforts  > 
General  Hill  to  repossess  them. 

In  conclusion,  I am  strongly  of  the  opinion  that  as  longps  I am  stror 
enough  to  hold  these  points  I should  do  so,  and  further  think  that  if  tl 
exigency  should  compel  me  to  abandon  either  that  it  would  be  a lo 
advantage,  inasmuch  as  by  holding  the  three  I can  operate  more  effec 

ively  with force  than  I could  with  the  same  force  concentrate 

at  one  or  two  of  them,  and  the  others  held  by  the  enemy. 

In  a naval  point  of  view  I of  course  yield  and  defer  to  your  Jiul 
ment,  but  it  is  my  conviction  that  were  either  of  these  points  held  1. 
the  euemj^,  a larger,  not  a smaller,  naval  force  would  be  necessary 
hold  the  Sounds,  irresi)ective  of  river  navigation  and  the  convoying 


vessels.  . .. 

These  views  are  sent  to  you  in,  I assure  you,  the  most  friendly  spir 
and  in  accordance  with  the  harmony  which  has  always  existed  betwej 
our  two  arms  of  the  service,  and  merely  that  by  exchanging  ideas  tJ 
result  most  to  the  interests  of  the  service  may  be  arrived  at. 

I have  the  honor  to  be,  admiral,  very  respectfully,  your  obedie

ister  to  the  enemy.  Our  great  error  has  been  in  occupying  too  many 
)Ositions.  There  was  an  excuse  for  scattering  our  forces  while  there 
vras  reason  to  believe  that  the  people  of  the  South  would  rally  around 
hem  as  nucleus  for  the  restoration  of  the  Union.  This  hope  is  now  gone, 
lud  as  our  only  chance  of  success  is  by  overpowering  them  by  prepon- 
lerance  of  force  or  wearing  them  out  by  cutting  off  their  commerce  with 
joreign  countries,  all  interior  positions,  unless  they  have  some  special

^aj.  Gen.  John  A.  Dix, 

Commanding  Department  of  Virginia : 

My  Dear  General  : I have  received  your  letter  of  the  24th,  and  in 
■ccordance  with  your  request  am  now  starting  as  strong  force  as  I can 
pare  to  make  an  attack  on  D.  H.  Hill,  at  Kinston. 


656 


NORTH  CAROLINA  AND  S.  E.  VIRGINIA. 


[Chap.  XXX. ; 


I shall  continue  this  demonstration  for  four  or  five  days,  and  if  in 
the  mean  time  you  do  not  defeat  Longstreet  I will  make  a new  demon- 
stration in  another  direction. 

Please  keep  me  constantly  advised  of  what  you  wish,  and  i will  aid 
you  to  the  extent  of  my  power. . If  I only  had  my  troops  back  from 
South  Carolina  I should  be  able  to  make  such  an  attack  up  the  Eoan-i 
oke  Kiver  as  would  make  Longstreet  retire  or  leave  Weldon.  I was 
half  tempted  to  run  up  to  Suffolk  and  look  at  your  defenses.  If  they 
are  properly  constructed  and  well  laid  out  General  Peck  ought  to  be 
able  to  hold  out  against  five  times  his  number.  At  W ashington  we  were 
unassailable  (after  the  first  day)  with  ten  times  our  number  around  us. 

Our  outposts  taunted  the  rebels  with  the  inquiry  why  they  did  not 
come  in  and  take  Little  Washington. 

Egotism  apart,  however,  every  line  of  defenses  should  have  at  about 
800  yards  (dependent  upon  the  natural  features  of  the  ground)  a self 
sustaining  work,  perfectly  inclosed,  which  cannot  be  taken  even  if  the 
enemy  penetrated  the  lines  on  the  right  or  left.  These  works  should  bel 
able  to  fire  even  to  the  rear.  Each  of  these  works  should  be  mounted 
with  heavy  guns  (long  32-pounders,  firing  shell,  are  very  good)  am 
completelv  manned.  The  garrisons  should  be  instructed  to  hold  theii 
works  to  the  last  extremity,  and  made  to  feel  their  entire  independence 
of  any  mishaps  to  other  portions  of  the  line. 

These  works  should  be  of  a strong  profile,  with  a wide  and  deep  ditcl 
without,  and  a palisade  in  the  middle  of  the  ditch  or  a good  abatis 
in  front  of  it.  Between  these  works  should  extend  a line  of  intantn 
intrenchments,  with  a good  ditch  and  parapet  flanked  by  the  fires  of  tin 

strong  works.  ...  , 

If  there  be  time,  the  infantry  intrenchments  (along  which  embrasure: 
for  light  field  pieces  may  be  roughly  made)  may  be  supplied  with  loop 
holes  for  infantry,  formed  of  rods  and  high  enough  to  protect  the  head 
of  those  firing.  If  you  have  any  timber  send  me,  and  at  once,  and 

will  do  all  that  I can.  , . \ i.  i n 

My  advance  toward  Kinston  are  already  in  front  of  the  rebels  at  Lor. 

Creek,  and  will  engage  them  to-morrow. 

Ever  yours,  most  truly,  j.  G.  EOSTEE, 

Major  General^  Commanding.

.'riday,  consists  of  five  regiments.  One  of  my  spies,  who  arrived  last

Cwo  thousand  troops,  who  were  there  a fortnight  ago,  have  come  to 
kffolk.  The  Navy  could  easily  have  prevented  the  enemy  from  in- 
renching  at  Port  Powhatan.  Everything  indicates  that  the  movement 
>n  Suffolk  is  a campaign  and  looks  to  Norfolk.  The  gauge  of  the  rail- 
oad  from  Petersburg  to  the  Blackwater  has  been  altered  to  correspond 
vith  ours  this  side.  If  you  can  spare  a few  thousand  more  troops  they 
vill  no  doubt  be  needed,  and  can  be  sent  back  the  moment  the  exigency 
s over.  The  extent  of  our  river  line  absorbs  a large  number.  The 
memy  has  cut  a broad  road  down  to  the  river,  and  indicates  a deter- 
aination  to  cross.

b the  mouth  of  Cape  Fear  Eiver.  It  is  said  that  by  the  occupation  of 
lis  island  both  channels  may  be  closed,  and  thus  prevent  the  entrance 
f contraband  goods  to  Wilmington. 

I informed  Mr.  Fox  that  no  additional  forces  could  be  given  to  you 
b the  present  time,  but  that  possibly  you  might  accomplish  this  object, 
liich  he  deems  most  important.  He  says  that  at  this  season,  while  the 
ater  is  smooth,  there  will  be  no  difficulty  in  landing.

ossible  should  be  used  in  fortifying  and  holding  the  position.  I un-

665 


States,  with  everything  necessary  to  their  comfort  and  with  the  remedial 
treatment  they  require.  While  exercising  these  offices  of  humanity  the 
troops  at  Williamsburg  have  been  several  times  attacked  by  your  forces, 
not  with  a view  to  gain  and  hold  possession  of  the  place  and  to  assume 
the  guardianship  which  has  been  extended  to  the  inhabitants  and  the 
tenants  of  the  asylum  by  us,  but  for  the  purpose  of  harassing  those  who 
were  performing  this  generous  service.  On  the  31st  ultimo  your  forces 
entered  and  endeavored  to  take  possession  of  the  town,  occupying  sev- 
eral houses  and  firing  upon  the  troops,  and  in  this,  as  I am  informed, 
they  were  aided  by  some  of  the  inhabitants,  who  have  been  living  for 
nearly  a year  under  our  protection.  More  recently  your  forces  entered 
the  town  and  took  possession  of  it,  placing  our  employes  in  the  insane 
asylum  under  parole,  carrying  off  some  of  the  servants,  and  depriving  its 
inmates  of  the  care  to  which  they  have  been  accustomed  and  which  their 
helpless  condition  renders  indispensable.  You  have  by  withdrawing 
your  forces  left  the  asylum  again  to  our  charity  and  compelled  Major- 
General  Keyes,  the  commanding  officer  of  the  troops  at  Yorktown  and 
Fort  Magruder,  to  supply  it  with  food  to  save  the  patients  from  starva- 
tion. These  raids,  under  the  peculiar  circumstances,  are  in  violation  of 
every  dictate  of  humanity.  Having  no  result  and  apparently  no  object 
but  annoyance  and  a useless  sacrifice  of  life,  they  are  also  in  violation 
of  every  principle  of  honorable  warfare.  I have  directed  Major-General 
Keyes  to  reoccupy  the  townj  and  that  the  aggressions  referred  to  may 
cease  I give  you  notice  in  case  of  any  repetition  of  them — 

1st.  That  the  inmates  of  the  asylum  will  be  sent  to  Kichmond  and  the 
United  States  relieved  of  the  burden  of  their  support  j 
2d.  That  any  house  which  may  be  taken  possession  of  for  the  purpose 
of  firing  upon  the  troops  stationed  there  will  be  razed  to  the  ground  j 
and, 

3d.  That  any  citizen  of  Williamsburg  not  belonging  to  a regularly 
organized  corps  Avho  shall  be  found  co-operating  in  these  attacks  and 
rising  in  arms  against  the  occupying  troops  will  be  put  to  death  as  a 
violator  of  the  laws  of  civilized  warfare. 

I am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

JOHN  A.  DIX,

Lieut.  Col.  Southard  Hoffman, 

Assistant  Adjutant- General^  Eighteenth  Army  Corps: 

Colonel:  The  troops  of  this  command  were  all  in  position  last  night. 
On  account  of  the  limited  number  of  cars  it  took  several  trips  to  bring 
everything  up.  Colonel  Amory^s  brigade  I sent  to  the  railroad  cross- 
ing at  Core  Creek.  He  took  possession  of  the  bridge  and  sent  a force 
immediately  across  the  creek  and  as  far  as  the  switch.  There  was 
nothing  there. 

I marched  here  (about  12  miles)  from  Colonel  Jones^  camp,  arriving 
ahttle  after  midnight.  I brought  with  me  the  brigade  of  Colonel  Lee, 
the  section  of  artillery,  and  one  company  of  cavalry,  with  Colonel  Jones 
iuid  his  regiment.  Plank  was  brought  from  Colonel  Jones’  camp  to  re- 
pair the  bridge  here,  and  it  was  at  the  bridge  at  1 this  morning.  A 
orce  was  sent  immediately  across  the  creek  here,  which  went  out  some 
distance  on  the  road,  but  found  nothing.  This  force  still  remains  across 


666 


NORTH  CAROLINA  AND  S.  E.  VIRGINIA. 


[Chap.  XXX. 


tlie  creek.  The  cars  were  running  to  the  creek  till  late  last  night,  and 
the  noise  of  the  whistles  was  constant  and  imposing. 

At  midnight  it  commenced  to  rain  very  heavily,  and  now  the  whole 
country  is  under  water.  The  men  are  patient  and  trying  to  keep  warm 
and  dry.  One  shower  succeeds  another  very  quickly,  and  we  are  wait- 
ing patiently  for  a lull  in  the  storm.  I communicate  with  Colonel 
Amory,  who  is  about  2 miles  from  here. 

It  is  my  impression  that  everything  has  retired  to  Kinston ; that  is, 
every  force  of  any  size. 

With  the  best  care  that  could  be  taken  a good  portion  of  the  men’s 
rations  will  be  soaked,  and  to-morrow  we  will  have  to  get  a supply. 
These  should  be  sent  to  Core  Creek  by  rail.  We  need  2,500  to  3,000 
rations  daily,  and  the  cavalry  horses  haT^e  no  forage.  There  are  two 
companies  of  them  here. 

This  I shall  send  by  Captain  Harris,  commissary  of  Colonel  Amory’s 
brigade. 

I am,  colonel,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant,

If  I have  misunderstood  General  Foster,  I deeply  regret  itj  but  it  is 
tterly  impossible  that  I could  do  so,  as  the  conversation  was  too  deli- 
ite  and  explicit.  I write  now  for  the  purpose  of  ashing  that  my  duties  as 
wimander  of  the  post  may  he  defined  by  an  order.  My  desire  is  to  serve 
ly  country  to  the  best  of  my  ability,  but  I can  be  of  no  benefit  to  the 
?rvice  in  my  present  position  unless  I either  have  some  instructions  to 
uitle  me  or  I am  allowed  to  proceed  according  to  my  own  judgment. 
By  General  Orders,  No.  2 (hereto  annexed),  the  defenses  of  the  post 
ere  placed  under  my  command.  This  morning  I commenced  throwing 
p an  earthwork  at  a point  to  the  right  of  Block-house  No.  3,  where 
reneral  Potter  indicated  that  General  Foster  desired  it  should  be  done; 
ut,  as  the  order  of  General  Prince  defining  my  duties  and  placing  the 
efenses  of  the  post  under  my  command  has  been  rescinded,  I do  not 
jel  at  liberty  to  proceed  with  this  or  any  of  the  other  works  necessary 
)r  the  defense  of  the  place  until  I shall  receive  an  explicit  order  to  do 
0,  as  Orders  No.  2 placed  me  not  only  in  command  of  the  defenses  of 
le  post  but  also  of  the  troops  stationed  here.  That  being  now  rescinded 
, leaves  me  without  any  command. 

I did  feel  a desire  to  aid  in  driving  back  the  enemy  that  now  seems 
) be  hovering  around  this  place.  In  fact  I was  in  hopes  that  I would 
e able  to  make  it  too  warm  for  them  to  have  even  a picket  within  20 
tiles  of  Washington,  much  less  to  be  allowed  to  remain  in  force  within 
or  7 miles  of  this  place. 

A Mrs.  Lucinda  Willard,  from  the  neighborhood  of  Beaver  Dam,  and 
bo  says  that  General  Potter  knows  her  very  well,  came  to  our  lines 
)-day  on  the  Plymouth  road  and  informed  me  that  the  enemy  was  en- 
imped  in  large  force  at  TrantePs  Creek,  and  that  they  intended  mak- 
ig  another  attack  upon  the  place,  both  by  land  and  with  a floating 
attery  which  they  are  to  bring  down  the  river,  and  that  their  object 
fis  time  is  to  burn  the  town.  She  says  that  the  rebel  soldiers  have 
een  writing  this  to  their  families  in  her  vicinity  for  the  past  three  or 
)ur  days.  I make  the  statement  for  what  it  is  worth.  If  General  Pot- 
‘r  knows  her  he  can  tell  whether  any  reliance  should  be  put  in  what  she 
\ys.  Her  statement  in  regard  to  the  troops  and  their  location  is  con- 
rined  from  other  sources.  However,  I think  it  would  be  well  to  have  a 
:roiig  work  erected  on  the  extreme  left  of  our  lines,  as  in  case  they 
loiild  take  it  in  their  heads  to  approach  the  place  b^^  the  river  and  at 
time  when  the  gunboats  might  be  engaged  below  the  bridge  they  could 
ive  us  some  trouble  unless  Ave  have  everything  ready  for  their  recej)-

Lieut.  Ool.  Southard  Hoffman, 

Assistant  Adjutant- General,  Eighteenth  Army  Corps: 

Colonel  : I have  the  honor  to  report  the  following  interesting  facts, 
showing  how  by  timely  orders  to  a grand  guard  I probably  saved  it 

from  capture:  , , ^ ^ ^ i 

On  visiting  the  pickets  over  the  river  day  before  yesterday,  the  day 
on  which  I took  command  here,  I found  a grand  guard  (1  captain,  2 lieu- 
tenants, and  70  enlisted  men  of  infantry,  and  2 cavalry  soldiers)  sta- 
tioned at  the  cross-roads.  Considering  them  so  much  out  of  place  as  to 
be  a mere  invitation  to  the  enemy  to  come  and  take  them,  I ordered  all 
the  vedettes  to  be  called  in  at  once,  so  that  no  time  should  be  lost,  and 
that  the  force  should  retire  with  all  dispatch  to  inside  of  Eed  Hill,  de- 
fining the  position  to  be  occupied.  This  was  at  11  o’clock  a.  m. 

I have  to-day  the  most  perfectly  reliable  intelligence  that  at  12  m. 
day  before  yesterday,  Daniel’s  brigade  (five  counted  regiments  aud 
some  cavalry)  arrived  near  the  chapel  which  is  1 mile  from  the  cross 
roads  toward  Greenville.  They  halted  half  a mile  before  reaching  the 
chapel  and  ^‘made  ready  for  a fight  aud  sent  forward  the  cavalry  U 
the  cross-roads.”  But  tiie  informant  does  not  know  why  the  cavalr\ 
soon  returned,  when  the  brigade  immediately  marched  back  on  the 
Greenville  road  and  made  their  headquarters  at  Taft’s  Store,  lo  milef 
from  here.

to  extend  to  the  Navy  very  considerable  facilities,  and  this  has  always 
been  kindly  done  and  gratel'ally  received.  There  is  a difference,  how-i 
ever,  between  lending  a spare  tug  or  wagon  already  provided  for  the 
use  of  the  Army  and  buying  such  a tug  to  be  given  to  the  Navy  wdth-i 
out  proper  authority  to  do  so.  In  vindication  of  your  policy  of  proAud- 
iug  an  army-navy  for  the  defense  of  the  Upper  Nansemond  you  speak 
of  your  gunboat.  Smith  Briggs,  as  being  one  of  your  chief  supports  at 
Suffolk  in  consequence  of  our  gunboats  being  withdrawn ; ” and  m your 
letter  to  me  of  the  22d  you  say:  “My  two  armed  steamers  are  to  remain 
there.  Yours  are  to  be  exposed  to  no  more  danger  than  mine,”  and 
you  encourage  me  by  a reference  to  the  safe  running  by  the  Vicksburg 
batteries  of  our  iron-dads  under  cover  of  night  with  high  water  and  a 

swift  current.  .t  , 

As  to  the  withdrawal  of  the  gunboats.  Lieutenant  Lamson  was  obliged 
to  drop  down  below  the  bar,  that  is  to  say,  from  the  Upper  to  the  Lower 
Nansemond,  on  account  of  the  abandonment,  against  the  earnest  re 
monstrance  of  Lieutenants  Cushing  and  Lamson,  of  the  captured  rebel 
battery  by  our  troops  after  it  had  been  held  by  the  cross-fire  of  the 
gunboats,  whilst  the  troops  so  strengthened  it  in  the  rear  with  rifle-pits., 
intrenchments,  embrasures,  and  artillery  as  to  make  it  almost  impreg 
nable,  and  which,  while  occupied  by  the  enemy,  had  harassed  the  gun 
boats  considerably  and  cut  off*  their  communications  by  commanding 
the  bar,  over  which  but  one  of  them  could  pass  at  or  near  low  water. 

Had  this  battery  been  held  it,  with  our  battery  nearly  opposite,  would, 
have  afforded  the  gunboats  a cover  above  the  bar,  whence  they  mighl 
at  any  time  of  tide  have  moved  up  in  front  of  our  earthworks,  whicl 
Lieutenant  Lamson  informs  me  now  line  the  right  bank  of  Nausemonc 
Creek.  Your  gunboat  West  End  dropped  below  the  bar  when  our  gun 
boats  did  so,  but  Lieutenant  Lamson  informed  me  it  refused  to  stop  to 
ferry  back  your  troops. 

As  to  your  other  gunboat,  the  Smith  Briggs,  I am  informed  she  nevei 
engaged  the  batteries,  but  has  laid  at  Suffolk  expending  navy  ammu 
nition,  which  has  been  freely  supplied  to  her,  in  shelling  the  woods 
I cannot  see  how  she  or  any  other  gunboat  could  have  proved  a “ hos 
at  Suffolk.”  It  would  seem  better  to  have  the  guns  mounted  m bat 
teries  ashore  than  on  gunboats  floating  in  the  ditch  before  the  battery  o; 
fort.  The  West  Branch  Battery  not  having  been  reoccupied  by  tin 
enemy,  it  was  picketed  by  you  or  us.  Some  of  the  navy  gunboats  wen 
to  go  above  the  bar  yesterday.  I suppose  when  the  boats  get  abov( 
the  battery  the  enemy,  if  in  force,  will  reoccupy  it. 

I hope  you  will  see  in  this  only  a purpose  to  put  myself  and  my  com 
mand  right  ou  the  record.  I close  with  the  earnest  assurance  that 
will  always  be,  as  I always  have  been,  happy  to  co-operate  with  you 
and  that  whatever  means  are  at  my  command  shall  be  at  your  servic 
Avithin  the  extent  of  my  authority. 

I have  the  honor  to  be,  general,  very  respectfully,  yours, 

S.  P.  LEE,

Sir:  I make  the  following  report  of  the  forces  under  my  command  a 
this  post  to  this  date: 

I was  sent  here  by  General  Palmer  February  28.  I have  one  compau 
of  Eighth  Massachusetts,  80  men;  one  of  the  Third  Massachusetts,  <

n • one  North  Carolina  company  of  about  20  men  ; two  armed  schoon- 
, with  26  men  each,  and  about  100  negroes  as  laborers, 
larch  12  I sent  a party  of  soldiers  from  the  North  Carolina  company 
0 the  woods  for  wood  with  12  negroes.  After  being  there  a short  time 
y were  attacked  by  about  40  guerrillas  and  1 negro  killed  and  2 
iinded  and  3 of  the  soldiers  taken  and  carried  away  prisoners.  Soon 
the  alarm  was  given  I sent  a company  in  pursuit,  but  they  having 
en  up  the  bridge  were  not  overtaken  by  our  forces, 
have  kept  the  negroes  employed  lately  in  throwing  up  an  intrench- 
Qt  and  have  it  nearly  finished.  I shall  then  send  those  that  are  not 
ided  here  to  New  Berne. 

Nothing  more  occurred  until  the  6th  of  April.  Captain  Sanders,  of 
North  Carolina  company,  with  a detail  of  7 soldiers  and  10  negroes, 
5 sent  down  the  river  in  a schooner  after  wood ; the  wind  blowing, 
y were  not  able  to  land  that  day ; he  returned  home  and  left  the  men 
board ; in  the  evening  they  went  on  shore  to  see  their  families,  and 
•e  all  taken  and  carried  away  to  Eichmond  prisoners,  leaving  that 
ipany  now  with  only  14  men  for  duty.  Had  we  a company  of  cavalry 
e I think  we  might  rid  this  section  of  the  country  from  the  guerrillas, 
it  is  now,  unless  we  go  out  in  a large  force,  we  are  liable  to  be  picked 
We  have  now  six  horses  and  one  yoke  of  oxen,  enough  to  do  our 
tning.  Previous  to  your  last  instructions,  under  General  Palmer’s 
er  I had  returned  to  the  persons  taken  from  10  horses  and  13  mules, 

. have  given  receipts  for  the  rest. 

V^ehaye  pceived  no  rations  since  I arrived  here,  although  I have  sent 
• requisitions,  and  I have  been  obliged  to  forage  upon  the  citizens,  and 
ae  Government  is  to  pay  for  them  it  will  be  much  more  expensive 
a if  sent  from  New  Berne,  as  provisions  are  scarce  and  high, 
he  negroes  are  very  much  in  need  of  clothing,  not  having  received 
! pay  or  clothing  from  the  Government  and  have  been  employed

Suffolk,  Va.,  May  1,  1863. 
General  D.  Butterfield,  Army  of  the  Potomac : 

There  may  be  portions  of  Longstreet’s  troops  with  your  opponents. 
If  so,  they  are  the  first  installments.  Deserters  and  contrabands  who 
came  in  yesterday  from  Hood’s  and  Pickett’s  divisions  agree  in  all 
points  with  others  that  have  fallen  into  our  hands.  The  pickets  ol 
Corse,  Garnett,  and  Law  are  on  all  the  roads  now.  There  have  been 
heavy  rains  here  for  a few  days.  Longstreet  had  two  railroads  in  about 
16  miles  of  his  line. 

JOHN  J.  PECK, 

Major-General. 

(Sent  by  General  Butterfield  to  General  Hooker  11.45  p.  m.) 


Fort  Monroe,  May  1,  1863. 

Maj.  Gen.  John  J.  Peck: 

Among  the  many  marvels  of  this  war  are  the  impossibility  on  oui 
part  of  getting  information  as  to  the  enemy  and  the  facility  withwhicl 
he  ascertains  everything  as  to  us.  I allude  especially  to  General  But 
terfield’s  dispatch  to  you  stating  that  Hood’s  and  Pickett’s  division! 
are  in  front  of  the  Army  of  the  Potomac. 

JOHN  A.  DIX, 

Major-General.

Commanding  Department  of  North  Carolina  : 


General:  I had  the  honor  to  receive  on  the  27th  ultimo  your  in- 
[eresting  and  instructive  communication  of  the  22d  ultimo,  giving  your 
riews  respecting  the  occupation  of  posts  within  the  limits  of  your  com- 
[fiand. 

I It  was  only  in  connection  with  the  occupation  of  such  posts  by  the 
lavy,  as  a part  of  their  defense,  that  the  subject  claimed  my  official  at- 
ention. 

I meant  in  my  communication  of  the  17th  to  refer  only  to  positions 
a the  Sounds  of  North  Carolina,  and  not  to  Fort  Macon  and  Beau- 
Drt  Harbor,  the  defense  of  which,  and  of  Hatteras  Inlet,  is  of  obvious 
ecessity. 

As  to  Eoanoke  Island,  I suppose  it  best  that  the  abandoned  rebel 
mrks  there  should  be  razed  and  the  obstructions  in  Croatan  Sound 
emoved.  Then  such  observation  or  police  as  would  prevent  any  at- 
empts  at  reconstruction  might  answer ; but  even  if  reoccupied  by  the 
nemy  we  could,  if  there  were  not  too  many  other  places  to  guard,  con- 
lentrate  and  dislodge  them.  But  this  position  does  not  receive  naval 
ccupation  at  present,  and  thelefore  is  only  referred  to  in  view  of  future 
emands.  Your  views  in  respect  to  New  Berne,  Washingtou,  and  Ply- 
louth  possess  great  force.  They  would  require  considerable  military 
; efenses,  however,  to  accomplish  all  you  have  in  view.  They  are  sickly 
'laces ; Plymouth  especially. 

The  enemy  can  build  gunboats  on  the  Tar  above  Washington,  and 
n the  Eoanoke  above  Plymouth,  though  their  facilities  would  be  bet- 
3r  at  the  towns  if  they  held  them. 

The  question  with  us  is  how  many  places  can  we  profitably  hold,  com- 
(•aring  the  advantages  with  the  expense  of  possession.  We  do  not  hold 
Mzabeth  City,  Edenton,  Hertford,  Winfield,  &c.,  nor  does  the  enemy 
^rive  any  visible  advantage  from  having  access  to  them. 

My  general  view  of  our  policy  is  to  take  places  which  the  enemy  has 
irtified  j to  level  his  works  of  defense,  and  then  to  leave  these  places  as 


682 


NORTH  CAROLINA  AND  S.  E.  VIRGINIA. 


[Chap.  XXX. 


they  were  before  the  rebellion,  unless  they  are  of  particular  military  im- 
portance, in  which  case  they  would  require  and  justify  proper  defenses. 

Where  a place  is  held  it  seems  to  me  that  the  military  occupation 
ought  to  be  as  complete  as  practicable  in  itself;  and  when  this  cannot 
be  done  the  occupation  becomes  one  of  questionable  propriety  to  the 
extent  that  gunboats  are  permanently  needed  for  its  defense. 

I do  not  desire  or  attempt  to  interfere  with  your  military  plans,  and 
I fully  appreciate  the  good  spirit  in  which  you  favor  me  with  your  views. 
It  is  certainly  my  wish  and  purpose  to  co-operate  heartily  with  you. 
I shall  be  glad  if  this  interchange  of  ideas  will  lead  to  such  an  examina- 
tion of  the  subject  as  will  show  in  connection  with  each  necessary  mili- 
tary occupation  precisely  what  kind  and  extent  of  naval  force  is  re- 
quired in  the  Sounds.  It  appears  to  me  that  the  naval  part  of  our  policy 
there  is  to  have  such  a force  as  can  co-operate  in  expeditions  with  the 
army,  and  in  the  mean  time,  by  cruising  and  as  guard  vessels,  preserve 
the  blockade  and  the  police  of  the  waters. 

Should  the  enemy  build  gunboats  on  the  rivers  above  the  towns  the 
naval  force  should  be  sufacient  to  destroy  his  vessels  before  they  unite 
or  after  they  have  combined. 

I have  the  honor  to  be,  general,  very  respectfully,  yours, 

S.  P.  LEE, 

Actg.  Bear- Admiral,  Comdg,  N,  Atlantic  Bloclcading  Squadron.

; I desire  to  acknowledge,  as  I always  have,  the  readiness  with  which 
my  calls  on  you  for  aid  have  been  answered.  In  regard  to  differences 
jof  opinion  between  us  concerning  our  respective  duties  I have  done  all

in  my  power  fco  confine  the  knowledge  of  them  to  those  immediately 
around  me  and  my  official  superiors.  How  difficult  it  is  to  carry  out 
such  a purpose  in  this  country  of  free  discussion  I need  not  suggest  to 
you.  My  own  public  conduct  in  this  department  has  in  more  instances 
than  one  been  criticised  in  a most  unjust  and  offensive  manner  by

ment my  attention  was  called  to  it  (for  I rarely  read  correspondents’ 
letters)  the  reputed  author  was  advised  that  he  had  been  guilty  of  a 
great  impropriety  in  using  the  words  highest  authority,”  which  was 
explained  to  be  a common  i)hrase  among  newspaper  correspondents, 
importing  that  the  statement  was  made  on  undoubted  information.  He 
was  also  advised  that  the  remarks  in  regard  to  yourself  were  strongly 
disapproved  by  me,  and  on  both  points  I was  assured  that  there  would 
be  no  cause  for  complaint  hereafter. 

The  last  paragraph  of  your  letter,  advising  me  that  Lieutenants  Lam- 
son  and  Cushing  were  authorized  in  their  discretion  to  go  into  the  Upper 
Nansemond  and  co-operate  with  my  forces  there  against  the  enemy,  is 
all  I can  ask,  and  I know  that  the  spirit  and  gallantry  those  officers 
have  exhibited  on  all  occasions  will  insure  to  us  all  the  aid  it  is  possible 
to  afford.

Fort  Monroe,  Ya.,  May  3, 1863—8  p.  m. 

Maj.  Gen.  H.  W.  Halleck, 

General-in-Chief : 

I have  just  returned  from  Suffolk.  General  Getty  crossed  the  Nan- 
semond,  near  General  Peck’s  headquarters,  to-day,  with  5,000  men.  He 
was  in  front  of  the  enemy’s  intrenchments,  2 miles  back.  A strong  dem- 
onstration will  be  made  on  the  enemy’s  right  flank  to-morrow  morning 
In  the  action  in  front  of  our  center  the  day  before  yesterday  we  lost  7 
killed  and  20  wounded.  The  enemy  acknowledge  33  killed  and  a large 
number  wounded.  We  cannot  ascertain  and  do  not  think  any  of  his 
troops  have  been  withdrawn.  To-morrow  we  shall  be  able  to  judge 
better  of  his  strength. 

JOHN  A.  DIX, 

Major-General.

►oint  to  his  attack  by  declaring  that  he  was  reflecting  your  feelings, 
ras  most  unwarrantable. 

This  correspondent,  in  the  same  inspired  communication  (for  in  that 
ight  be  has  presented  his  reflections  to  the  public),  also  charges  me 
7ith  being  at  fault  for  the  reoccupation  by  the  rebels  of  their  aban-

liver.  This  reoccupation  was  a military  act  done  in  your  department. 
Vbeu  Colonel  Ludlow  informed  me  of  it  on  his  return  down  James 
liver  in  a flag  of  truce  I did  not  wait  for  you  to  ask  me  to  co-operate, 
)ut  I went  immediately  to  confer  with  you  on  the  subject.  Your  reply 
vas  that  you  could  do  nothing,*  that  the  enemy  was  on  this  side  of  the 
flackwater  in  greater  force  than  yourself;  but  you  asked  me  if  I could 
lot  shell  them  out.  I confess  that  I was  a little  surprised  at  this  ex- 
)ectatiou,  in  view  of  the  failure,  from  want  of  army  co-operation,  of  a 
)etter  force  than  I had  to  shell  the  enemy  out  of  Fort  Darling,  which 
lad  no  rebel  navy  to  support  it. 

The  reoccupation  of  Fort  Powhatan  was  the  easy  and  natural  effort 
>f  the  enemy,  who  had  remained  in  possession  of  the  Blackwater  in 
i'ont  of  Suffolk  (between  Suffolk  and  Fort  Powhatan)  for  the  last  eight 
nonths.  Where  an  active  enemy  holds  miliiary  possession  of  a country 
II  force  he  may  not  only  reoccupy  his  forts  on  his  river  front,  but  he 
nay,  where  there  is  no  military  interference,  build  forts  on  the  bluffs  of 
he  river  where  he  had  none  before.  One  of  our  gunboats,  as  proposed, 
)r  several  of  them,  aided  by  the  one  iron-clad  I then  liad,  could  not 
lave  driven  him  from  Fort  Powhatan  after  he  had ’reoccupied  it. 

Under  the  circumstances  of  this  case  the  unfounded  and  injurious 
issaults  made  by  a correspondent  at  the  fort,  who  is  under  your  imme- 
liate  authority  and  who  professedly  writes  from  military  intelligence 
iominunicated  to  him  there,  it  seems  both  proper  and  decent  that  his

s understood  by  the  public  to  write.

Fort  Monroe,  Va., 

May  6,  1863 — 10  a.  m. 


I embarked  5,000  men  yesterday  and  last  night  at  Ntorfolk,  and  hope 
:o  have  them  at  their  destination  to-morrow  morning.  We  had  a heavy

the  squadron  without  a transport,  tender,  dispatch,  mail,  or  picket 
boat,  save  one  tug.  When  on  the  14th  of  April  you  telegraphed  me 
that  three  of  the  improvised  gunboats  were  disabled,  and  asked  for 
more,  I obtained  temporarily  and  sent  to  the  Nansemond  four  tugs, 
half  the  Potomac  steam  flotilla. 

This  recital  shows  what  earnest  efforts  were  made  to  relieve  you.  It 
must  be  very  apparent  to  every  candid  and  intelligent  professional 
mind  that  had  General  Longstreet  really  intended  to  force  a crossing 
of  the  Upper  Nansemond  with  the  reputed  means  at  his  command  these 
few  light  pieces,  mostly  field  pieces,  on  the  open  decks  of  a few  mer- 
chant vessels  could  not  have  prevented  his  doing  so  there.  The  same 
number  of  field  pieces  would  have  made  a better  resistance  behind 
earthworks  ashore  than  on  frail  little  steamers  afloat.  Hence  in  my 
instructions  of  the  13th  ultimo,  sent  to  Lieutenants  Cushing  and  Lam- 
son  that  day  and  night,  these  views  were  expressed  by  me  to  be  com- 
municated to  you.  Your  theory  therefore  that  this  conviction  was  the 
result  of  the  rough  handling  the  boats  received  in  fighting  the  enemy’s 
earthworks  on  the  14th  falls  to  the  ground.  It  was  my  manifest  duty  to 
let  you  know  that  the  Uavy  had  not  the  means  to  make  the  military 
lefense  expected  of  it.  Had  I undertaken  the  defense  imposed  without 
i word  of  warning  as  to  the  sufficiency  of  the  naval  means  as  a substi- 
tute for  military  defense  to  protect  your  rear  from  a real  attempt  by 
the  enemy  to  cross  the  Uansemond  Creek,  the  failure  that  must  have 
ensued,  so  disastrous  to  the  army  and  nation,  would  have  been  charged 
Lipou  the  Uavy.  I did  send  Fleet  Captain  Crosby  to  Suffolk  on  the  19th 
Lo  withdraw  the  boats  if  practicable  from  the  Upper  Hansemond. 

The  situation  was  this  : You  had  been  largely  re-enforced,  and  had 
i gallant  army,  22,000  strong,  at  Suffolk.  You  had  just  erected  earth- 
^vorks  and  rifle-pits  along  the  right  bank  of  the  Nansemond  suitable  to 
.its  defense.  The  enemy  had  made  no  attempt  to  cross  Hansemond 
Creek,  the  blockade  of  which  he  had  established.  His  earthwork  at 
West  Branch,  which  commanded  the  bar  at  the  mouth  of  Uansemond 
Creek,  had  cut  off  the  communications  of  the  gunboats  whilst  yours  were 
q)en  ; had  thoroughly  disabled  one  and  seriously  damaged  three  other 
:)oats,  besides  killing  and  wounding  a large  proportion  of  their  small 
•rews.  The  enemy’s  rifle-pits  and  artillery  on  the  left  flank  were  a se- 
lous  annoyance  to  the  boats  but  did  not  seem  to  threaten  the  safety 
)f  the  post.  Your  detachments  had  twice  failed  to  support  Lieutenant 
Camsoii  and  capture  this  battery  and  raise  the  blockade  (which  was 
ifterwards  so  easily  done),  and  our  transports  and  tenders  were  sus- 
aiiiiiig  in  an  unequal  and  unnecessary  contest  with  the  enemy’s  earth- 
>vorks  much  damage.  Nevertheless,  when  you  that  day  (the  19th)  by 
elegraph  desired  the  retention  of  the  gunboats  in  the  Upper  Nanse- 
noiid  1 promptly  replied  by  telegraph  and  directed  Lieutenant  Lamson 
hrough  you  to  remain  with  the  boats.  You  most  unfairly  omit  this 
roiii  your  statement  of  the  case  and  go  on  to  charge  me  with  having 
'vitlidrawn  the  gunboats,  when  the  fact  is  I gave  no  such  orders  to  do 
io  after  the  one  I just  revoked  at  your  instance  and  through  you. 

On  the  20th  you  ordered  this  earthwork,  which  our  troops  had  held 
luder  the  cross-fire  of  the  gunboats  and  had  greatly  strengthened,  to 
^0  abandoned.  Lieutenant  Lamson  reported  to  me  that  this  evacuation, 
‘aiiiestly  opposed  by  him,  obliged  him  to  withdraw  the  boats  from  the 
Cpper  to  the  Lower  Nansemond  from  just  above  to  just  below  the  bar, 
mder  West  Branch  Battery  and  commanded  by  it  a distance  of  half  or 
liree-quarters  of  a mile.  Thus  your  orders  and  not  mine  occasioned 
be  withdrawal  of  the  gunboats.  In  your  communication  of  the  21st 
^'ou  admit  your  ability  to  hold  the  Nansemond  without  the  boats.

Last  fall  Commodore  Livingston,  at  my  suggestion,  leveled  the  work 
at  Helena  which  commands  the  navy -yard. 

I respectfully  suggest  to  you  that  it  would  be  of  great  advantage  to

Rear-Admiral  S.  P.  Lee, 

Comdg.  N.  Atlantic  Bloclcading  Squadron^  Hamgytoyi  Beads,  Va. : 

' Sir  : I have  the  honor  to  acknowledge  the  receipt  of  your  letter  of 
May  1,  repeating  some  of  yonr  views  on  the  subject  of  posts  on  the 
Sounds  in  this  department,  and,  as  always,  yonr  views  claim  my  care- 
ful consideration. 

In,  as  it  were,  a joint  department  like  this  it  is  a matter  of  discrimina- 
tion what  points  to  hold  as  of  greater  benefit  to  both  arms  of  the  serv- 
ice. The  points  on  the  coast  are  of  course  equally  important  for  all  par- 
ties. Roanoke  Island  is  of  great  advantage  to  us  as  a strategical  point; 
would  be  to  the  enemy.  If  the  island  were  abandoned  and  the  works 
were  razed  I have  no  doubt  that  it  would  be  occupied  by  the  eneinj^ 
via  Rag^s  Head  and  across  Roanoke  Channel.  At  this  point,  from  the 
shallowness  of  the  water,  gunboats  could  not  prevent  the  occupancy 
and  could  not  prevent  the  erection  of  batteries,  even  were  it  known  that 
it  would  be  attempted ; whereas  that  position  could  be  held  by  a small 
force  on  the  island  against  a large  one  crossing. 

Experience  has  shown  us  the  facility  with  which  sand  batteries  can 
be  erected,  and  also  ])roved  that  their  power  of  withstanding  fire  is 
treater  than  stone.  It  would  require  but  a few  weeks  to  again  fortify 
Roanoke  Island  (should  the  enemy  have  it),  and  probably  the  taking  of 
it  has  shown  them  the  falsity  of  their  previous  line  of  defense;  and  I 
believe  the  division  might  lose  more  men  than  were  withdrawn  from 
iny  force  as  garrisons. 

As  to  Washington  and  Plymouth  my  views  were  given  in  my  letter 
M the  22d  ultimo.  While  I have  force  sufficient  it  seems  to  me  impor- 
ifcant  to  hold  the  rich  grain-growing  counties  lying  in  the  pockets  held 
by  these  towns,  and  also  as  strategical  points  for  harassing  the  enemy 
so  long  as  I have  force  sufficient  for  any  offensive  movements ; but  such 
:nay  not  be  the  case  long. 

Again,  if  the  enemy  should  construct  gunboats  up  the  Tar  and  Roan- 
)ke  Rivers  they  probably  could  not  be  made  sufficiently  formidable  to 
lefeat  the  naval  forces  at  Washington  and  Plymouth ; the  naval  as  well 
IS  land  batteries  could  assist  in  the  defense.  It  is  not  likely,  however, 
:bat  naval  vessels  crossing  through  the  Sounds  would  be  in  force  equal 
Lo  encounter  the  combined  forces  at  Washington  and  Plymouth,  in 
^hich  case  (the  enemy  always  being  in  a position  to  make  concerted 
Itiiovements)  a concentration  of  the  vessels  from  several  might  be  made 
Tor  attacking  detached  vessels,  in  which  case  the  result  might  be 
lisastrous.  Of  these  probabilities  you  of  course  are  the  best  judge, 
but  merely  in  accordance  with  our  mutual  desire  to  exchange  ideas  for 
file  general  good  I give  it  as  my  opinion  that  were  the  towns  of  Wash- 
ngton  and  Plymouth  abandoned  the  mouths  of  the  rivers  so  situated 
^vould  be  the  right  and  best  places  for  the  guard-boats,  and  that  the 
presence  of  the  assistance  on  land  would  necessitate  the  presence  of  a 
‘large  naval  force  to  be  as  effective  as  the  present  guarding  force. 

Would  the  class  of  boats  in  service  here  be  of  much  use  in  outside 
■service  ? 

I inclose  herein  a’  slip  cut  from  a Raleigh  paper,  which  shows  the 
^iews  held  by  the  enemy  upon  the  subject  of  our  abandonment  of  the 
ounties  of  Albemarle,  the  advantage  gained  by  them  of  food,  &c. 

I have  the  honor  to  remain,  admiral,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient 
servant, 

J.  G.  POSTER, 

Major-  General,  Commanding.

of  Norfolk.  Why  it  was  ever  occupied  I do  not  know.  "i

I also  learn  from  various  sources,  so  that  I count  on  it  as  reliable  to

small,  not  exceeding  five  regiments,  and  that  there  are  few  troops  at 
Goldsborough.  Of  the  five  regiments,  one  is  at  Gum  Swamp  and  one 
at  AVise’s  Forks,  and  the  regiment  at  Gum  Swamp  is  open  to  a move- 
ment on  its  rear  and  might  be  cut  off.  If  it  is  thought  desirable  under 
existing  circumstances  to  seize  Kinston  and  Goldsborough  I would  re- 
quest to  be  allowed  to  strike  the  railroad  somewhere  north  of  Golds- 
borough, in  order  to  intercept  re-enforcements,  &c.  AYith  one  good  in- 
fantry regiment  added  to  my  own  and  three  or  four  troops  of  cavalry 
and  a section  of  artillery  I feel  confident  I could  reach  that  railroad 
with  little  or  no  opposition  and  break  it  up  extensively,  that  is,  pro- 
vided the  intention  be  kept  entirely  secret. 

The  enterprise  would  justify  some  labor  and  risk  in  reference  to  tbe 
capture  of  Goldsborough  only,  but  as  connected  with  a simultaneous 
movement  from  Suffolk  on  Weldon  it  might  materially  interrupt  the 
enemy’s  communications  and  influence  the  war.

Maj.  Gen.  H.  W.  Halleck, 

General-in-  Chief : 


Fort  Monroe,  Va., 

May  16,  1863 — 1 p.  m. 


Colonel  Foster  is  covering  our  work,  which  is  in  good  progress,  on 
the  railroad  near  Carrsville.  Has  been  engaged  with  the  enemy  more 
or  less  for  two  days.  A lively  artillery  fire  has  been  kept  up  on  our 
workmen.  Yesterday  the  enemy  advanced  within  canister-range,  but 
was  driven  back  with  considerable  loss.  On  our  side  a caisson  was 
riddled,  a horse  killed,  and  9 men  wounded.  The  iron  is  arriving  in 
Norfolk.  When  we  get  on  the  other  road  we  shall  probably  have  some 
sharp  fighting. 


JOHK  A.  MX, 

Major-General.

General  : Your  letter  of  the  14th  is  received  and  your  wishes  have 
all  been  anticipated.  The  moment  I received  your  telegraphic  dispatch 
saying  that  you  approved  my  views,  I sent  Major  Stewart  to  examine 
the  new  line,  and  it  will  be  fortified  under  his  direction.  It  has  been 
given  out  that  we  are  to  fortify  it  as  a second  line,  and  a show  of  strength- 
ening the  defenses  at  Suffolk  is  to  be  kept  up  until  it  is  ready. 

I have  just  returned  from  Suffolk ; the  enemy  is  on  this  side  the  Black- 
water  and  in  considerable  force.  Colonel  Foster  is  between  him  and 
our  working  party  with  8,000  men.  We  hope  to  finish  our  work  on  the 
Weldon  road  by  Wednesday.  When  we  go  to  Zuni  we  shall  send  a 
still  larger  force. 

My  man  came  in  from  Eichmond  to-day.  He  says  that  only  one  divis- 
ion of  Longstreet’s  force  went  north  of  Eichmond,  and  that  it  returned 
to  Petersburg,  being  too  late  for  the  battle  of  Fredericksburg.  He  con- 
firms my  former  statements  that  the  force  before  Suffolk  was  near  40,000, 
and  he  says  this  whole  force  is  at  Petersburg,  ou  the  Blackwater,  and 
back  of  Franklin,  on  the  Weldon  road. 

The  Eichmond  has  met  with  an  accident ; he  could  not  ascertain  pre- 
cisely what,  but  thinks  it  was  some  damage  to  her  machinery.  The  two 
iron-dads  on  the'stocks  are  getting  on  slowly.  He  thinks  they  cannot 
be  completed,  before  August,  but  he  judged  from  what  he  saw  tljat 
workmen  had  been  transferred  from  one  to  the  other,  indicating  an  in- 
tention to  bring  one  out  as  soon  as  possible. 

He  is  satisfied  that  troops  have  recently  been  brought  to  Eichmond 
from  Georgia  and  South  Carolina  and  sent  on  to  Fredericksburg.  It 
was  said  at  Eichmond  that  Lee  was  to  attack  Hooker  and  drive  him 
back  to  the  Potomac. 

I am,  very  respectfully  and  truly,  yours, 

JOHN  A.  MX, 

Major-General

11  the  latter  road  will  amount  to  a campaign  and  we  must  look  for  some 
harp  fighting,  for  I do  not  believe  5,000  tons  of  railroad  iron  will  in

ENERAL  Orders,  ) Hdqrs.  Dept,  op  N.  0.,  Eighteenth  A.  C., 

No.  81.  j New  Berne.,  May  20,  1863. 

The  commanding  general,  in  common  with  the  officers  and  men  of 
is  command,  is  called  upon  to  mourn  the  loss  of  a most  gallant  officer, 
)1.  J.  Eichter  Jones,  Fifty-eighth  Pennsylvania  Volunteers,  who  fell 
the  head  of  his  regiment  on  the  evening  of  May  23,  whilst  repelling 
i attack  on  the  outposts. 

Colonel  Jones  won  the  admiration  of  all  in  this  department  by  the 
defatigable,  able,  and  gallant  manner  with  which  he  filled  the  ardu- 
18  duties  of  commander  of  the  outposts.  He  died  whilst  yet  enjoying 
e triumph  of  a victory  won  by  his  valor  and  counsel.  To  the  service, 
this  dejiartment,  and  to  his  regiment  this  death  has  been  a sad  loss ; 
id  to  all  here,  and  to  those  at  home  whom  he  loved,  the  commanding 
neral  offers  his  most  sincere  sympathy.  May  his  bright  example  lead 
any  to  tread  the  arduous  path  of  duty  witli  as  pure  an  appreciation  of 
ity  and  with  as  firm  unswerving  tread  as  he. 

All  the  flags  in  this  department  Avill  be  carried  at  half-mast  for  the 
ree  days  following  the  receipt  of  this  order,  and  at  this  post  half-hour 
ms  will  be  fired  from  Forts  Totten  and  Eowan  from  sunrise  to  sunset 
-morrow.  May  27. 

By  command  of  Maj.  Gen.  J.  G.  Foster:

I hope  you  may  get  the  troops  which  you  so  greatly  need  for  the 
3cupation  of  Smith’s  Island  and  the  attack  on  Wilmington. 

Your  views  respecting  the  occupation  of  Plymouth,  Koanoke  Island, 
^d  Washington  are  certainly  very  forcible.  I will  at  all  times  use 
rery  effort  to  sustain  you  in  holding  your  positions,  and  especially 
bile  you  are  supported  by  so  few  troops.  I have  instructed  Coni- 
lander  Davenport  to  make  every  exertion  to  support  you  at  this  crit- 
:al  period.

id  Washingtou  complete,  so  as  to  require  little  or  no  gunboat  defense, 
wer  vessels  will  be  required  in  the  Sounds,  and  yet  allow  a sufficient 
lovable  force  there  to  keep  the  police  of  its  waters,  prevent  such  es- 
ipes  as  those  of  the  Arrow  and  Emily  up  the  Chowan,  and  prevent 
iolations  of  the  blockade.  Though  the  vessels  in  the  Sounds  are  not 
lapted  to  outside  cruising  a portion  of  them  would  be  very  useful  for 
lockade  and  other  duty  here. 

I have  just  written  urgently  to  the  ^^Tavy  Department  to  try  and  get 
3u  more  troops  and  artillery. 

I have  the  honor  to  be,  general,  very  respectfully,  yours,

1 went  with  Major-Generals  Peck  and  Keyes  to  West  Point  yester 
day,  and  on  consultation  with  General  Gordon  it  was  unanimously  de 
cided  to  withdraw  the  troops,  throw  them  up  the  Peninsula  abov( 
Williamsburg,  aud,  in  conjunction  with  the  force  under  Keyes,  attacl 
the  enemy  at  Diascund  Bridge,  which  is  as  near  Pichinond  as  Wes 
Point.  There  are  at  West  Point  only  4,700  men,  and  they  will  be  re 
duced  to  4,000  shortly  by  the  discharge  of  a regiment.  General  Keyei 
has  only  5,000  men  at  Gloucester  Point,  Yorktown,  and  Williamsburg 
and  it  is  very  desirable  that  he  should  have  this  re-enforcement.  I have 
lost  three  regiments  and  shall  lose  fourteen  more  b}^  expiration  o 
service.

nublic  transports  from  one  place  to  another  in  this  department,  or  to

General  S.  G.  French: 

General  : I fear  very  much  that  unless  the  business  of  building  the 
bridge  and  repairing  the  railroad  be  pushed  our  expedition  will  be  a 
very  discreditable  tkilure  to  us  all.  Capt.  [Charles  H.]  Dimmock  has 
returned  to  Petersburg  without  my  seeing  him,  so  I do  not  know  what 
arrangement  he  has  made;  but  there  are  no  materials  whatever  here— 
no  timber,  no  tools,  and  no  car-logs  to  haul  the  timber.  The  bridge 
can  best  be  built  somewhere  on  the  railroad,  and  when  this  is  fini.s]ied 
transported  down  to  Zuni;  but  if  the  enemy  choose  to  they  can  prevent 
it  until  they  are  driven  away.  Whatever  we  are  to  do  must  be  done' 
quickly,  or  all  our  trouble  will  be  in  vaiu. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  J.  PETTIGEEW,

Sir:  Some  of  the  leading  farmers  and  citizens  of  Bertie  County  had 
i consultation  on  the  15th  instant  in  Windsor,  it  being  Monday  of 
m])eiior  court,  for  the  purpose  of  making  representations  to  Your  Ex-

)ointed  to  visit  Raleigh  and  see  you  in  person,  but  he  not  being  able  to 
to  until  about  October  1, 1 was  requested  in  the  mean  time  to  lay  before 
rou  in  writing  the  points  agreed  to  be  presented  and  the  reasons  which 
odiiced  the  gentlemen  present  to  ask  some  action  upon  them. 

This  county  is  almost  entirely  surrounded  by  the  waters  of  the  Al- 
jemarle  Sound  and  the  Roanoke  and  Chowan  Rivers,  all  of  which  are 
lavigable  to  the  largest  of  the  enemy’s  steamers,  while  the  Caskie  River 
uid  Salmon  Creek,  running  into  the  very  heart  of  the  county,  are  navi- 
rable  to  his  steamers  of  highest  draught.  Upon  these  water-courses  lie 
lie  main  body  of  the  excellent  farming  lands  of  the  county,  and  several 
honsarid  slaves  are  upon  these  lands.  The  gunboats  of  the  enemy  are 
raversing  these  waters  almost  daily.  Occasionally  the  enemy  hind  a. 
ew  troops  at  unexpected  iioints,  but  so  far  have  committed  veiy  little 
lepredation.  The  military  post  at  Plymouth  is  upon  the  very  border 
)f  the  county  and  is  accessible  by  the  water-courses  above  named, 
ihere  is  not  a Confederate  soldier  here,  and  not  the  least  show  of  pro-

Hon.  Secretary  of  War  : 

Sir  : When  I was  assigned  to  the  command  of  this  district  by  th 
direction  of  General  Lee  I assumed  the  general  control  of  the  con 
scription  or  recruiting  business  in  the  State.  So,  after  doing  so, 
deemed  it  advisable  to  issue  the  inclosed  order,  in  connection  with  th 
order  and  proclamation  of  Governor  Vance.  The  good  effect  of  tha 
order  has  been  very  perceptible.  Your  telegram*  to  Major  Mallett  c 
yesterday’s  date  will  set  aside  this  order  and  cause  great  complaiul 
. i respecfully  suggest  that  men  be  not  forced  into  regiments,  but  b 
allowed  the  choice  assured  in  my  order.  Major  Mallett  only  using  sue. 
influence  as  he  can  to  direct  their  choice.  Should  a sudden  emergenc. 
require  the  use  of  400  or  500  men  in  the  vicinity  of  Bichmond  it  won!' 
be  better,  in  my  judgment,  to  order  the  camp  guard  there  for  a week  o 
so  than  to  compel  conscripts  to  go  to  those  regiments. 

I am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant,

Executive  Department  of  North  Carolina, 

September  18,  1862. 

Whereas  information  has  reached  me  that  certain  persons,  unmindful 
f the  calls  of  patriotism  and  forgetful  of  the  duties  of  good  citizens,  are 
sing  their  influence  to  prevent  obedience  to  the  law  of  Congiess  known 
s the  conscription  law,  and  that  others  are  attemiiting  to  organize  an 
pen  resistance  to  its  execution  ; and  whereas  such  conduct  being  not 
nly  in  direct  violation  of  law,  but  also  detrimental  in  the  highest  degree 
3 the  cause  of  our  country,  it  becomes  my  sacred  duty  to  prevent  and 
Bpress  the  same  by  all  the  means  in  my  power : 

Now,  therefore,  I,  Zebulon  B.  Vance,  Governor  of  North  Carolina,  do 
}sue  this  my  proclamation  warning  all  such  persons  to  desist  from  such 
inpatriotic  and  criminal  conduct,  earnestly  hoping  that  allAvhoare  dis- 
’•cliued  to  defend  their  homes  themselves,  either  by  reason  of  age,  in- 
rmity,  or  cowardice,  will  cease  to  dissuade  those  who  are  willing,  and  no- 
tying  positively  all  i)ersons  contemplating  an  armed  resistance  to  the 
il‘  there  really  be  any"  such  misguided  and  evil  disposed  persons  in

His  Excellency  President  Davis: 

Dear  Sir  : Pardon  me  for  addressing  you  in  regard  to  a matter  tli; 
should  ordinarily  come  before  the  Quartermaster-General,  but  its  u 
portance  justifies  me  in  bringing  the  matter  directly  to  your  notice. 

Large  quantities  of  harness  are  made  in  this  State  by  contract  wi 
the  Confederate  Government  agents.  The  prices  paid  being  more  rein 
nerative,  almost  two-thirds  of  our  leather  is  made  into  harness  inste. 
of  shoes.  As  shoes  are  now  our  greatest  need  I respectfully  sugge 
that  the  Quartermaster-General  cease  to  contract  for  leather  liaine 
and  allow  the  whole  product  of  our  tanneries  to  go  into  the  manutactii 
of  shoes.  Harness  sufficiently  strong  for  all  reasonable  inirposes  c: 
be  made  of  heavy  cotton  goods.  Much  of  it  is  in  use  in  this  >Stm  , * 
is  found  to  answer  every  end.  So  far  as  my  observation  goes  it  v 
enable  us  to  double  the  amount  of  shoes  produced. 

I need  not  remind  you  of  the  importance  of  this  item  for  tlic  am 
nor  of  the  great  difficulty  we  are  realizing  in  getting  a supply.  ^ 
Hoping  you  may  think  favorably  of  the  suggestion,  I remain, 
respectfully,  your  obedient  servant,  ^ VANCd-

most  cheerfully  send  three  regiments  and  a corresponding  force  of  ar- 
tillery to  the  vicinity  of  Leech ville  but  for  two  considerations : First,  I 
have  not  got  them  to  spare ; secondly,  with  the  power  of  the  enemy

The  force  I sent  last  week  to  Plymouth  I hope  is  now  on  the  borders  of 
Beaufort  and  Washington  Counties,  and  may  bring  out  some  supplies. 
You  will  readily  perceive  I cannot  handle  my  small  force  as  I would 
wish,  because  if  I were  to  withdraw  them  from  any  point  to  operate  on 
another  for  any  length  of  time  it  would  be  but  to  expose  that  point 
from  which  they  were  withdrawn.  If  I take  the  troops  from  Kinston 
to  operate  toward  Beaufort  County  it  exposes  Goldsborough  and  Wil- 
mington. If  I send  them  from  here  it  leaves  25,000  in  front  of  me  with 
only  a march  of  40  miles  from  Zuni.  I am  doing  all  I can  to  draw  sup- 
plies from  the  eastern  parts  of  the  State,  and  even  in  this  much  depends 
on  the  cheerful  co-operation  of  the  people. 

Yours,  very  truly, 

S.  G.  FEENCH,

Engineer  Bureau,  October  30, 1862. 
Col.  Walter  Gwynn,  Goldsborough,  W.  C.  : 


Colonel:  I have  to  acknowledge  the  receipt  of  your  letters  of  the 
22d  and  24th  instant.  In  accordance  with  your  wish  your  son  has  been 
applied  for,  and  as  soon  as  the  detail  is  granted  he  will  be  ordered  to 
report  to  you  in  Tarborough  for  duty. 

I have  just  learned  from  a letter  of  General  S.  G.  French  to  General 
G.  W.  Smith  that  100  negroes  are  ordered  to  assemble  at  Hamilton. 
You  will  therefore  take  immediate  steps  to  receive  and  set  them  to 
work. 

In  your  letter  of  the  24th,  alluding  to  the  defenses  of  Neuse  Eiver,  you 
write  the  works  embrace  the  river  batteries  and  will  require  10,000  men 
for  their  defense.  You  further  estimate  that  an  armament  of  thirty-four 
guns  in  all  will  be  necessary.  These  are  works  of  vastly  greater  mag 
uitude  than  I have  ever  contemplated  or  can  approve.  In  my  letter  of 
instructions  of  the  9th  instant  I particularly  called  your  attention  to 
the  fact  that  the  garrisons  of  such  forts  as  you  might  construct  would  be 
necessarily  small.  Instead,  therefore,  of  building  forts  defending  the 
river,  in  turn  to  be  defended  by  covering  works,  I decidedly  prefer,  as 
a general  thesis,  and  without  special  and  controlling  circumstances,  one 
work  commanding  the  river  with  strong  land  as  well  as  water  fronts, 
defiled,  if  necessary,  to  protect  it  from  attacks  on  commanding  ground. 
1 most  earnestly  therefore  call  your  special  attention  to  prompt  studies 
and  actions  to  carry  out  these  views.  In  my  judgment,  with  rare  excep 
tions,  a permanent  garrison  for  each  position  of  one  regiment,  is  the 
utmost  that  can  be  reasonably  hoped  for. 

Very  respectfully. 


J.  F.  GILMEE, 

Colonel  and  Ch  ief  of  Engineer  Bureau.

Subsistence  Department,  0.  S.  A., 

Richmond^  November  2, 18G2. 

His  Excellency  Gov.  Zebulon  B.  Yance,  Raleigh^  N,  G.: 

Sir  : It  is  very  desirable  to  exhaust  the  hogs,  beeves,  pease,  beans, 
and  potatoes  of  that  part  of  North  Carolina  which  lies  within  the  lines 
of  the  enemy  or  accessible  to  them.  The  President  called  my  attention 
to  information  derived  from  you  on  the  subject,  and  the  representations 
made  in  response  to  inquiries  have  been  of  a discouraging  nature.  I 
venture  to  apply  to  you  for  action  thereon.  It  is  obvious  that  those 
charged  with  such  an  undertaking  should  be  reliable  business  men, 
whose  integrity  and  energy  should  be  personally  known  to  those  among 
whom  they  are  to  operate.  Neither  myself  nor  anj^  one  in  my  office  bas 
such  knowledge  of  the  country  or  the  people  of  lower  North  Carolina 
as  to  enable  me  to  make  the  proper  selections  and  the  necessary 
arrangements  to  the  above  end.  That  being  the  case  I write  to  ask  if 
you  will  allow  your  agency  to  be  used  in  this  matter  by  having  tbe 
whole  devolve  upon  you,  except  so  far  as  existing  arrangements  go. 
They  run  thus  far : Mr.  Jacob  Parker  has  a contract  for  packing  hogs 
at  Warrenton,  and  has  the  following  counties  allotted  to  him  for  pur- 
chase, viz:  Pranklin,  Warren,  Nash,  and  Halifax.  In  addition,  Maj.  W. 
H.  Smith  has  made  certain  arrangements  with  Mr.  H.  Hayes,  of  Har- 
rellsville,  which  he  will  detail  to  you.  Tlie  balance  of  the  district 
spoken  of  it  is  proposed  to  put  under  your  charge,  with  these  remarks: 

1st.  That  as  this  Bureau  has  already  more  captains  and  majors  than 
it  ought  to  have  it  is  not  expedient  to  appoint  more,  except  in  case  ol 
absolute  necessity,  but  to  operate  by  agents,  wiiose  agencies  can  cease 
when  their  business  with  tbe  Department  closes. 

2d.  That  the  points  of  delivery  of  the  hogs  should  be  fixed  with  ret 


Chap.  XXX.] 


COKKESPONDENCE,  ETC. CONFEDERATE. 


765 


ereuce  to  the  packing-houses,  both  in  and  out  of  the  State  of  North 
Carolina,  so  that  such  as  can  go  conveniently  to  the  packeries,  which 
Major  Smith  has  established  or  will  establish,  may  do  so,  and  such  as 
are  more  convenient  to  Petersburg  can  go  to  that  point,  whence  they 
can  be  brought  to  this  place. 

3d.  That  it  may  be  necessary  to  procure  both  bags  and  transportation 
to  get  out  the  pease  and  potatoes  and  any  bacon  that  may  be  attainable. 
As  to  the  transportation,  Mr.  Hayes,  in  a letter  to  Major  Puffin,  says 
that  a few  teams  and  wagons  can  be  bought  in  his  region.  If  they  can 
be  bought  at  prices  satisfactory  to  yourself  you  will  be  authorized  to 
buy  them,  and  when  they  are  done  with  they  can  be  disposed  of  in 
some  satisfactory  manner.  As  to  the  bags,  it  would  be  very  desirable  to 
secure  the  services  of  some  of  the  factories  of  North  Carolina  in  order 
to  get  them,  and  as  they  have  not  been  called  on  up  to  this  time  it  is 
to  be  hoped  that  they  will  now  be  able  to  serve  the  needs  of  this  Bureau. 
One  of  the  greatest  difficulties  now  is  to  get  bags,  and  there  are  not 
half  enough.  Can  you  not  get  them  ? Please  try. 

I have  been  induced  to  ask  you  to  undertake  the  above  service  in  con- 
sequence of  your  communication  to  the  President,  and  my  notice  of  your 
address  to  the  people  of  your  State,  indicating  a readiness  to  help  the 
cause  in  general. 

I have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

L.  B.  NOPTHPOP.

Col.  Walter  Gwynn, 

In  eharfje  of  Defenses  in  Eastern  North  Carolina : 

Colonel  : I have  to  acknowledge  the  receipt  of  your  letter  of  the 
29th  instant  relating  to  the  defenses,  disbursements,  &c.,  in  Eastern 
North  Carolina.  A requisition  for  $30,000  in  favor  of  Lieut.  W.  G. 
Bender  has  been  made. 

I am  glad  to  hear  that  so  satisfactory  a iiosition  for  the  defense  of  the 
Koanoke  Piver  has  been  found  at  PainbowBend.  The  line  of  infantry 
to  cover  miles  to  the  pond,  causing  the  enemy  to  make  a detour  of  15 
miles,  seems  a good  suggestion.  It  is  not  possible  at  present  to  furnish 
all  the  armament  required,  still  platforms  and  i^ositions  should  be  pre- 
pared for  formidable  river  batteries  (a  part  of  these  platforms  should  be 
prepared  for  siege  carriages).  You  will  most  probably  have  to  exercise 
your  ingenuity  in  mounting  the  guns,  as  the  supplj^  of  guns  is  very 
limited.  There  are  only  two  i)ile-drivers  in  this  vicinity,  both  steam, 
with  2,000-pound  hammers,  and  in  constant  usej  they  are,  moreover, 
mounted  on  boats.  They  should  be  sought  for  in  the  section  where  you 
are,  and  if  they  cannot  be  found  seek  to  have  them  made  where  you 
are;  and  failing  in  that,  if  you  will  send  on  drawings  of  the  hammers, 
i^c.,  required,  I will  order  them  to  be  executed  at  the  Tredegar  Works. 
While  our  founderies  and  machine-shops  are  so  overtasked,  and  the 
price  of  labor  and  iron  so  high,  I do  not  think  screw-piles  at  all  advisa- 
ble. Before  approving  the  suggestion  of  repairing  the  steamboat  Cora, 
it  is  necessary  for  the  Bureau  to  have  an  approximate  estimate  of  the 
cost.  Communicate  with  Muj.  Gen.  S.  G.  French  respecting  provisions 
and  transportation  and  request  his  co-operation.  Capt.  C.  H.  Dimmock, 
engineer  in  charge  at  Petersburg,  will  be  requested  without  delay  to 
forward  you  the  required  amount  of  intrenching  tools.  Your  call  for 
stationery  will  be  promptly  attended  to.

Navy  Department,  C.  S.  A., 

Richmond^  November  4, 1862. 

His  Excellency  Zebulon  B.  Vance, 

Governor  of  North  Carolina  : 

Sir  : Commander  Cooke,  sent  by  me  to  North  Carolina  to  obtain  iron 
for  plating  the  gunboats  being  built  in  and  for  the  defense  of  the  State, 
has  returned  without  having  accomplished  this  object.  He  reports  that 
you  have  the  control  of  a quantity  of  railroad  iron,  and  I therefore  ad- 
dress myself  to  you  upon  the  subject. 

To  enable  the  boats  to  resist  the  guns  of  the  enemy  their  armor  must 
be  at  least  4 inches  thick,  placed  at  an  angle  of  at  least  36^.  This  armor, 
from  the  limited  power  of  our  mills,  we  are  compelled  to  roll  into  plates 
2 by  7 inches  and  10  feet  long,  and  to  put  them  on  the  vessels  in  two 
courses. 

If  you  wall  let  the  Department  have  the  rails,  and  facilitate  its  trans- 
portation to  Bichmond,  they  will  be  immediately  rolled  into  plates  for 
the  vessels  in  question  and  for  such  other  defenses  as  we  may  build  in 
the  waters  of  your  State. 

Commander  Cooke  will  remove  the  iron  if  you  consent  to  its  transfer, 
and  will  arrange  the  compensation  according  to  his  instructions. 

Please  telegraph  your  reply. 

I am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

^ ' S.  E.  MALLOEY,

rop,  Commissary-General,  to  collect  with  my  own  agents  all  the  supplies

there  at  work.  Two  of  the  richest  counties  in  the  State  are  Gates  and
